tasks.title: A project level, with the world placed in it
tasks.detail: The project loads /Engine/Maps/Entry -- an empty engine map -- and a subsystem spawns the planet, the sun, the atmosphere and the ship into it. So the world exists only while code is running, and there is nothing to open, look at or select. A real map, with the things that are not generated placed as actors, and the generated ones attached to something a person can find.
tasks.acceptance: The project opens on its own map, the world's fixed actors are visible and selectable in the editor, and the scripted flight runs from it unchanged.

notes.text: The project opens on /Game/Maps/Ledger, built by tools/make_level.py and holding exactly three actors: Sun, SkyLight, WorldPostProcess. Listed and kept as evidence in docs/comparisons/project-level/level-actors.txt. The level says WHAT EXISTS and the code says HOW IT BEHAVES: ULedgerWorldBuilder finds a placed actor and configures it, falling back to spawning so a world with no level still comes up lit. That fallback matters -- before this, the engine's Entry map contributed a PlayerStart and the code spawned a second one. Two consecutive flights on the new map are BYTE-IDENTICAL, worst channel difference 0, via compare_captures.py --between. What I could NOT establish: the captures differ from the previous references by a structural residual of 25 to 32. That is not the map's doing -- a control run on the old engine map differs from the same references by the same amounts (town 28.97 either way), and the lighting configuration is provably identical on both, logged at world build: sun rotation R(P=-50.11,Y=-147.53), intensity 11, atmosphere sun on, sky 3.2 with real-time capture, exposure 0.03-8.0 bias 0.10. So the references were already stale against the current build before this task, from a commit I did not identify, and I did not pretend to. Re-baselined against a run that is now reproducible.

Finished what ADR-0006's third tier asked for: the level now holds the planet, the atmosphere and the settlement as well as the sun, sky light and post-process -- six actors, read back from disk. The builder finds and configures them before they begin play, and a body switch rebuilds the same planet in place rather than destroying and respawning three actors. tools/make_level.py was never idempotent despite saying so: it had only run once, with no map present. Re-run, does_asset_exist answered False for the map so the delete never happened, new_level refused, the save was refused, and the report said PASS from the list of actors it had asked for. It now opens an existing map and replaces only the actors it owns, and the verdict comes from loading the saved file again. docs/comparisons/proper-world/

evidence.caption: The placed world, lit: baked buildings and pad, snowfields and sea, under a sun 44.6 degrees up -- after per-pixel atmosphere transmittance
The level read back from disk: six actors, each once

tasks.title: Materials as saved assets, generated once
tasks.detail: Every material is RF_Transient and built as a node graph on each launch inside an editor-only block, which is why LedgerSurfaceCooked.cpp returns null for all of them and a packaged build has no look at all. The graphs stay in C++ and stay the source of truth -- that is what makes them diffable and is worth keeping. A commandlet runs them once and saves the result, and the game loads assets. The same arrangement the surface textures already use.
tasks.acceptance: Every material in the game is a saved asset; a build with the editor stripped renders the terrain, water and underwater passes correctly; and regenerating produces no diff unless the C++ changed.

notes.text: Three materials -- M_Terrain, M_Water, M_Underwater -- are now saved assets in /Game/Materials, baked by 'UnrealEditor.exe <project> -game -bakematerials'. Report kept at docs/comparisons/project-level/bake-materials.txt. The graph builders stay in C++ and stay the source of truth, which is the part worth keeping: a material that is code diffs, reviews and merges, and one that is a binary asset does none of that. The bake runs them once into real packages; CreateTerrainMaterial and friends now LOAD the asset. EVIDENCE, three parts. (1) The flight logs 'materials: terrain M_Terrain, water M_Water' where it used to log the transient names Material_1 and Material_0, so it is loading assets rather than building graphs. (2) Captures against the reference: residuals 0.00 to 1.57 against a 2.5 limit, so a baked asset renders the same as the graph it came from. (3) Two consecutive bakes are BYTE-IDENTICAL, 3 of 3, which is the 'regenerating produces no diff' half of the gate. Fallbacks are deliberate and loud: a fresh clone with no baked assets still runs because the editor builds in memory and warns that it did, and '-livematerials' skips the asset entirely for working on a graph. NOT DONE and named rather than hidden: CreateFlatMaterial is not baked, because it takes a colour and a roughness and the settlement wants a different pair per building -- that is a material instance per colour, which belongs to the instancing task. So a packaged build still has no material on buildings or the ship hull. That is now a small specific hole instead of the entire look of the game.

[2026-09-09] CORRECTION to the evidence above. The claim that two consecutive bakes were byte-identical, 3 of 3, was wrong. The second bake had silently failed to write -- SavePackage will not overwrite an existing file and SAVE_NoError was hiding the failure -- so the comparison was of each file against itself. That is the same self-confirming measurement the turntable's camera check made, and I made it again the same day. Found while wiring T419's one-command regeneration, which ran the bake a second time and reported 'could not write the package' for all three. The bake now deletes the previous file first and reports the real save result. What is actually true: Unreal packages embed GUIDs and are NOT byte-reproducible. Of 73 generated assets, exactly one is stable across regenerations -- Maps/Ledger.umap, which is the only one tracked in version control, so nothing churns. The materials and textures are derived and gitignored, and their equivalence is established by their settings read back off the assets and by the render matching the reference, not by their bytes.

The bake had not been re-run since M_Star (T077) and M_Clouds (T094) were added, so both were built in memory on every launch. Re-run, and extended: MPC_LedgerWind, the wind collection T093's vegetation was meant to read and which had never existed, and M_Foliage, which leans the canopies with it. M_Foliage then failed to compile silently into the default material -- a collection node binds by parameter GUID and the builder set only the name. One helper sets both, for the cloud material too, and the collection's parameters get deterministic ids so a re-bake does not orphan the materials baked against it. 8 of 8, zero materials built in memory at runtime.

tasks.title: Asset generation as an editor commandlet
tasks.detail: The mechanism the generators of ADR-0005 plug into: a generator is a function from parameters to geometry, and this is what runs it offline, names the package, saves it, and records what produced it. One command regenerates everything from source, so a change to a generator is a rebuild rather than an afternoon of clicking.
tasks.acceptance: One command regenerates every generated asset from its definition; a second run leaves the version-controlled ones byte-identical and the derived ones equivalent by settings and render; and every generated asset records the generator that made it.

notes.text: tools/generate_assets.py regenerates every generated asset in the project from its definition, in one command: the level, the 69 imported surface textures, and the three baked materials. 'python tools/generate_assets.py' takes about a minute; --only <step> runs one; --list says what each step makes and why. Index kept at docs/comparisons/project-level/generated-assets.json. EVIDENCE: a full run reports 'level ok -- the map exists, surfaces ok -- 69 textures imported, materials ok -- VERDICT: PASS', and a second full run does the same rather than failing on the first. Two bugs it found, both the same shape -- a generator that worked exactly once. make_level.py called new_level, which refuses to overwrite, so every run after the first failed to validate the destination. The material bake called SavePackage, which will not overwrite an existing file, and SAVE_NoError was swallowing the failure -- which is also how T418's byte-identical evidence came to be wrong, since the unwritten files compared equal to themselves. Both now delete first. Steps are judged BY THEIR ARTIFACT, not by exit code: both Unreal entry points return non-zero on a successful run -- the import commandlet validates an unused global block and fails on it, and the editor's shutdown does not reliably return zero -- so a generator that trusts exit codes either fails on success or succeeds on failure. Provenance: each baked material carries Ledger.Generator, Ledger.Source and Ledger.Command as Unreal metadata, so it travels with the asset and shows in the details panel. No timestamp, deliberately: an asset that embeds when it was made can never be compared against a re-run.

tasks.title: Static mesh output with Nanite, LODs and collision
tasks.detail: What the commandlet actually emits. Nanite enabled where it belongs, automatic LOD chains, simplified collision matching the silhouette, and distance-field generation. None of this is available to a procedural mesh and all of it is free once the output is a static mesh, which is the whole argument of ADR-0006 in one task.
tasks.acceptance: A generated hull comes out as a static mesh with Nanite on, a full LOD chain, collision matching its silhouette and a mesh distance field, with no manual step.

notes.text: The ship hull is now a static mesh asset at /Game/Meshes/SM_ShipHull, baked by 'UnrealEditor.exe <project> -game -bakemeshes' and by tools/generate_assets.py as a step. LedgerMesh::Bake takes the same FLedgerMeshBuilder arrays the runtime uses and hands them to Unreal's own static mesh build, so the shape is described once and has two destinations. EVIDENCE, read back from a FRESH PROCESS rather than from the process that set it -- 'I set the flag' and 'the asset has it' are different claims: tools/verify_meshes.py opens the saved asset and reports '144 tris, nanite on, lods 1, collision yes, dist field yes, by LedgerMesh::Bake'. VERDICT PASS. Kept at docs/comparisons/project-level/verify-meshes.txt. Both things this unlocks were previously impossible: Nanite cannot be enabled on a procedural mesh component at all, and the mesh distance field is what Lumen's software tracing needs -- its absence across the whole project is why Lumen had to be forced onto hardware ray tracing in the first place. On 'a full LOD chain': the asset has one source model, and that is the right answer for a Nanite mesh rather than a shortfall. Nanite does LOD per cluster, so a hand-built chain would be both redundant and, on 144 triangles, meaningless. Said plainly rather than counted as met. NOT DONE: only the hull is baked. The settlement's buildings and trees are still runtime procedural meshes, because they want a material instance per colour and that is the instancing task.

[2026-09-09] CORRECTION. This task reported 'nanite on' for SM_ShipHull, read back from the saved asset -- which was true of the asset and false of the running game. Both the editor and the packaged build were on Shader Model 5, and Nanite requires SM6, so Nanite was configured and not running. Found by packaging: a packaged build states its feature level in the first hundred lines of its log, and the editor had been saying the same thing for two days. DefaultGraphicsRHI is DX12 with PCD3D_SM6 now, and the editor reports 'Using Highest Feature Level of D3D12: SM6' with raytracing=1. The asset-level verification in this task was correct as far as it went; it just did not go as far as asking whether the feature was available at all.

tasks.title: Instanced rendering for repeated and scattered assets
tasks.detail: Three hundred and forty-two trees are three hundred and forty-two procedural mesh components today, each with its own draw and its own generation cost on the game thread. Once assets are static meshes they instance, and a forest becomes one draw. The scatter framework in M02 decides where they go; this decides what they are placed as.
tasks.acceptance: A settlement's trees and props render as instanced draws, the draw count is independent of the instance count, and the measured game-thread cost of placing them falls against the current build.

notes.text: Trees are now instances of a baked static mesh: two UHierarchicalInstancedStaticMeshComponents, 174 and 168 instances, replacing a single merged procedural mesh of 43,092 runtime-generated vertices. MEASURED, steady state, two consecutive runs: settlement build 3.0 and 3.2 ms against a 5.4 ms baseline, of which loading both tree meshes is 1.2-1.4 ms and placing all 342 instances is 0.0 ms. Draw count is independent of instance count by construction -- two components whether there are 342 trees or 3,420. Hierarchical rather than plain instanced, so a group of trees behind a hill is culled as a cluster; the merged mesh was one primitive, drawn whole or not at all. First readings were 38.9 ms and then 8.8 ms and I nearly recorded the task as a regression on them; both were first-load-after-bake, where the asset's derived data is built on demand. THREE WRONG GUESSES before the trees rendered correctly, each looking like the last: they came back black, and I blamed a missing material assignment, then an sRGB decode on the vertex colours, then Nanite. The actual causes were two. A material without bUsedWithInstancedStaticMeshes is silently swapped for the default on an instanced component, and BuildFromMeshDescriptions creates no material slots at all -- so SetMaterial(0, ...) succeeded, reported the material back, and drew nothing. The component was asked what it had and answered '0 material slots'. Vertex colours were then dropped entirely in favour of a material slot each for trunk and canopy, which is how this is normally done and depends on none of it. A correction to the task's own text: it claimed 342 trees were 342 procedural mesh components. They were one.

tasks.title: Asset layout, naming and ownership in the content tree
tasks.detail: Where generated assets live, what they are called, and how a stale one is found. Boring, and the alternative is a content directory nobody can navigate in two years and a set of orphans nobody dares delete.
tasks.acceptance: Every asset's package path is derived from its definition rather than typed, and a generated asset with no definition behind it is reported by a validator naming the file.

notes.text: Every asset's package path is derived from its definition -- /Game/Materials, /Game/Meshes, /Game/Surfaces and /Game/Maps, each root owned by one generator -- and tools/verify_assets.py walks the whole content tree and fails on anything without a Ledger.Generator tag or outside a known root. Evidence: 76 assets checked, VERDICT PASS, kept at docs/comparisons/project-level/verify-assets.txt. Materials and meshes tag themselves as they are baked. The 69 textures are imported by Unreal's own commandlet, which knows nothing about this project, so tools/tag_surfaces.py writes their source and licence on afterwards FROM THE MANIFEST rather than from a second copy of the same facts. The validator caught itself first: its opening version reported '/Game/Maps 0' and passed, having never looked at the level, because get_assets_by_path does not return World assets. A validator that quietly checks nothing is worse than none, because it is believed. ONE HONEST EXCEPTION, written down rather than waved through: the level cannot record its generator in the asset. Package metadata set before a map save is dropped and metadata set afterwards is not persisted by save_asset -- both were tried, and an actor tag on the world settings did not take either. Its provenance is kept beside it in build/make-level.txt and the validator checks that line, so the level is held to the rule rather than exempted from it.

tasks.title: Terrain component type, measured rather than assumed
tasks.detail: After this milestone the terrain is the only runtime-generated geometry left, and it owns the game-thread cost failing the frame budget: 20 to 31 ms through every low-altitude phase against 16.7, with the GPU at 5 to 9. UProceduralMeshComponent was the prototype's choice and has never been compared against anything. Measure it against the alternatives on generation, upload and draw cost before deciding to keep it.
tasks.acceptance: A written comparison of at least two component types over the same flight, with generation, upload and draw cost measured for each, and a decision recorded with its numbers.

notes.text: Measured. UProceduralMeshComponent kept: over the same flight it uploads 121,918 patches to the static backend's 8,212, and finishes with 6 holes against 2,584. The static run's p99 is lower (29.0 vs 33.1 ms) only because it is drawing a starved world -- compare_captures puts the worst channel difference between the two runs at 199 against a limit of 16.

The comparison also produced the answer to a question nobody had asked: the terrain tick's cost was never the upload. Breaking ALedgerPlanet::Tick into phases put the LOD tree walk at 24 ms and upload at 7. UpdateTree was taking a full fractal elevation sample per visited node per frame for a value that never changes; caching it on the node took the ridge sweep from 18.8 ms of terrain to 11.2 and the flight p99 from 43.3 to 35.1.
docs/comparisons/terrain-component.md, five runs kept under docs/comparisons/terrain-component/

evidence.caption: The static backend starved: 2,584 holes, town and trees on open water
The written comparison, with both runs' raw reports

tasks.title: Shader compilation and PSO caching
tasks.detail: Building material graphs at runtime means compiling shaders at runtime, which is a stall the moment anything new comes into view. Once materials are assets their shaders cook, and the pipeline state objects need collecting so that first sight of a surface is not a hitch.
tasks.acceptance: A packaged build shows no compilation stall on first sight of any material, and a first run's frame-time trace matches a second run's within the stated tolerance.

notes.text: PSO precaching is on and takes effect; the two D3D12 driver disk caches cannot be enabled from project config -- read-only CVars read before it is applied, still logging r.D3D12.PSO.DiskCache=0 under both RendererSettings and SystemSettings. 28 PSOPrecacheState:Missed in cold AND warm runs, identical, so precaching is not covering them. 973 frames over the stall threshold, worst 116.5 ms. First run vs second: overall 17.2 then 17.8 ms (noise), but the town phase 17.0 then 20.0 -- 18% apart with nothing changed, so the run-to-run tolerance is not demonstrable yet. Needs ConsoleVariables.ini or a command-line route for the read-only CVars, and a stall attribution pass to find what the 973 actually are. Reports in docs/comparisons/packaged/.

The two D3D12 driver disk caches are unreachable, not merely unset. Tried RendererSettings, SystemSettings, [ConsoleVariables] (the earliest project-owned section, applied in PreInit) and -dpcvars on the command line; all four give 'CVar deferred - dummy variable created' followed by 'Not using pipeline state disk cache per r.D3D12.PSO.DiskCache=0'. The RHI reads the value in the pass that registers it. The lines are out of DefaultEngine.ini rather than sitting there looking like a setting somebody chose. They were also the wrong lever: they are the driver's copy, not the engine's, and the engine's answer is a recorded .upipelinecache shipped with the build.

Run-to-run half of the acceptance now measurable, because the fixture is reproducible: cold and warm packaged runs under -useFixedTimeStep agree to within 2% on every phase mean (overall 16.4 vs 16.6 ms) and 12% on p99. The previous attempt had the town phase 18% apart with nothing changed; that was the free-running fixture. Still failing: 34 PSOPrecacheState:Missed, IDENTICAL cold and warm, so precaching is not covering them and nothing carries them between runs. Also: the 22 stalls in the cold run land on the capture timestamps -- taking a screenshot stalls its own frame and the recorder counts it, so stall attribution has to exclude capture frames first. Evidence in docs/comparisons/packaged/pso/.
unblocked

Stall attribution done. The recorder now drops frames while a screenshot is outstanding -- a fixed two-frame skip was tried first and removed only nine of twenty-two, because the request is served whenever the render thread gets to it, and picking a larger number until the list looked clean would have been picking the answer. Count 22 -> 12. What is left lands on t=124 (coast teleport), t=132 (underwater teleport) and t=140 (start of the climb): the frames where the camera moves somewhere new or the tree collapses. None coincides with a precache miss. So the 34 misses are 30 in the warm-up window and 4 in flight, and the flight's stalls are the terrain's cache-copy problem rather than shader compilation. Remaining work for the acceptance is a recorded .upipelinecache to take the 34 to zero.

Recording pipeline built end to end: stable keys from the cook, a clean flight exit so the recording flushes, 38 recorded PSOs -> 82 stable -> a 38-PSO binary cache at Content/PipelineCaches/Windows/Ledger_PCD3D_SM6.stable.upipelinecache, which is the exact path and name FPipelineFileCacheManager constructs. The runtime never opens it -- no FShaderPipelineCache lines in the log at all -- and the miss count is unchanged at 34. STOPPED DELIBERATELY: PSOPrecacheState:Missed is reported by the PSO precaching system and the bundled cache is a different mechanism, so a working cache might not move that counter. Four package-and-fly cycles went into a number that may not be connected to the change. Prerequisite for finishing is a meter that measures the bundled cache; the other candidate is that nothing calls OpenPipelineFileCache.

MET, both halves. Cause of the last wall: BuildCookRun DELETES loose non-asset files from Content/ during the cook, so the cache built into Content/PipelineCaches/Windows was gone by staging -- the log said 'Could not open FPipelineCacheFile' naming the exact path, under a string I had not grepped for. tools/pipeline_cache.py builds from the committed .spc and installs into the staged build after packaging. PSOPrecacheState:Missed 34 -> 0, cache opened with 38 entries, precompile finished with no jobs remaining. Second half: tolerance stated for the first time at 10% on phase means; eight of eleven phases agree to 0.0% between two cold runs, worst 6.3% on underwater, the one phase whose settle wait times out. Correction: I had claimed the miss counter might be the wrong meter for a bundled cache. It was the right meter.
docs/comparisons/packaged/pso/README.md; reproduce with tools/pipeline_cache.py

tasks.title: Package the technical slice and run it without the editor
tasks.detail: The narrow version of what M12 does properly later: prove it packages and runs at all. Today it cannot, and every milestone spent adding content on top of a build that has never shipped once is a milestone spent finding out later.
tasks.acceptance: A packaged Windows build launches with no editor present, flies the scripted flight, and writes its captures and frame-time report.

notes.text: A packaged Windows build launches with no editor present, flies the whole scripted flight, and writes its eight captures and its frame-time report. build/package/Windows/Ledger.exe, 901 MB, packaged by RunUAT BuildCookRun. Evidence kept in docs/comparisons/packaged/. Two real failures found, which is what packaging was for. FIRST: nothing was cooked. Generated assets are loaded by path string at runtime, so no asset in the project references them and the cooker never saw them -- the first packaged build came up reporting 'SkipPackage: /Game/Materials/M_Terrain, the package to load does not exist on disk or in the loader' for every material and mesh, and rendered a planet with no material. Fixed by naming the directories in DirectoriesToAlwaysCook. SECOND: the flat material could not be baked at all, because it took its colour as a constant and the settlement wants a different one per building -- so buildings, trees and the hull rendered as black cut-outs on correctly textured ground. Its colour and roughness are parameters now, one baked asset with a dynamic instance per user, and LedgerSurfaceCooked.cpp is empty of fallbacks for the first time. NOT MET, and it belongs to the milestone gate rather than this task: the packaged captures do not match the editor's within tolerance, worst channel 193. And the reason is worth more than the mismatch -- BOTH builds report 'Using Highest Feature Level of D3D12: SM5' and raytracing=0. Nanite and Lumen hardware ray tracing both require SM6, so neither has been running since I enabled them, in either build. Every claim I have made about Lumen HWRT and about Nanite being on the hull needs re-checking against that.

tasks.title: Write down the asset creation strategy
tasks.detail: What is baked, what is streamed, what is placed, and how a new kind of thing gets added to each. ADR-0006 records the decision; this is the document somebody follows. It exists because the current architecture was never chosen -- it is what the prototype happened to do -- and the way that happens again is by leaving the choice implicit.
tasks.acceptance: A document that answers, for any new asset type, which tier it belongs in and what producing one involves, with a worked example for each of the three tiers.

notes.text: docs/asset-strategy.md. Answers, for any new asset type, which of the three tiers it belongs in and what producing one involves, with a worked example for each: a new prop and a new material for baked, a new placed actor for placed, and for streamed the honest answer that there is no example and the test is 'write down how big the file would be'. It also carries the five traps this milestone actually hit, each of which cost an afternoon and none of which is guessable: vertex colours do not survive the trip from procedural mesh to baked-and-instanced; a material without bUsedWithInstancedStaticMeshes is silently swapped for the default; BuildFromMeshDescriptions creates no material slots so SetMaterial succeeds and draws nothing; generators must be idempotent because new_level and SavePackage both refuse to overwrite; and a number taken straight after a re-bake measures the first load of freshly built derived data, which is how the settlement read 38.9 ms, then 8.8, then 3.0 with nothing changed. Plus what is and is not in version control, why .uasset files are not byte-reproducible, and a closing section naming the seams that are still open.

tasks.title: Playable proof: the packaged build flies the same flight
tasks.detail: Per ARCH Rule 6 the milestone ends with something that runs: a build with no editor, flying orbit to ground to orbit, producing captures that match the editor build.
tasks.acceptance: Captures from the packaged build match the committed references within the perceptual tolerance, and its frame-time report is no worse than the editor build's.

notes.text: Not met, and the reason is a flaw in the harness rather than in the build. Packaged against the editor's references, on the same SM6 configuration: 4 of 8 captures pass and 4 fail -- town 4.16, coast 8.26, surface 10.13, sweep 14.70, against a 2.50 limit. The four that fail are exactly the phases where the ship is moving fastest and terrain is streaming; town, the slowest, is closest to passing. CAPTURES ARE TRIGGERED ON GAME TIME, so a build with a different frame rate reaches a given timestamp having streamed a different amount of terrain, and the images differ for a reason that has nothing to do with rendering. Two builds with different performance can never match a time-triggered capture. The fix is to trigger on STATE -- altitude reached, distance travelled, patches resident -- which also makes the existing editor-to-editor comparison mean something stronger than it does now. Frame-time half of the gate: packaged overall 17.2 ms against the editor's 17.5, so the packaged build is not worse. Evidence in docs/comparisons/packaged/.

CORRECTED DIAGNOSIS. My first explanation was that captures fired before terrain had streamed, and it was wrong. Captures now wait for PendingBuilds and JobsInFlight to reach zero before firing, and seven of eight settle on the first 0.1 s poll -- the terrain was already idle. The comparison barely moved: coast 8.26 to 7.93, sweep 14.70 to 14.68, town 4.16 to 4.16. THE ACTUAL CAUSE, with evidence: the packaged run logs 926 stalls against the editor's 543, from the same seed and the same start position. The flight model integrates at a fixed 120 Hz step with a capped catch-up -- MaxStepsPerFrame 16, accumulator zeroed when capped -- so a stall DROPS simulated time rather than spiralling, which is deliberate and is what the SurvivesAHitch test protects. A build that stalls more has flown less far by any given timestamp, so a time-triggered capture photographs a different place. Nothing to do with rendering, and nothing a settle can fix. THE FIX is to trigger captures on ship state -- altitude crossed, distance travelled -- so the image is a function of where the camera is rather than of how fast the machine is. That is a rewrite of the harness's scheduling, which is timer-driven throughout, and it is worth doing because it also makes the editor-to-editor comparison mean something stronger. The settle wait is kept: it is correct on its own terms, and it is now labelled as not having been the problem.

THIRD DIAGNOSIS, and this one was tested before it was written. Both previous explanations were about the packaged build. Neither was checked against the obvious control: run the EDITOR build twice and compare it with itself. Seven of eight shots disagree, coast by a mean of 7.67 -- against the 8.26 that had been blamed on the packaged build. The fixture cannot reproduce itself, so no comparison against it meant anything. Cause: the flight is driven by game time, game time advances by however long the last frame took, so position, LOD state and Lumen history are all functions of the frame rate. -useFixedTimeStep -fps=60 takes the worst channel across the set from 128 to 21 and six of eight shots pass outright. Evidence in docs/comparisons/repeatability/.
unblocked

MET. Two causes, both found by testing rather than reasoning. (1) The fixture could not reproduce itself; -useFixedTimeStep -fps=60 pins it. (2) With it pinned, the same four shots still failed -- the four with sky in frame -- because UVolumetricCloudComponent takes its material from its own class default, nothing in the project names that asset, and the cooker never saw it. The packaged log said 'the package to load does not exist' and the build rendered a clear sky. /Engine/EngineSky added to DirectoriesToAlwaysCook. Gate now: eight of eight captures match, worst residual 0.89 against a limit of 2.50. Frame times packaged 16.6 ms mean / 27.6 p99 against the editor's 18.0 / 29.0 over 8,760 frames each -- not worse. Both still fail the 16.7 ms budget, which is the terrain work's problem and not this task's.
docs/comparisons/packaged/README.md

tasks.title: Source a PBR surface library and audit its licences
tasks.detail: Quixel Megascans through Fab, decided 2026-09-08. The first version of this task said the scans are free for Unreal use, which is wrong and was corrected by reading the listings: Megascans *3D assets* have a free tier that is UEFN reference-only, while Megascans *materials* are free outright under the Fab Standard License. Materials are what terrain needs. See docs/asset-licensing.md. Needs an Epic sign-in once, which is manual. Twelve to sixteen ground surfaces spanning the biomes the climate model will produce: sand, gravel, scree, granite, sandstone, grass, moss, snow, mud, clay. Every set records its source and licence in a manifest as it arrives — a project that audits licences later is one that finds out at ship time that it cannot.
tasks.acceptance: A manifest lists every surface set with source and licence, and a validator fails the build on any texture present without an entry.

notes.text: Needs an Epic/Fab sign-in, which is a manual step only the user can do. Everything around it is built: the manifest format, the validator that fails the build on any texture with no recorded source and licence, and its CI job.

Quixel Megascans materials via Fab, free under the Fab Standard License; the licence audit is in docs/asset-licensing.md and was read rather than remembered. Manifest and validator enforce it in CI. The library itself is being populated a set at a time; the first, Rippled Sand, is in and imported.

tasks.title: Texture import pipeline for surface sets
tasks.detail: Pulled forward from M12, because sixteen sets imported by hand is sixteen chances to get a normal map's colour space wrong and one afternoon wondering why the lighting is inside out. Channel packing — roughness, ambient occlusion and height into one texture — compression settings per map type, sRGB flags, mip and streaming policy.
tasks.acceptance: A surface set dropped into the source directory is import-ready with no manual step, and a validator rejects wrong channel layout or colour space with a message naming the file.

notes.text: tools/import_surfaces.py takes a Fab texture-set zip and needs nothing else: it reads the scan's real-world size from the bundled metadata for tiling, keeps albedo and normal, packs AO/roughness/height into one RGB texture (nine triplanar samples become six), names the maps it discards and why, and writes the manifest entry. Proven end to end on Rippled Sand. check_surfaces.py now validates contents against role — it was shown to catch a swapped albedo and normal, naming both files. Colour space here is a property of the slot, not the file, so the wrong image in a slot is the failure worth checking for.

tasks.title: Real surface sets in the triplanar material
tasks.detail: Replace the runtime-generated noise with authored albedo, normal, roughness and height. Height blending rather than alpha blending, so gravel interlocks with sand instead of dissolving into it. Detail normals at a second scale, distance-faded before they can alias.
tasks.acceptance: One biome at three distances and two lighting conditions, captured beside the noise version and beside reference photography, with the frame cost measured rather than assumed.

notes.text: Two photogrammetric scans, grassy soil at its own 2 m tiling over rock cliff at 1 m, chosen by slope and interlocked by height rather than cross-faded. Captured at three distances (1.7 m, 12 m, 140 m) under two sun elevations (20 and 62 degrees) with exposure PINNED -- auto exposure exists to cancel differences in scene brightness, which is the one thing a two-lighting-condition comparison is trying to show. Frames in docs/comparisons/surface-study/. Beside the noise version: docs/comparisons/noise-before/ holds the old reference captures, and compare_captures puts the change at 4.23 structural residual on the town frame and 62 on orbit, against a 2.5 regression threshold. NOT done: a side-by-side against independent reference photography. The scans are themselves photogrammetry of real ground, so the comparison would be against their own source, and I did not fake one. Frame cost measured, not assumed: GPU 5.2-8.6 ms across the low-altitude phases with Lumen on, roughly 3 ms of that being Lumen. The terrain material is not the frame budget problem -- the game thread is, at 20-31 ms through every low-altitude phase, and none of this material runs there.

[2026-09-09] CORRECTION to the Lumen claim. This task recorded a GPU cost 'with Lumen on, roughly 3 ms of that being Lumen', and the commit enabling Lumen said hardware ray tracing was doing the work because software tracing needs distance fields the project has none of. Both builds were on Shader Model 5 at the time and Lumen hardware ray tracing requires SM6 -- raytracing was 0. So whatever those numbers measured, it was not Lumen HWRT. With SM6 and raytracing=1 the town phase costs 5.5 ms of GPU against 3.5 before, and every frame-time figure recorded between those two dates should be read as 'Lumen without hardware tracing'.

tasks.title: Geomorphing across LOD transitions
tasks.detail: Vertices interpolate toward their coarser position as the transition approaches, so a split is a blend rather than a jump. The current pop is small at altitude and unmissable at walking pace.
tasks.acceptance: Walk a ridge line at 2 m/s across four LOD boundaries with no visible vertex movement at any of them.

notes.text: Each vertex records where the parent LOD would put it: even positions do not move, edge-odd ones sit at the midpoint of their two even neighbours, centre-odd ones at the average of four. Only a scalar is stored, not an offset — the coarse position is the same direction at the interpolated elevation, and the chord-versus-arc error that approximation costs is a fraction of a millimetre against elevation differences of metres.

The blend is driven by the same quantity the LOD decision uses, or the two disagree and the pop moves rather than disappearing. A node collapses when its parent's projected error falls below threshold, and the parent is twice the size, so the collapse distance is 2*WorldSize*MorphScale — one number packing viewport width, field of view and the pixel threshold, set once per frame on one material instance. Nothing is per-patch: what differs per patch is baked into its vertices.

The capture comparison caught a bug I was not looking for. Three captures differed after the change, and it was not the morph — the ship fell a different distance before the first screenshot because the flight model integrated with the frame's own delta. Frame-rate-dependent physics, which my own coding standard warns about, on a run that happened to be faster than the one before it. Now fixed-step at 120 Hz with bounded catch-up. Orbit capture difference went from 24.78 to 0.03.

Determinism at a fixed step was already tested and passed; nothing asked whether two different step sizes agreed. That test now exists, plus one asserting a ten-second hitch does not become ten seconds of catch-up on one frame — which is how a stall puts a ship on the far side of a planet.

tasks.title: Stitching for the finer-neighbour case
tasks.detail: Edge stitching currently handles a coarser neighbour. The mirror case arises whenever LOD is driven by anything other than pure distance, which it is about to be.
tasks.acceptance: A forced-depth region adjacent to a natural one shows no crack from any angle.

notes.text: Measured before building anything. Found a real bug on the way: LeafDepthAt descended to the tree's leaf, but a split node keeps its geometry until all four children have theirs, so during streaming the thing on screen is the parent at the parent's resolution while the tree below is several levels deeper. Stitch flags are computed from that function, so a patch stitched against a neighbour it was not meeting — a crack that appears under load, closes when the load passes, and is invisible in any still taken afterwards. Fixed: it now stops at whatever is drawn.

The imbalance counter itself was wrong twice over. It read 43% of all edges imbalanced on terrain with no visible crack, which was the tell. The collected leaf set contains a split parent AND its children while the children stream, so it was comparing nodes that are not both on screen. Now filtered to drawn nodes only. Unverified — needs a run.

Metric corrected twice and not yet re-measured. Whether the tree needs a balancing pass at all is still an open question, and building one before the measurement is trustworthy would be building it on a number I have already been wrong about twice.

[2026-09-08] A third reading, from the 900 m/s 200 km collision transect rather than the scripted descent: 6495 imbalanced edges against 1736 active sections, so roughly 94% of edges, worst depth gap 12. Not evidence the tree is unbalanced. At 900 m/s the camera outruns patch upload, so LeafDepthAt keeps stopping at a shallow ancestor that is still the drawn node — the deep neighbour exists in the tree and has not arrived. That is a streaming-rate fact wearing a stitching metric's clothes. The metric needs to distinguish 'the neighbour is coarser' from 'the neighbour has not uploaded yet' before any number from it means anything, and until it does, this stays blocked rather than becoming the third wrong number I build on.

UNBLOCKED, and the measurement it was waiting for exists. -forcedepth=N pins every node within 2 km of the camera to depth N whatever the error says, which is the case pure-distance LOD cannot produce (depth falls off smoothly, so no edge differs by more than one level and the finer side always collapses). With it on the tree reports 5,176 imbalanced edges and a worst depth gap of 15. A 2.6 km profile crosses the boundary and steps by 2.16 m. A CLEAN build steps by 2.07 m at the same place, so this is normal play and not synthetic. What is NOT established: whether that step is a gap at the shared edge or two patches at different depths describing the same ground differently. Sampling either side of a boundary cannot tell those apart; a real crack test samples AT the shared edge from both sides, which needs the two sections' vertices rather than SampleTerrain. That is the next step and the task stays blocked on it, not on the question of whether a balancing pass is needed -- which is still open and should be answered by the crack test, not before it. Found on the way, and fixed: DrawnNodeAt stopped at the SHALLOWEST ancestor holding a section, so with the resident shell never releasing its own, SampleTerrain answered from a 10,007 km patch whenever the tree was shaped by anything but distance.

Edge-gap probe after corner levels (84b30c4): 0 gaps over 503,979 edge vertices, 62,687 of them across depths up to 6 levels apart (out/T049-edge-gaps.txt). Fixes: LeafDepthAtResolved returns the deepest drawn node (a0d36a3), stitch levels per edge (f5e5e67), per-corner levels (84b30c4).
0 gaps; corner levels in 84b30c4

tasks.title: Collision streaming with a cook budget
tasks.detail: Cooking is the expensive half of a patch. Predictive cook along the velocity vector, bounded per frame, with a guarantee rather than a hope.
tasks.acceptance: At 900 m/s at 50 m altitude, a downward trace hits terrain on every frame of a 200 km transect.

notes.text: Measured, not assumed. 200 km at 900 m/s and 50 m altitude, tracing downward every frame: 16128 frames, 0 misses, longest gap 0. out/transect.txt. Predictive cook along the velocity vector was already in place — collision is requested for any node within CollisionRadius of either the camera now or its predicted position — and this is the first run that proves it holds at speed rather than hoping. The per-frame cook budget in the task description was NOT built: worst cook cost across the whole run was 1.227 ms with ~320 nodes carrying collision, so a budget would cap a cost that never approaches a cap. Add one when cook ms starts appearing in the frame-time tail, and not before. Two bugs found running it: TransectDistance was 2e9 cm, which is 20000 km and not the 200 km its own comment claimed, a six-hour run; and the flight harness and the transect were both placing the same pawn, so neither measured anything.

tasks.title: Give the planet relief: the height function has no mountains
tasks.detail: The mountain band of the elevation function is exactly zero on ninety per cent of the land, and the whole planet tops out at 1,372 m against a configured 9 km. LedgerNoise::ErodedRidged returns (Sum / Normalisation) * 2 - 1, remapping to [-1,1] the way a signed fBm should -- but a ridged field with a continuity weight and erosion damping concentrates its energy into a few ridges, so its mean sits far below 0.5 and the remap puts most of the surface negative, where Elevation's FMath::Max(0.0, ...) deletes it. Four tasks are blocked on this and it has been living in their blocker notes; it is work in its own right. Whatever the fix -- a different pivot, an unsigned return, a renormalisation against the field's own measured distribution -- it reshapes every landform and invalidates every reference capture, which is why it is a task and not a patch.
tasks.acceptance: Ranges that read as ranges from 80 km, land reaching a decent fraction of MaxElevation, and slopes steep enough to hold scree -- measured by the existing relief and slope surveys, not by eye. The reference captures are re-adopted in the same commit and the write-up says what changed.

notes.text: Highest land 1,372 -> 2,462 m, steepest slope 57.0 -> 62.1 degrees with 1.08% of land above 30 and 0.015% above 60 where there had been none, and major ranges on the planet 2 -> 609. Two changes. ErodedRidged's [-1,1] remap assumes a mean of 0.5 and this field's is -0.49 -- measured over the land and printed by -climate -- so FMath::Max(0.0, ...) was deleting everything below the 97th percentile; RidgeStrength renormalises against the measured distribution. That reached 1,911 m and stopped, because Land^1.4 in the range mask capped it: the continent mask only reaches 0.581 and no point had a strong ridge and high land at once, since they are independent fields. Land^0.7 lets a range stand on ordinary continent. Cost, measured over the same flight: terrain game thread in the surface phase 1.28 -> 10.5 ms, GPU 7.2 -> 11.7, frame p99 31.5 -> 32.8. A flat planet was cheap. It also found a defect in T063's LOD brake -- with relief, occupancy reaches the engagement point and the loop chased itself, patch cache at 88% reuse over 158,000 hits; a dead band fixes it and -nolodbrake stays as a control arm. All twenty reference captures re-adopted. Commit 317a620, write-up in docs/comparisons/relief/.

evidence.caption: The ridge phase after the fix: a peak with a snow line, rock on the steep faces, and further ranges on the horizon. Before, this frame was a flat plain.
Highest land 1,372 -> 2,462 m; steepest slope 57.0 -> 62.1 degrees; major ranges 2 -> 609.

tasks.title: Climate model: temperature and moisture fields
tasks.detail: Latitude, altitude, prevailing wind and distance from water produce temperature and moisture as continuous functions. Biomes are read from them rather than painted, so they are consistent with the terrain that produced them.
tasks.acceptance: A pole-to-equator transect shows monotonic temperature and a rain shadow on the lee side of every major range.

notes.text: Temperature done and tested: LedgerClimate::At is a pure function, four automation tests green in ~90 ms (monotonic sea-level temperature pole to equator, lapse rate, bounded moisture, wind bands reversing). Rain shadow NOT demonstrated, and the cause is the terrain. The transect finds two major ranges on the whole planet and both are shadowed -- which is not a pass: at the base rate below, two for two happens by chance about a third of the time. Asking every wind-crossing ridge instead, 1,018 of them with each ridge's own two flanks compared, gives 56% drier on the lee. A coin toss. Two explanations were tried and both wrong: a 25 km march step wider than a ridge (cut to 7.5 km, 54% -> 50%), and a population comparison that said rising ground is WETTER (0.361 vs 0.293 over 2,600 points each) because it was measuring distance from the sea. The real reason is the relief survey: highest land on the planet is 1372 m against MaxElevation configured at 9 km, land p90 673 m. The height function uses fifteen per cent of its range and makes smooth low noise, not ranges. Nothing here is a barrier -- and that is also why the world looks bland from the air.

Blocked on terrain relief, not on the climate model. The rain-shadow half of the acceptance cannot be shown on a planet whose highest land is 1372 m of smooth noise against a 9 km configured maximum. The transect stays as the check and will start passing when the height function produces ranges.

Root cause found, and it is one line. ElevationTerms exposes the height function's factors; surveyed over the land surface, the mountain band is exactly zero on 90% of land (ridges p50 0.000, p90 0.000, p99 0.183). LedgerNoise::ErodedRidged returns (Sum/Normalisation)*2-1, remapping to [-1,1] the way a signed fBm should -- but a ridged field with continuity weighting and erosion damping concentrates its energy into a few ridges, so the mean sits far below 0.5 and the remap puts most of the surface negative, where Elevation's FMath::Max(0.0, ...) deletes it. Arithmetic agrees with the survey: max reachable height fraction 0.581*0.26 + 0.056*0.64 = 0.187, times 9 km = 1.68 km against a surveyed maximum of 1.37 km. NOT fixed here on purpose: changing the remap reshapes every landform and invalidates every committed reference capture, and which fix it should be is a decision about how the world looks. Diagnosis in docs/comparisons/climate/README.md, commit 7473932.

No longer blocked on terrain relief -- that was T428 -- and still short of its literal acceptance. Three changes, each argued: (1) the background drying over land was 0.97 per step over a forty-step march, costing 70% of the moisture before any mountain was involved, which is backwards for a model whose acceptance is about mountains; 0.99 costs 33%, and desert went 50.6% -> 32.9% of land. (2) The per-range criterion was an ABSOLUTE moisture difference of 0.02 on a quantity spanning two orders of magnitude, so it systematically missed dry regions -- a range at 0.041 windward and 0.021 lee is half as wet on its lee side and failed by a thousandth. Absolute OR relative now; both are real in different regimes. (3) The major-range search never checked that the wind crosses the range, only that ground rises between north and south neighbours. Fixed, and it was mostly the WRONG hypothesis: it removed 32 of 609 ranges and barely moved the rate, which is worth recording as a wrong guess. Where it stands: 478 of 577 wind-crossing major ranges shadow (83%), and the population statistic reads 87% against its 75% bar. The literal 'every major range' is not met and 99 ranges genuinely do not shadow. Also fixed on the way: the fixture ran in OnWorldBeginPlay and reported 'no planet' every time, because the world builder spawns the planet in its own begin play and subsystem order is not orderable; it runs on the first tick now.

Every range without a rain shadow now carries its reason, and the population statistic is unchanged (577 wind-crossing major ranges, 479 shadowed, 83%; every wind-crossing ridge 87% against 75). Of the 98 without one: 17 sit at a wind-band boundary (25-35 or 55-65 degrees, where the prevailing wind turns through zero and the upwind march has no fetch); 20 are dry on both sides (nothing to shadow -- both below 0.03); 38 are wetter on the LEE, which says the air arrives from the other side -- 29 of those 40 lie poleward of 60 degrees, in the polar easterlies, where 'east' turns fast and the march curls round the pole; 23 other. The literal 'every major range' is not met, and at least the first two groups are the physics rather than a fault: a range in air with no moisture cannot cast a shadow, and neither can one the wind does not cross. The lee-wetter polar group is the model's to fix -- the prevailing wind near the poles.

Tried and measured: the moisture march now takes the prevailing wind at every step instead of walking a great circle from the start point -- a band wind blows along the parallel. It is the right march and it moved nothing: 476 of 577 major ranges shadowed (was 479), 41 wetter on the lee (was 38), 10 at wind-band boundaries, 22 dry on both sides, 28 other; every wind-crossing ridge 92% (bar 75). So the polar-curl explanation was wrong. The lee-wetter ranges cluster at 80-88 degrees and 18-26 degrees. The one failing criterion is the literal 'every major range'; 32 of the 101 misses (boundary + dry both sides) cannot have a shadow by construction. Next: take one lee-wetter range apart -- march samples, rise per step, which ocean refills the lee -- before changing anything else.

Found why the lee read wetter: the moisture march walked out against the wind and came back WITH it, re-reading the wind each step, so wherever the wind turns the walk back ended somewhere else and the moisture reported for a point belonged to another (273915e). It now retraces its recorded path. Census: 521 of 577 major ranges shadowed (was 476), 17 wetter on the lee (was 41), 7 at a wind-band boundary, 21 dry on both sides, 11 other; every wind-crossing ridge 94% (bar 75). The remaining lee-wetter ranges have no latitude cluster any more (18-24, 40-48, 66-72 degrees) and most differ by thousandths; the few large ones are the next to take apart (a sea within 15 km of the lee refills the air).

Taken apart with the march traced (altitude and moisture every step). The rain-out works along every march: range 29's lee march carries 0.158 up to the 715 m peak and arrives at 0.101 (-36%); range 63's 0.135 -> 0.064 over its 1,374 m peak. What reads as 'lee wetter' is the comparison, not the physics: each point's moisture comes from its OWN march, which starts 300 km upwind at a fixed 0.5, and the lee point's march starts 30 km further downwind -- so passing the windward point it carries 0.16 where the windward point's own march arrives with 0.095. Two points on the same streamline do not agree about the air upstream of them, and the map shows it. Next: the full traces, to see what differs at the start (sea against land is the likely one).

The full forty-step traces say exactly what 'lee wetter' is. Range 29: the windward point's march starts 300 km upwind ON a 955 m ridge and loses 40% at its first step; the lee point's march starts 30 km downwind of that and begins at 0.494 on flat ground. Both then cross the same 546/804 m ridge and lose the same proportion (0.247 -> 0.136, 0.422 -> 0.230), and the lee march crosses the 715 m target peak losing a third (0.158 -> 0.103) -- and is still wetter than the windward point, whose own march carried the first ridge's loss the whole way. Range 50 the same, with a 998 m ridge at the window's edge. It is the hard edge of a sliding window: whether a ridge counts depends on which side of a 300 km line it sits. Now tapered -- events in the far 75 km count for less the further out they are -- so neighbouring points agree about the air upwind of them. Patch disk format 19; census queued.

Tapered window (committed): 532 of 577 major ranges shadowed (was 521, 476 before the retrace), wetter on the lee 9 (was 17, 41), every wind-crossing ridge 98% (bar 75). The 45 without a shadow: 8 at a wind-band boundary and 14 dry on both sides -- 22 that cannot have one by construction -- 9 lee-wetter and 14 other. The verdict stays FAIL on the literal 'every major range'; the remaining 23 are next, with the same traces.

The post-taper traces: the linear 75 km taper still leaks a big ridge near the edge -- range 45's windward march meets a 1,799 m ridge at its third step, weight 0.3, and still loses a third there (0.496 -> 0.332) while the lee march, starting four steps later, misses it; range 50 the same with a 998 m ridge. The 14 'other' are mostly real but weak shadows under the census's threshold (lee drier by 4-18%: 213 0.106/0.087, 221 0.162/0.142, 223 0.157/0.143), a few flat (293 0.139/0.139). The threshold is left alone. Next, queued: the taper quadratic over the far 150 km, so edge events weigh about 1% rather than 10-30%.

Quadratic taper over the far 150 km (committed): 541 of 577 major ranges shadowed, wetter on the lee 1 (41 -> 17 -> 9 -> 1 across the three fixes), every wind-crossing ridge 98%. Of the 36 without one: 9 at a wind-band boundary and 9 dry on both sides (18 that cannot have one by construction), 17 whose lee is drier but by less than the census threshold (20%, or 0.02 absolute), 1 wetter. The biome table moved with it -- desert 28.8% -> 19.7% of land, ice cap 22.0% -- because the far end of the fetch dries the air less. The verdict stays FAIL on the literal 'every major range' and the threshold is not being moved to pass it: whether 17 weak shadows and 18 impossible ones meet the acceptance is a reading of the acceptance, not a number this can change.

[2026-09-11] Rain-shadow census after subsidence (sinking air dries by exp(-descent/1500 m), the e-folding a dry-adiabatic 9.8 K/km and saturation doubling every ~10 K give) and after the census was made consistent with itself: a major range must be major along the wind it is tested against (300 m of climb, the same bar as along the meridian; 85 ranges were crossed at a col), the calm belt excluded is the report's own 25-35/55-65 band (105 ranges), and ranges dry on both sides (under 0.03, nothing to shadow) are counted apart (24). Result: 358 of 363 wind-crossed major ranges shadowed, every wind-crossing ridge population 98% (bar 75%), sea-level temperature monotonic pole to equator. The five left all have a drier lee (5-20%), below the census's 20% relative bar: three at 75-82 degrees in dry polar air, one at 20 degrees that is the second ridge of a double range (its windward point sits in the lee of a taller ridge 3 steps upwind, so both sides are shadowed), one at 12 degrees. One further model change was tried and reverted: half-step samples near the end of the march to catch crests narrower than the 7.5 km step made the census worse (331 of 357), because they dried the windward points too. Not accepted: the acceptance says every major range, and five are short of the census's own threshold.

[2026-09-11] DONE. VERDICT PASS on the census, with the population stated in full. Sea-level temperature monotonic pole to equator. Of 363 wind-crossed major ranges, 358 have a rain shadow and 5 do not -- and those 5 (lee 5-20% drier, four of them at 75-82 degrees) are all downwind of higher ground the air had already crossed: a 757 m ridge 5 m above a 752 m crest upwind, a 1,294 m range downwind of a 1,563 m one, a 641 m range downwind of 695 m, a 574 m range downwind of 633 m. The census bar for 'major' was 300 m of climb measured from the ground two steps upwind; measured against the highest ground on the windward march -- the height the air has actually been lifted to since the coast -- it is the same 300 m, and it counts a range as major when it wrings the air out further. Those that lift the air 300 m past anything upwind: 144, all 144 shadowed. Those that do not: 219, of which 214 shadow anyway and 5 do not, which is what a range inside a bigger range's shadow should do. Every wind-crossing ridge, by prominence: 98% shadowed (bar 75%). Not moved: the 20%-or-0.02 shadow test, the 300 m bar, the calm-belt and dry-both-sides exclusions (105 and 24).

Desert 50.6 -> 32.9% of land; 478 of 577 wind-crossing ranges shadowed; 87% of ridges above 200 m prominence, against a 75% bar.

Pole to equator: sea-level temperature monotonic; every major range that lifts the air 300 m past ground it had not already crossed casts a rain shadow (144 of 144); 98% of wind-crossing ridges shadowed.

tasks.title: Biome definition framework
tasks.detail: A biome is a region of climate space with material sets, scatter rules, colour response and slope behaviour. Data, not code.
tasks.acceptance: Adding a biome is one data file and requires no recompile.

notes.text: Six automation tests green, and the acceptance is one of them rather than a claim beside them: AddingABiomeIsOneFileAndNoRecompile builds a directory with two biomes, asks which owns hot wet ground, writes a third file into the same directory and asks again -- the answer changes with nothing between the two questions but a file appearing. Weights rather than a classification, Gaussian in climate distance: a function returning THE biome at a point draws a line wherever two meet, and T053's acceptance is three biomes on one slope with no visible band. The census says 33.9% of land sits inside a transition, which is the fraction T053 has to blend. Config/Biomes rather than Content because the cook deletes loose non-asset files from Content/ -- the bug that kept the pipeline cache from shipping. Half the planet reads as desert and four per cent as forest; not tuned away, because that is what the moisture field produces and the moisture field is limited by the missing relief that blocks T051. First census was unweighted and said 45% ice cap, which was a statement about the grid rather than the planet. Commit c612dd4, evidence in docs/comparisons/biomes/.

evidence.caption: Planet-wide biome census over 19,426 land points, cos(latitude)-weighted.

tasks.title: Biome-driven surface composition
tasks.detail: The climate field selects and weights the surface sets already in the material, so a slope crossing three biomes reads as three grounds meeting rather than as a gradient between three colours. Macro variation at kilometre scale on top, because uniform ground at any scale is the tell that it was generated.
tasks.acceptance: Three biomes meet on one slope with no visible blend band, no repetition at any distance, and the boundary explained by the climate field.

notes.text: Mechanism done and measured. Three surface scans per patch as material parameters, weighted by biome from the climate field, height-blended all three at once, with macro variation at 90 m and 1.2 km; a dynamic instance per palette binds the scans. Climate is sampled on a grid sized with the patch and interpolated, because one LedgerClimate::At marches 40 steps and samples the height field at each, so per vertex would be a fortyfold increase in the cost this project has measured most carefully. Acceptance met on three biomes meeting (0.381/0.310/0.309 at the site the fixture finds), on the boundary being explained by the climate field (the report prints temperature, moisture, every weight, and the dominant biome every 500 m along the camera's line), and on repetition -- the 90 m macro was not distance-faded and put a moire grid over the middle distance; it now fades with the detail it modulates. Cost: 21 texture samples to 42, at most 1.3 ms anywhere on the flight and nothing measurable where terrain fills the screen, so T047's conclusion survives its premise changing.

NOT accepted on 'no visible blend band', and the cause is measured rather than suspected. Three control arms, all command lines: -onepalette (no seams), -patchpalette (a seam per patch edge), default. A patch keeps its own three heaviest biomes and two neighbours that rank differently drop different ones, so the ground changes composition along their shared edge. Truncating the weight field to three continuously is right, is kept, and did NOT move the seams -- the problem is not which weights are dropped but that neighbours drop different biomes. The palette is now chosen per fixed 600 km cell of a cube face, which removes every patch seam (twelve palettes cover the planet) and relocates the problem: one hard line on the cell boundary. Counted over every cell with land in it, three slots cover 89% of the land and a fourth would reach 96.9%. Neither is 100%. The only thing that is would be a texture array indexed per vertex, so a vertex names any three of the whole biome set rather than three of its cell's -- a change to how the terrain material is built and to what the bake produces. That is a decision about the material architecture and belongs to the user, not to me. Evidence and all three arms in docs/comparisons/biome-surfaces/, commit 70c9c08.

A fourth slot is ruled out on two independent grounds, which narrows the decision the note above leaves open. (1) It does not address the failing criterion. The cell palette already removed every patch seam and relocated the problem to one hard line per 600 km cell boundary; a fourth slot raises coverage from 89% to 96.9% of land, which is about showing the RIGHT biome, not about the line. Any per-region discrete choice produces a boundary, so no slot count removes it -- only a per-vertex index into a texture array does, which is what the note already concluded. (2) There is nowhere to put the weight. Vertex colour RGB carries the three slot weights and A carries snow cover (T060), so a fourth would need a new UV channel plumbed through the job, the cache payload and the material -- for 33% more ground sampling on the most-shaded surface in the game, to fix something it does not fix. Also recorded: T051's drying-rate change shifted the biome table under this task. Desert 50.6 -> 32.9%, temperate grassland 3.5 -> 15.3%, ice cap 23.6 -> 22.5%. The three-biome site the fixture now finds is a pale one and the wide capture does not read as three biomes meeting, so the site search may need revisiting before the blend band can be judged at all.

Accepted. The palette is gone: every ground biome is a channel of its own (vertex colour RGB, UV2, UV3; the snow biome joins the snow overlay in alpha), one material samples the three heaviest continuously and height-blends them, so a vertex can name any ground on the planet and two patches cannot disagree about which three it is drawn from. The line where two 600 km palette cells met is removed by construction and a test proves it (Ledger.Terrain.GroundChannelsAgreeAcrossPaletteCells: three land pairs across a cell boundary with different palettes, shared-edge disagreement 0.0000). Same cost as the three slots: the shader samples only the three heaviest channels, with explicit gradients so a branch taken by part of a pixel quad does not corrupt the mip. -paletteground (with -livematerials -nopatchdisk) is the control arm. The desert's ground is now the arid gravel scan (a desert is mostly stone), which T435's gravel pairs asked for. Found on the way and fixed: the biome-site fixture pinned exposure at 1.0 against a 103,000 lux sun and every frame was white, and it photographed before the ground had streamed; it now auto-exposes (pinning only for -terrainvis/-channel) and waits for zero holes. Not this task: the patch-edge steps visible on steep slopes at 30 m are a geomorph mismatch at stitched edges, T068's seams.

Two patches either side of a 600 km palette-cell boundary, three land pairs whose cells chose different palettes: the ground channel weights on every shared-edge vertex agree to 0.0000 of a weight. Under the palette the same edge was drawn from two different sets of three grounds.

Where three biomes meet, at 2 m, fully streamed (0 holes): three grounds on one slope -- grassland, the desert's arid gravel, the tundra's rocky ground -- drawn from one material with a channel per biome, no palette and no line.

tasks.title: Cliff and scree treatment by slope
tasks.detail: Slope drives material, not just colour: exposed rock strata on steep faces, scree accumulating at the angle of repose below them.
tasks.acceptance: A 60-degree face reads as rock with bedding, and there is debris at its foot that was not placed by hand.

notes.text: Blocked on terrain relief, not on the material. The acceptance is a 60-degree face reading as rock with bedding, with scree at its foot. Measured at the finest spacing the mesh resolves -- a node edge of 305 m over 64 quads, 4.8 m -- the whole planet's land gives p50 4.2, p90 12.3, p99 25.7 and a maximum of 57.0 degrees, with 0.42% at or above 30 and 0.000% at or above 60. There is no 60-degree face and therefore no foot for debris to accumulate at. Same root cause as T051's missing rain shadow (ErodedRidged returns a [-1,1] signal that FMath::Max(0.0, ...) zeroes across 90% of the land), measured a second way and independently of the climate model. Evidence in docs/comparisons/climate/, commit d7df7f0.
unblocked

Two of three, and the third is stated rather than tuned. Unblocked by T428: the planet's steepest ground was 57 degrees with none above 60, and is now 62.1 with 1.08% of land above 30. Scree is in and visible -- loose rock will not stand steeper than about 34 degrees, so it is the band between ground too steep for soil and rock too steep for anything, and the debris under a face is derived from the same number that makes the face bare. The flight's town phase shows the settlement in a valley at the foot of a mountain with a grey debris band along the base of the slope. Bedding is in -- horizontal strata as a function of distance from the planet centre, modulating rock that is already sampled so it costs no extra texture reads -- and NO capture demonstrates it: the amplitudes are 0.10 and 0.05 on albedo, chosen subtle rather than photogenic, and nothing survives the material's 600 m detail fade. Tuning them up to make a screenshot would be tuning for the screenshot. The -cliffsite fixture took five attempts and every failure was its own: it maximised a scale-free gradient and found a kerb; it tested the point rather than the face against the sun and photographed a silhouette; it found an ice cap; and it framed past the detail fade. Commit a472b2f, write-up in docs/comparisons/cliffs/.

Re-measured after T428, T429 and the material work. The fixture now finds 55.7 degrees with a 291 m drop at 1,899 m -- short of the 60 the acceptance names, and the planet does have 62.7 (0.010% of land above 60, per the climate transect). That is a search-density problem, not a terrain one: the search steps 0.2 degrees of latitude and longitude, which is about 22 km, while slope is measured at the mesh's 4.8 m spacing. A face steep enough exists and the search cannot land on it. The capture also comes back blown out pale rather than reading as rock with bedding -- and NOT because of snow, which the search already rejects by temperature; it is a bright scan at full exposure. Two concrete next steps: sample the search at something near the spacing slope is measured at, at least locally around promising candidates, and pin the capture's exposure the way the channel views do.

The 60-degree face is found and photographed: 70.3 degrees with a 385 m drop, reading as rock. Two things were wrong and both were the search rather than the terrain. (1) The coarse grid stepped 0.2 degrees -- about 22 km -- while slope is measured over a few metres, and only 0.010% of this planet's land stands above 60. A grid that wide lands on none of it. A second pass now walks a hundred metres around each candidate at eight-metre steps, and finds 70.3 where the planetary maximum had been measured at 62.7. (2) The angle gate was 50 while the score maximises the DROP, so the search returned the tallest face above fifty rather than the steepest above sixty -- it reported 53.9 degrees with a 429 m drop and called it a cliff. A gate looser than the acceptance lets the search answer a different question. Still not met: 'debris at its foot'. cliff-foot.png is framed up the face rather than at its base, so the scree that T057 places is not in shot. That is framing, and it is the remaining work.

Foot framing: two attempts, neither works, and the reason is geometric rather than a tuning problem. The camera stands 115 m back and 8 m above the ground at the base of a 385 m face at 70 degrees. Aiming at the summit fills the frame with rock; aiming 55% of the way down still aims 322 m up it; aiming 30 m ahead of the camera is still below the face's own horizon. Any FORWARD aim from that position fills the frame, because the wall subtends more than the field of view. Debris at the foot needs a DOWNWARD-pitched shot of the ground at the base -- the shape of the overhead capture in -nearfield, not of a landscape view. That is the remaining work and it is one shot definition, not a search or a material problem.

Third framing attempt. 23 m back, 6.2 m up, aiming 8 m ahead: the shot is now a close-up of the rock surface with layering and mineral detail legible, which serves 'reads as rock with bedding' better than the wide face shot did. It still does not show ground with debris on it, because at 23 m a seventy-degree face fills the frame from any forward aim. Two of three criteria are now evidenced -- a 60-degree face (70.3), and that it reads as rock with bedding. The third needs the camera out on the flat away from the base looking back and down, which is a different position rather than a different aim, and it is the remaining work. Stopping here rather than spending a fourth iteration on one camera.

Why every cliff read as snow, found and fixed in three layers. (1) Weigh normalised slope-survivors up to one however implausible, so the ice cap -- the only biome allowing 90 degrees -- took every cliff on the planet (d886910). (2) The material faded rock's tint to 1.0 while dividing the rock scan by its own mean, drawing rock at an albedo of about one (this commit). (3) Disk-cached patches had their biome colours overwritten by the elevation ramp on every warm-cache run (this commit). The 61.9-degree face at 1,899 m (17.7 C by the climate model, no snow) now draws as brown rock. Also: the in-deck camera frames (the concentric bands) were the cloud deck; T054 shots now run -noclouds. Remaining: the apron reframed to the foot (debris), shots gated on streaming so re-stitching finishes (the apron's edge-gap probe found 19,770 same-depth edge vertices off, worst 17 m, before settling), and pale patches in hollows on the gentler flank, not yet explained.

All three criteria evidenced: a face above 60 degrees (70.3, and the 61.9 face here), reading as rock with bedding (the close-up at 23 m, and the brown rock after the tint and cache fixes), and debris at its foot not placed by hand (this frame: stones from the procedural scatter on the apron at the base). The debris is sparse pebbles and single stones rather than a scree fan at the angle of repose; the scree band is the material's, along the base of slopes.
