tasks.title: Hydrology: flow accumulation and river networks
tasks.detail: Rivers derived from the height field by flow accumulation, carving their own valleys, reaching the sea. The erosion model already computes slope; this is what slope is for.
tasks.acceptance: Every river reaches the sea or a basin, none flows uphill, and the same seed produces the same network.

notes.text: Five automation tests green, and the acceptance is three of them rather than a claim beside a screenshot: NoCellFlowsUphill, EveryCellReachesTheSeaOrABasin, SameSeedSameNetwork. The other two earn their place -- FlowIsConserved catches a wrong accumulation, which would otherwise give a plausible network with every river the wrong size, and SameSeedSameNetwork is the only place a race in the parallel neighbour pass could show up. A fixed lattice rather than the quadtree, because which way a river runs depends on ground a thousand kilometres away and two patches at different LODs would answer differently; 256 per cube face, 39 km cells, 393,216 of them, built in 0.1 s. The bug worth recording: neighbours were found through the sphere, and DirectionToFace inverts FaceToCube but not CubeToSphere's area-evening warp, so every neighbour link joined cells that do not touch. Every test passed -- the graph was consistent, downhill, acyclic, conserved and deterministic. It just was not a map, and the tell was in the report (32,605 basins, longest river 0 km), not the tests. Neighbours are now resolved in cube space and CellRoundTripsThroughItsCentre is the test that was missing. The corrected planet drains 46.6% to the sea and 53.4% into 1,985 closed basins against Earth's 18% endorheic, which is what a height field with no erosion looks like; pit-filling is left undone because the acceptance allows a basin as a terminus. Commit 2d45266, write-up in docs/comparisons/hydrology/.

evidence.caption: Whole-planet drainage: 393,216 cells, 1,985 basins, largest catchment 394,000 km2, longest river 1,173 km.

tasks.title: Caves and overhangs
tasks.detail: A height field cannot express an overhang. A sparse volumetric layer over the height field, meshed only where it is non-trivial, so the cost is paid where there are caves and nowhere else.
tasks.acceptance: Walk into a cave mouth, through a passage, and out the other side, with collision and lighting correct throughout.

notes.text: Partial, and the acceptance cannot be finished here. It asks to WALK into a mouth, through a passage and out the other side with collision and lighting correct throughout; there is no pawn with legs until M09, so two of the three things that sentence asks to be correct cannot be checked at all. What works and is photographed: the cave field (26.6% of the surface is cave country; the first mouth leads to a passage of 1,123 cells spanning 680 m and 648 m deep, meeting the sky at 35 cells with its two furthest mouths 120 m apart -- the acceptance's substance measured by flood fill without a mesher), and the hole in the surface, which is a deletion because a height field cannot have a hole. What does not: the wall mesh runs on 745 patches and is visible from outside, but is NOT verifiably closed -- a camera 18 m under the mouth sees uniform sky, so from in there every surface is back-facing, and whether that is winding or coverage is unanswered. Not started at all: LOD (caves pop in at the 1.2 km patch boundary), brick seams (left open rather than capped, so a crack rather than a wall across the passage), a material for cave rock, and any light inside. Meshing is behind -cavemesh and off by default so no other measurement in the repository is affected. Write-up with all of this in docs/comparisons/caves/, commit 4d3312d.

[2026-09-11] COLLISION: walked, end to end. -caves -cavewalk -cavemesh sweeps a 40 cm x 1.8 m capsule on the floor along the breadth-first route between the two furthest real mouths of the passage the survey keeps (it now tries every lit mouth, up to eight: 361 m apart, 456 m of route) -- 0 steps blocked, 0 without a floor. What it took: cave walls wound towards the air by where the air is (they faced into the rock on some cube faces, so from inside every wall was a back face and the camera saw sky), bricks sampled one cell past their edge and on a shared altitude lattice so neighbours join, 64 layers rather than 24 (at 12.5 m a layer the narrowing towards a mouth closed in the mesh), cave rock coloured as the tundra's rocky ground with no snow (unset, it was full snow cover), the collision proxy cut at mouths (it was a lid over them), a breach counted only where the ground itself is open, the walker standing on the floor rather than at lattice cell centres, and stepping over anything a 60 cm lift clears. LIGHTING: plausible -- walls lit and shadowed by the sun, the floor in shade -- but not clean: thin slits of sky between bricks of different depth (the apron joins only equal-depth neighbours), stones floating on the rims of the cut, and sliver triangles where the land was deleted. The passage this route follows is also mostly open to the sky (it meets it at 101 cells), a slot canyon more than a cave. Not accepted until those are fixed.

[2026-09-11] Two fixes measured by photograph, neither enough: (1) stones are now kept off any grid quad the land lost a triangle from (the land is cut per triangle at its centroid; testing the cave field at the stone's own point left stones on rim triangles), and (2) each cave brick samples the union of its own altitude range and those of the three neighbours whose seams it joins (bricks hang from the ground at their own centres, so a seam was drawn over one brick's range only). The walk still passes (0 blocked, 0 floorless, 456 m, 481 climbed), but the slits of light down the shadowed wall and the pale shards and stones along the rims are still in the photographs -- so the slits are not (only) the range mismatch; the next suspect is bricks of different patch depth meeting, whose lattices do not share vertices. Not accepted.

[2026-09-11] The walk passes again after three regressions of this session's making were fixed -- skirts hanging into the passage (now left off cave patches), cave sections losing collision to the per-frame allowance (the in-place upgrade now covers section 2), and a stack overflow in HomeAir: 456 of 456 m, 0 blocked, 0 without a floor. Tried against the slits of light down the shadowed wall, each measured by photograph and none of them moving it: bricks given the union of their neighbours' altitude ranges; bricks joining their own first edge so seams overlap; the land cut by triangle corners instead of centroids (the rim is now a lip over the opening, not a sawtooth). The slits are none of those. Enlarged, they are narrow windows through the wall with the grass of the hillside behind: the passage runs close under a slope, the rock between is a fin thinner than one cell of the cave lattice (BrickAcross 32 across a patch, several metres a cell), and surface nets do not mesh what the samples miss. Two fixes, both design: a finer lattice on cave patches (about 3x the samples, and a thinner fin still fails), or a minimum wall and roof thickness near the ground surface in the cave field (changes the passages the walk and survey were built on). Also on the rim: stones on the land lip over the opening, which from the floor show their shadowed undersides. Not accepted.

[2026-09-11] The thin-fin theory is wrong. At 64 cells across (from 32) the walk still passes (456 of 456 m, 0 blocked, 0 without a floor) but the windows in the shadowed wall multiplied and came out evenly spaced along its top: they scale with the lattice, so they are a join the surface-nets mesher misses between cell columns, not rock the samples cannot see. Reverted to 32 (four times the samples for nothing). They were in the first walk photographs too, before any of this session's cave changes, so they are the mesher's, not a regression. Next: dump the cave mesh of the brick holding the wall and find which edge's quads are absent -- the four-cell join around each crossed edge requires all four cells to have vertices, and a cell whose sign changes only along an axis the join loop does not visit would leave exactly a column-wide hole. Not accepted.

[2026-09-11] The windows are back faces, found by two control arms on the 90% frame (chain151). -cavedoubled (every cave triangle drawn from both sides): the wedges are gone. -cavenoland (the cave patches' whole land surface removed): the wedges are unchanged, so the land plays no part -- everything in that frame is cave mesh. Per-triangle winding (chain149) had not moved them either: the fold at the rim defeats the towards-the-air test for some faces whichever way it is asked. So the cave section is now two-sided, the back a copy of the vertices with the normals flipped so it lights as the side it is; the walk still passes both arms (456 of 456 m, 0 blocked, 0 without a floor). Photographs of the two-sided mesh queued.

Walked end to end with collision and lighting correct throughout (chain155): 456 of 456 m, 0 blocked, 0 without a floor, and the photographs at 10, 50 and 90 per cent show the walls whole and lit as the sun falls. The last defect -- slits of sky along the shadowed wall top -- was cave faces wound away from the camera where the fold at the rim defeats the towards-the-air winding test (-cavedoubled removed them, -cavenoland did not); the section is two-sided now, the back a flipped-normal copy. The walk is a capsule sweep rather than a pawn with legs, which arrives in M09.

A passage of 1,123 cells spanning 680 m with two mouths 120 m apart, measured by flood fill without a mesher.
The walk: a capsule 40 cm by 1.8 m swept on the floor from one mouth to the other, 456 m -- 0 steps blocked, 0 without a floor, 488 steps climbed (ground rising under it, cleared by a 60 cm lift).

90% of the way: the passage here is open to the sky, walls lit on one side and in shadow on the other. The thin slits of light down the shadowed wall are seams between cave bricks of different depth, still open.

90% of the way, after every fix: the walk clean, the clouds now three decks. The slits down the shadowed wall are holes in a rock fin thinner than the cave lattice's cell -- the passage and the hillside beyond it nearly meet.

tasks.title: Asset review harness: turntable, framing and lighting rig
tasks.detail: One command puts a generated asset on a stand and photographs it: eight yaw angles, three framings from silhouette to close, and two lighting rigs, at pinned exposure. Scheduled before the first generator that needs it, and for the same reason the capture comparison was built before the material work. ADR-0005 makes every asset in the game an iterated one, and iteration is only affordable if looking at the result is cheap and honest. It was not: three separate readings of the surface captures were wrong -- a camera underground, an exposure in stops mistaken for lux, a camera standing inside a building -- and each cost an hour because the picture was believed before the arithmetic.
tasks.acceptance: One command turns any generated asset into a contact sheet on disk, with the camera provably outside the geometry, exposure fixed across every frame, and two consecutive runs agreeing within a stated tolerance rather than by eye.

notes.text: 48 shots: 8 yaw x 3 framings (silhouette, standing, close) x 2 rigs (raking key with almost no fill, soft filled), exposure pinned, backdrop plane held square to the camera. out/turntable/, three kept in docs/comparisons/turntable/. Four bugs between writing it and the first usable frame, and each one produced the same symptom -- a black or empty image -- which is why each was mistaken for the last: GetActorBounds(true) counts only COLLIDING components, and the hull's collision is off, so the subject measured 1 m and the camera-outside check passed 48 times against the same empty bounds it was derived from; then bounds measured over the whole actor, which on this pawn includes a 52 m camera boom, so framings were three times too far and the ship was a speck; then the backdrop was an inside-out sphere by negative scale, which does not work and also enclosed the stage in its own shadow; then two stage lights plus the world's sun produced 'multiple directional lights competing for forward shading', resolved by a brightness tie-break. The user spotted that last one from the on-screen warning after I had cleared it by grepping the log, where it does not appear. Determinism: byte-identity was the original gate and is NOT achievable with Lumen -- its probes accumulate over frames and two runs came back 42/48, then 46/48, then 42/48 identical, differing by a mean of 0.06 of a channel and never more than 9. The gate now states a tolerance and the runs pass it at worst-channel 3 against a limit of 16. compare_captures.py --between does the comparison.

Its acceptance does not hold as the tool judges it: two consecutive turntable runs compared with compare_captures.py --between give a worst single channel difference of 39 against a limit of 16 (48 shots, 2026-09-11). What that failure is, measured: 2 of 48 shots over the limit, median worst-channel 10, and in the worst shot exactly ONE pixel of 2,073,600 exceeds it -- isolated, no differing neighbour, at a backlit silhouette edge -- with a mean channel difference of 0.107 over the whole frame. The renders agree to a tenth of a channel; a single stray sample decides the gate. Blocked on the owner's call rather than fixed quietly: either attempt a fix (the harness settles 64 frames a shot; a longer settle may not touch a stochastic edge sample), or restate whether 'worst single channel' over two megapixels is the right statistic for 'do two runs agree'. Widening the limit to clear the gate is the one thing I will not do unasked.

THE DECIDING STATISTIC HAS A WIDER SPREAD THAN THE LIMIT IT IS JUDGED AGAINST -- from records already on this task, no new run needed. Tonight's terrain work established the discipline that a difference means nothing without a floor, and check 11 has never had one. Applying it to the numbers already recorded here: THE SAME FIXTURE, UNCHANGED, HAS PRODUCED WORST-CHANNEL 3 (2026-09-09, this task's first note: 'the runs pass it at worst-channel 3 against a limit of 16'), 9 ('never more than 9' in the byte-identity exploration recorded in the same note), AND 39 (2026-09-11, the evidence attached). Across those same runs the MEAN channel difference stayed between 0.06 and 0.107. So the statistic that decides this gate varies 3 to 39 run-to-run on a fixture nobody changed, while the statistic that is stable says the renders agree to about a tenth of a channel. A limit of 16 sits INSIDE that spread, which means the check currently passes or fails by luck: a real regression could pass at 3, and an unchanged build fails at 39. It cannot discriminate in either direction, and that is a property of the statistic rather than of the renderer. WHAT THIS DOES AND DOES NOT SETTLE: it does not tell the owner what the criterion should be -- that is still theirs, and I am still not widening a limit to clear a gate. It does remove the framing I offered earlier, which treated this as a matter of taste. It is measurable, it has been measured, and the measurement says the current test is not a test. A CONCRETE ALTERNATIVE, offered for the owner to accept or reject: judge two runs on the MEAN (already in the tool as REPEAT_MEAN_TOLERANCE 0.5, and the measured runs pass it at 0.107 with room to spare) PLUS a neighbour-aware worst -- count a pixel only when at least one adjacent pixel also differs beyond the limit. That is standard firefly rejection and it does not weaken the test for real changes, because a real change moves a region and never a single isolated sample. The failing shot's worst pixel is explicitly isolated with no differing neighbour, so it would be rejected; a genuine material or lighting change would not be. ALSO RULED OUT TONIGHT, so nobody spends a run on it: raising FramesToSettle. The constant is 64 and its comment records WHY -- 24 left Lumen's probes reconverging -- and at 64 two runs differed by 'never more than 9'. A reading that jumps from 9 to 39 at unchanged settle is not under-convergence, so more settle frames cannot touch it.

MEASURED THE FAILURE SHOT BY SHOT, FROM FRAMES ALREADY ON DISK -- no new run needed, and it argues against the fix route I was about to take. Across the 48 shots of the two runs already captured: MEDIAN worst-channel 7; SECOND-WORST SHOT 14, already under the limit of 16; and exactly ONE shot over it, raking-silhouette-05 at 39, carrying ONE pixel above the limit in the sampled quarter with a mean frame difference of 0.107. So 47 of 48 shots pass comfortably and the gate is decided by a single stray sample on a raking-lit silhouette edge -- a firefly, which is what a stochastic sampler produces at a backlit edge. WHY I AM NOT TAKING THE FIX ROUTE: the candidates are pinning Lumen's screen-probe temporal accumulation or TSR's jitter (the harness pins NO sampling cvars at all today, so either is a real change). Both alter how EVERY review sheet is rendered, and this fixture exists to make asset review cheap and honest -- its output quality is the product. Changing the renderer for all 48 shots, in every future review, to suppress one pixel in two million is disproportionate to the cause, and disabling anti-aliasing outright would stabilise the comparison by degrading the artefact the fixture is for, which is gate-gaming by another route. Raising FramesToSettle is already ruled out on the code's own history (64 frames gave 'never more than 9'; tonight gave 39 -- not under-convergence). WHAT THE MEASUREMENT NOW SUPPORTS, and it is a change of my position: restating the statistic is the better ENGINEERING answer, not merely the easier one. The deciding number swings 3, 9, 39 across runs of an unchanged fixture while the mean holds at 0.06-0.107, so a limit of 16 sits inside its own noise and the check cannot discriminate a real regression from a lucky roll in either direction. The concrete proposal stands: judge two runs on the MEAN (already computed, REPEAT_MEAN_TOLERANCE 0.5, measured 0.107) PLUS a neighbour-aware worst that counts a pixel only when an adjacent pixel also differs beyond the limit. The failing pixel is isolated with no differing neighbour and would be rejected; a real material or lighting change moves a region and would not. THIS REMAINS THE OWNER'S CALL. I will not widen a limit to pass a gate, and I have not; recommending that a statistic be replaced with one that measures agreement is a different act, and it needs the owner's yes.

evidence.caption: Two consecutive turntable runs compared as check 11 asks: worst single channel 39 against a limit of 16, 2 of 48 shots over it, median 10 -- and one isolated pixel in two million decides the worst shot, with a mean frame difference of 0.107.

tasks.title: Scatter framework: rocks, vegetation, debris
tasks.detail: Deterministic placement from biome rules, GPU-instanced, LOD'd, with density that survives the frame budget at ground level.
tasks.acceptance: Ten thousand visible instances at 60 fps, identical placement across runs, and nothing floating or half-buried.

notes.text: Acceptance met and measured. 42,408 instances at a median 16.6 ms over 2,296 sampled frames at the three-biome site -- sixty, and four times the ten thousand asked for. Wall clock rather than DeltaSeconds, because the fixture runs under -useFixedTimeStep and the engine's delta is a constant that would have reported a perfect sixty however slowly the frame ran. Identical placement across runs is a bit-for-bit test: every position is a hash of the patch key and a cell index and nothing else. Nothing floating took three attempts and the third found a real bug -- the mesh is a bilinear interpolation of the height field sampled every 4.8 m and wanders up to 1.222 m from it, so a tree placed at the exact value floats or sinks by that much; placement now reads the patch's own vertices. The two failed attempts are recorded because both passed: one compared the height function against itself, and one needed to invert CubeToSphere's warp, which DirectionToFace does not do, so it skipped every instance and reported 0.000 m over four hundred it never looked at. Sixteen instanced-component buckets rather than one: one component per variant costs 13.4 ms to rebuild at a forest site, sixteen buckets with two rebuilt per frame costs 0.3 to 1.2 ms. Known and named limit: scatter stops dead at the finest-LOD ring with no fade or impostor, which is visible in the evidence and is T059's task. Commit fddfc8a, write-up in docs/comparisons/scatter/.

Correction to the note above: the limit was described as 'a hard edge where the scatter stops', from the thirty-metre frame. The six-hundred-metre frame (docs/comparisons/scatter/ring-edge.png) shows rectangular clumps at about the size of a 305 m patch with gaps between them, not a clean edge -- and why a distance-driven LOD produces blocks rather than a disc is not established. Also recorded: the obvious remedy makes it worse. Carrying scatter two size steps further with fewer candidates per patch is cheap (97,777 instances over 905 patches, 1.5 ms, still sixty) and looks far worse, because a fixed candidate count over a patch means areal density falls with the square of patch size, so patches one LOD step apart differ eightfold. Reverted; the reasoning is in LedgerScatter.h. Density has to be a function of position rather than of which patch a point falls in, which means a world-fixed candidate lattice -- T059's work. Commits 33081f7 and 2e8486a.

evidence.caption: 42,408 instances at a median 16.6 ms. The hard edge in the middle distance is where the finest-LOD ring ends; that is T059's business.

tasks.title: Vegetation with wind response
tasks.detail: Trees and grass that move with the wind field M04 will provide, and stop moving when it stops.
tasks.acceptance: Wind speed changes and vegetation responds within a second, at every LOD including the impostor.

notes.text: Blocked on two things that do not exist, and the acceptance names both. It asks that vegetation respond to a wind speed change 'at every LOD including the impostor'. There is no wind field: the task's own detail says 'the wind field M04 will provide', and that is T093 (Wind field queryable by everything), sixty tasks away and not started. LedgerClimate::PrevailingWind is a fixed banded direction for the moisture march, not a field with a speed that changes. And there is no impostor: that is T059, the very next task. The mechanism could be built against a stand-in -- a material with world position offset driven by a wind weight painted into the tree meshes, plus a global speed and direction parameter -- but it would be responding to a parameter nothing sets, at an LOD tier that does not exist, and the acceptance could not be run either way. Recorded rather than half-built so the shape of it is on the record: the work is a wind weight in tools/generate_assets.py's tree meshes and a foliage material, and it wants doing after T059 and T093.

Delivered against the trees that exist; the impostor clause cannot be met because there is no impostor. M_Foliage leans the canopy by world position offset from MPC_LedgerWind (the one wind T093 publishes), lean = dir * saturate(v^2/900) * (z/18m)^2 * 150 cm plus gust. Measured: the wind probe changes the wind and all five consumers (ship, precipitation, audio, vane, materials) follow within a second. Photographed fairly for the first time: Ledger.Wind.Scale changes the wind at a fixed clock -- the earlier pair had jumped 72 hours and compared two suns -- and the crown moves ~115 px downwind with the base fixed. Two lighting faults found on the way and fixed: the sky light's real-time capture delivered nothing (every shaded face (0,0,0), Lumen on or off; a static capture fixes it), and M_Foliage multiplied the tint by a vertex colour that already carried it, an albedo near 0.01. STILL OPEN: the acceptance says 'at every LOD including the impostor'. The trees have one LOD (46 triangles) and T059 did not build impostors (its own note: 'NOT BUILT'). Either the acceptance is amended to the LODs that exist or an impostor tier is built first; that is a scope decision, not a technical blocker.

Accepted. The impostor now exists and is drawn: each tree has an impostor mesh of its own (SM_Tree_A_Impostor, SM_Tree_B_Impostor: trunk, canopy and upper canopy on two crossed cards, 16 triangles, normals from the cones so a card is lit as the volume it stands for) on its own instanced component, drawn from 250 m where the full trees stop. A mesh LOD was tried first and the engine rebuilt the second LOD from the first whatever it was handed -- through BuildFromMeshDescriptions and through committed source models alike, with a valid 16-triangle description reported for LOD 1 and 46 triangles built -- so the manual LOD is the one that works. Both sets use M_Foliage, whose lean is a function of the instance's local height and the one wind collection, so the impostor leans with the tree it stands in for: forced to impostors (-treeimpostor hides the full trees), the canopy moves downwind within 30 frames of a calm-to-gale change, and the frames differ from the full-tree ones in 240,135 pixels concentrated on the tree, which is what says the impostor is what was photographed (the first attempt differed in 6,602 scattered pixels and was the full tree both times). All five consumers agree within a frame; the probe's vegetation row had read NEVER under -treephoto because it compared the collection's across-the-up wind with the full 3D field, and now compares like with like.

The wind probe: flight, vegetation, particles, audio and the settlement vane all followed the change within one frame (0.02 s); vegetation now compared with the across-the-local-up wind the collection actually carries.

tasks.title: Far-field impostors and horizon detail
tasks.detail: Beyond the last real LOD, the planet needs to keep its silhouette. Impostors for scatter, and a horizon that does not go smooth.
tasks.acceptance: A mountain range 80 km away has a silhouette and reads as terrain rather than as a gradient.

notes.text: Two halves, and both are blocked for different reasons. The acceptance is 'a mountain range 80 km away has a silhouette and reads as terrain rather than as a gradient'. There is no mountain range: measured at the mesh's own 4.8 m spacing, the whole planet's land is p50 4.2, p90 12.3, p99 25.7 degrees of slope with a maximum of 57, and the highest land is 1,372 m against a configured 9 km. At 80 km the horizon drop alone is about 500 m, so the tallest thing on the planet would be a bump on it. Same root cause as T051 and T054 -- ErodedRidged returns a [-1,1] signal that FMath::Max(0.0, ...) zeroes across 90% of the land. The other half, keeping the scatter's silhouette past the last real LOD, has a measured design constraint from tonight rather than a blocker: a candidate count fixed per patch cannot thin with distance without drawing the patch grid in trees (tried, 97,777 instances at 1.5 ms and visibly worse, reverted). It needs a candidate lattice fixed to the world so density is a function of position, and that is the work when the task is unblocked. Evidence in docs/comparisons/climate/ and docs/comparisons/scatter/.

Unblocked by T428 and met against its acceptance. The blocker was arithmetic: at 80 km the horizon drop is 502 m, so on the old planet the highest land (1,372 m) stood 870 m proud and subtended 10 px -- a bump, and no impostor work makes a bump read as a range. It is 2,891 m now, standing 2,389 m proud and subtending 29 px, and the photograph shows snow-capped summits with a ragged profile rather than a gradient. NOT BUILT, and named rather than implied: the impostors in the task's title. The acceptance does not ask for them. The design constraint for that work is already measured and stays with it -- a candidate count fixed per patch cannot thin with distance without drawing the patch grid in trees (tried: 97,777 instances at 1.5 ms, visibly worse, reverted); it needs a candidate lattice fixed to the world so density is a function of position.

[2026-09-11] THE PLANET FROM ORBIT IS NOT COVERED BY THIS TASK, AND NOTHING ELSE COVERS IT EITHER -- recorded here because this is the nearest thing the roadmap has. The owner reported that planets from space look 'awful and like almost low poly/animated, not realistic like Star Citizen', and the orbit capture bears it out. DIAGNOSIS, from the code and the surviving frame: from ~12,000 km the whole planet resolves to about 540 patches at depth 3 to 4, so vertices sit 10 to 20 km apart; the terrain material takes its ground palette straight from VertexColor (LedgerTerrainMaterial, the three slot weights masked off the vertex colour); and the sea is generated on the SAME vertex grid as the land (Job.Side in LedgerPatchGenerator), so both sides of every coastline step together. That is exactly the rectangular coastline in the capture: it is COLOUR RESOLUTION, not polygon count, and adding triangles is the expensive way to fix a shading problem. Two further defects, separate causes: no clouds at all over the disc, because the volumetric layer's TracingMaxDistance is 250 km and the viewer is far outside it; and a limb with no visible scattering halo, which is mostly honest physics -- 60 to 100 km of atmosphere on a 6,344 km radius is about 1% of the disc -- rather than a bug. THE FIX, designed but not yet written: a planet-wide albedo sampled from the same climate and height functions the patch generator already uses, at a resolution independent of the mesh, cross-faded in as patches coarsen. The material already has everything needed -- NodeSize comes from UV1.y, ToCamera from the camera position, and the graph's own comment warns that the blend must be driven by the same quantity the LOD decision uses or the two disagree; SampleParameter() binds a texture into the generated graph. One source fixes land and sea together because they share the grid. WHY THIS TASK DID NOT CATCH IT: T059's acceptance is 'a mountain range 80 km away has a silhouette', which is a horizon problem from the ground. Nobody ever wrote a task for the planet seen from space, which is why it has never been measured. NOT YET PROVEN BY EXPERIMENT: the A/B that would confirm it (default 250 px screen error against 60 px, -terrainerror= added for it) died mid-flight when the disk filled -- both arms lost, captures truncated to zero bytes.

evidence.caption: Snow-capped peaks on the horizon at 80 km: a ragged profile with distinct summits, not a gradient.
2,891 m of land against a 502 m horizon drop: 2,389 m proud, subtending 29 px.

tasks.title: Snow, ice and seasonal cover
tasks.detail: Cover driven by the climate field and the season, accumulating by altitude and latitude, affecting material and scatter.
tasks.acceptance: The same location has snow in winter and not in summer, and the snow line moves with altitude.

notes.text: Partial. The acceptance's two claims are met as properties of the climate function and are four green tests: 55 N at 800 m reads 0.00 snow in summer and 1.00 in winter, and 45 N reads 0.00 at sea level and 1.00 at 4,000 m. The snow line is not a parameter -- it is where surface temperature crosses zero, so it moves with altitude because the lapse rate was already there, and a test walks it from the equator to 80 degrees and fails if it ever rises poleward. Seasons are opposite by construction (the term is odd in the sine of latitude) and the equator has none. Snow rides the vertex colour's alpha, the one channel the biome weights left free, and scatter reads it. What is missing is the look: a snow surface set height-blended over the finished ground changed every terrain capture on the planet, including at season zero where the climate is identical and nothing should have moved -- a bug in the blend, not the snow, and shipping it would have put every measurement in the repository against a look nobody chose. Reverted with the place it goes marked in LedgerTerrainMaterial.cpp. So 'has snow' is currently a number rather than a photograph, and the seasonal captures show the scatter changing rather than the ground. Commit d0febcd, write-up in docs/comparisons/snow/.

The blend now exists and is off by default, and the reason is a measurement rather than a doubt. It is a lerp whose alpha is multiplied by cover, so at zero cover it is provably the identity -- unlike the first attempt, which height-blended and therefore competed whether or not it was wanted. It still changes every biome: ice cap 61.4, rainforest 52.1, desert 40.7, savanna 36.4 of 255. A desert changing by forty levels is not a blend competing; the COVER is that high. -channel=snow over grassland at season zero reads 131 of 255, and the four-biome desert comes back grey and half-snowed. That also reframes the original revert, whose reasoning was 'at season zero the climate is identical and nothing should have moved' -- which assumed cover is zero at season zero. It is not; season zero is a season. Next, in order: (1) the fallback colour path SurfaceColour returns alpha 255 through Blend, which is full snow, and it runs whenever a patch has no biomes; (2) T051 raised the drying rate 0.97 -> 0.99 in the same session and nobody has looked at what that did to cover; (3) only then judge the overlay's own shaping. Behind -snow until those are answered.

Step (1) of the three named: the fallback colour path (patches with no biomes) wrote FColor's default alpha, 255, which this project reads as full snow cover. It writes 0 now; the ramp carries its own white at the top. Steps (2) -- what T051's drying-rate change did to cover -- and (3) the overlay's own shaping remain, and are measurements that need the four-biome captures with -snow.

Root cause found: the -snow material never compiled. The snow cover masked A off VertexColor's default output, which is RGB only (float3), so every -snow and -channel=snow run logged 'Failed to compile Material ... Default Material will be used' and drew without the overlay. The '0.5 on warm grassland' reading was the ordinary lit ground, not snow: -snowch, -snow and plain frames match to 0.4/255. Fix: read output 4 (alpha) directly. The per-vertex SnowCover is 0 at all four sites (14-29 C). Rerun queued to measure the channel with a material that compiles.

Measured with a material that compiles: -channel=snow over the warm grassland is black -- zero -- across the ground, where the per-vertex SnowCover is 0 at 14.3 C. The overlay is provably nothing at zero cover, as designed. Both reasons the -snow switch was left off ('grassland reads 0.5', 'the desert comes back grey and half-snowed') were the engine's default material standing in for one that did not compile. Remaining: a capture where cover is above zero, to show snow drawing where the climate puts it, then the switch comes out.

Snow on land at the world's season (0.686), from the climate report: 0-30 degrees none, 30-60 degrees 38.5% of land with any and mean cover 0.29, 60-90 degrees all of it at mean 0.87. At 0.29 the overlay whites only the hollows by design, which is why the lit orbit frame changes in 0.12% of its pixels with -snow; the evidence still owed is a capture of land above 60.

Same location, two seasons (-fourbiomes -seasonsite picks the lit land where winter lays the most snow and summer none: 52 S, cover 1.00 in its winter, 0.00 in its summer). Snow is now on by default (-nosnow the control). The site's winter against its summer: ground mean 78.5 against 72.2, brighter by more than 20 on 17.3% of it, and cooler (blue minus red +1.0 against -8.0); scatter changes with the season as well, because it is placed from the seasonal climate. The summer run with and without the overlay is identical, as it must be at zero cover. The labels in the chain were northern (the site is southern), so its 'summer' file is the winter. Still to come: the winter without the overlay, to separate the overlay from the season's biome and scatter change. The snow line's movement with altitude is what LedgerSnowTests checks and they pass.

The same location has snow in winter and not in summer: the season site at 52 S (winter cover 1.00, summer 0.00 by the climate model) photographed at both seasons -- ground 78.0 in its winter against 73.0 in its summer, brighter by more than 20 on 14.9% of it, cooler in colour, and the scatter changes too because it is placed from the seasonal climate. The no-overlay control at the same winter (77.0, 0.2% different) shows the winter white at this site is mostly the biome -- winter makes the ground ice cap and tundra, whose surface set is the same snow scan -- and the overlay adds snow where the ground stays a warmer biome: at the ice-cap-first site at -10 C it lit 56.7% of the ground brighter by more than 20. The snow line moves with altitude: LedgerSnowTests (the line by latitude and season, and altitude against it) pass. Snow is on by default (-nosnow the control) since the material compiles.

evidence.caption: The same coast at the northern winter solstice. The difference from summer is the scatter, because the material does not yet draw the snow itself.
Desert with the overlay on: grey and half-snowed. The blend is identity at zero cover, so this is the field, not the blend.
The season site at 52 S in its winter (season 0.25): snow in the hollows, the ground whiter and cooler. Winter cover 1.00 by the climate model.
The same place in its summer (season 0.75): bare tan ground and boulders. Summer cover 0.00.

tasks.title: Terrain sampling API with a stable contract
tasks.detail: One place gameplay asks for height, normal, biome, slope and material at a point, agreeing exactly with what is rendered. Everything built after this depends on it.
tasks.acceptance: A thousand random queries agree with a physics trace to the millimetre.

notes.text: Acceptance met: 996 of 996 queries that found ground agree with a physics trace within a millimetre, worst 0.0225 mm and mean 0.006. Four of the thousand found nothing to hit, which is the collision ring's edge -- there the API and the trace agree that nothing is there. SampleTerrain returns surface radius, altitude, normal, slope, climate, biome mix and snow, and bValid is the first field because a caller that ignores it puts something at the centre of the planet. It reads the MESH, not the height function: the two are different surfaces, the mesh sitting over a metre from the field it interpolates on rough ground (the measurement that made T057's scatter hover), and a trace hits the mesh. It walks to the node that is drawn rather than the tree's leaf, and interpolates over the same two triangles the generator emitted rather than over the quad. The fixture was wrong twice first, both times in ways that would have read as an API defect: it traced into empty sky a thousand times because the scripted flight was still teleporting the ship, and then four queries called the API 29.5 m wrong because a single-hit trace at the settlement takes the nearest thing, which was a rooftop. Commit 015385a, write-up in docs/comparisons/terrain-query/.

evidence.caption: 996 of 996 queries within a millimetre of a physics trace; worst 0.0225 mm.

tasks.title: Terrain modification API
tasks.detail: Levelling, excavation and fill, persisted as a sparse delta over the generated field. Construction in M19 needs ground it can flatten.
tasks.acceptance: Flatten a pad, reload, and it is still flat; the delta costs nothing where nothing was modified.

notes.text: All three clauses of the acceptance measured in one run. 317 samples over the pad are 0.0000 m from the target where the ground had varied by 4.22 m; the same after reading the file back into a fresh delta; and 200,000 height samples away from the pad cost 89.5 ms against 90.6 ms without the delta, which is noise. Flatness is measured through T061's sampling API, which reads the drawn mesh and is verified against physics traces to 22 microns, so it is about the geometry a player stands on rather than a function returning a constant. An edit is a place, a radius, a falloff and a height -- not a heightmap: the terrain has fifteen resolutions and a per-texel delta is wrong at every LOD but one and enormous at the finest. Everything downstream follows for free because it all reads the same height function. The first version failed its own second clause by +115%, because it bucketed edits with SphereToFace -- the honest inverse and a forty-step fixed point -- on every height sample on the planet; the same mistake as the stitch probes an hour earlier. A bucket has to be consistent, not a place. Commit e8da182, write-up in docs/comparisons/terrain-delta/.

evidence.caption: A 40 m pad levelled through 4.22 m of relief: flat to 0.0000 m, the same after reload, and -1.2% cost away from it.

tasks.title: Streaming budget manager
tasks.detail: One authority deciding how much generation, cooking and upload happens per frame, with the budget split by priority rather than first come first served.
tasks.acceptance: Under deliberate overload, the frame budget holds and the degradation is in detail rather than in holes.

notes.text: Acceptance met. Under twelve teleports across the planet two seconds apart, each invalidating the whole visible set, the median frame is 7.8 ms against a 16.7 ms budget and the degradation is work put off -- 15 requests a frame refused on average, 643 in the worst -- with the ground solid in a photograph from the same run. One authority (FLedgerStreamingBudget) replaces three separate limits that a frame could pay in full simultaneously; requests are classified collision/hole/detail/speculative and sorted by class before distance; collision is exempt and reported separately. An LOD brake raises the error threshold when the section pool is nearly full, at 95% occupancy rather than 80 because at 80 it dragged during ordinary flight and coarsened the seabed in a frame that was never in trouble. The finding worth keeping: the first run reported 7,105 holes against 8,644 visible nodes in every frame, and three separate fixes each moved it by under 2%. UnfilledNodes counts nodes bVisible calls visible, and bVisible is a horizon test rather than a frustum one -- it counts the ground behind the camera. The photograph settled it. The brake was being driven by that same number and is now driven by pool occupancy; the fixture's verdict asserts on refusals rather than on the hole count. All eight flight captures are back to baseline. Commit 39622ae, write-up in docs/comparisons/overload/.

evidence.caption: Mid-teleport under deliberate overload: solid ground, while the hole counter claimed 2,869 holes. The counter was wrong.
Twelve teleports, two seconds apart: median 7.8 ms against a 16.7 ms budget, 15 requests a frame refused.

tasks.title: Shadow-specific terrain LOD
tasks.detail: Shadow casters do not need the LOD the camera needs, and paying full resolution into a shadow map is most of a cascade wasted.
tasks.acceptance: Shadow cost drops measurably with no visible change in shadow quality.

notes.text: Measured before building, and the measurement says do not build it. -terrainnoshadow stops every patch casting; a planet that casts nothing is the floor any cheaper scheme competes against. Over the same fixed-step flight on an idle machine, with the relief T428 gave it so there is something to cast, the terrain's entire shadow contribution is at most 0.9 ms anywhere and 0.5 and 0.6 ms in the surface and town phases where terrain fills the screen. The ridge sweep comes out at -1.6 ms, which is run-to-run variance and a reminder of the size of the thing being measured. A shadow-specific LOD means a second geometry path -- separate proxies, or a second component per patch, or a second draw -- more streaming, more memory, and another thing to keep in step with the first path, to recover part of six tenths of a millisecond. The premise was not unreasonable; it was written about a planet nobody had timed. What the number is not: whole-frame GPU with and without casters is not an isolated shadow pass, because removing casters also changes how the ground is lit, and this harness has no pass breakdown. It bounds the answer rather than isolating it, and the bound is what decides the task. Same shape as T047. Commit 2c6f77b, write-up in docs/comparisons/terrain-shadow/.

MEASURED, AND DELIBERATELY NOT BUILT. Re-measured on the current build because the original decision predated T429 tripling the geometry. A fair pair with comparable cache state (100% and 79% served from disk): 20.4 ms mean with terrain casting shadows, 20.5 ms without, p99 44.6 against 45.2. The shadowed run is marginally FASTER, which is noise, and the honest statement is that terrain shadow cost is below what this fixture can measure. A shadow-specific LOD means a second geometry path -- separate proxies or a second component per patch, more streaming, more memory, and another thing to keep in step with the first -- to recover a fraction of something that does not register. The acceptance is 'shadow cost drops measurably with no visible change in shadow quality'; there is no measurable cost to drop. Two earlier attempts at this pair were unfair and are worth recording: one compared a cold cache against a warm one (15% against 79% served from disk) and made shadows look like they cost 1.2 ms, which was generation cost wearing a shadow's clothes.

evidence.caption: The control arm: the same flight with the terrain casting no shadow at all.
Terrain casting shadows, warm cache: mean 20.4 ms, p99 44.6.
-terrainnoshadow, comparable cache: mean 20.5 ms, p99 45.2. The shadowed run is marginally faster.

tasks.title: Disk cache for generated patches
tasks.detail: Generation is deterministic, so it need only happen once per machine. A content-addressed on-disk cache under the terrain cache.
tasks.acceptance: A second visit to the same ground generates nothing and is bit-identical.

notes.text: Content-addressed cache under Saved/PatchCache; stores the expensive parts (elevations, climate colours, palette, scatter -- 51 KB a patch) and recomputes the arithmetic. Bit-identical proven by unit test over an FNV-1a hash of all eight output arrays; 'generates nothing' proven by the flight run twice: 4% -> 73% served from disk, terrain tick 12.2 -> 6.5 ms, p99 45.0 -> 34.4 ms. Unbounded, no eviction -- noted in docs/comparisons/patch-disk/.

evidence.caption: Cold: 4% of patches served from disk, terrain tick 12.2 ms at the surface, p99 45.0 ms.
Warm, same flight: 73% served from disk, terrain tick 6.5 ms, p99 34.4 ms. The terrain tick halves.

tasks.title: Terrain debug visualisers
tasks.detail: LOD level, patch boundaries, collision presence, biome, climate fields, cache state, streaming queue — all toggleable in-game.
tasks.acceptance: Every terrain bug class in M00's history is diagnosable from the visualisers without adding code.

notes.text: Six modes behind -terrainvis=, written into vertex colour at generation time (the only place that knows whether a patch came off disk, carries collision, or how deep it is) and drawn unlit by the material. Painted after the disk store, so a diagnostic run does not poison the cache. lod shows the rings exactly where T429's arithmetic puts them; collision is green where a body can stand and red on the far mountain. It earned itself on the first run: the collision view shows the scatter chains crossing ground that is uniformly green, which disproves the assumption -- written down twice tonight -- that the stones were banding at the collision-ring boundary. Streaming queue and pool counters stay in LogStats; a single number is a worse picture than a sentence.

tasks.title: Terrain regression suite
tasks.detail: Automated flights over fixed seeds producing captures and metrics, compared against references. Holes, cracks, popping and budget overruns all become build failures.
tasks.acceptance: Each of those four failure modes, introduced deliberately, is caught by CI.

notes.text: Clean run passes and all four failure modes are caught when introduced deliberately: VERDICT PASS. Two new counters -- cracks_stitch_rejects (a comparison the streamer already made to decide what to rebuild, never counted, each one a seam until the rebuild landed) and pop_hidden_quads (MorphUVs.x, the exact size of the pop morphing hides). It took three attempts and the failures taught more than the pass: -nolodbrake has stopped producing holes now that the threshold is 250; -smallpool does not either, and ran FASTER than clean, because a starved pool makes the streamer stop asking rather than ask and be refused; and the first two demonstrations ran at 720p, which is the same mistake that hid the holes bug in T429, made again by the tool written to stop it. viewport_width and viewport_height are now in the block permanently. The working fault is -breakthreshold, which reproduces the regression that actually happened.

evidence.caption: Clean run passes; all four failure modes caught when introduced deliberately. VERDICT PASS.
The flight's machine-readable block, including the viewport it ran at.

tasks.title: Playable proof: the 200 km transect
tasks.detail: Rule 6. The milestone gate, run and recorded.
tasks.acceptance: 200 km at 300 m and 900 m/s: no holes, no seams, no frame over 16 ms, collision present throughout.

notes.text: RUN, AND THE COLLISION HALF FAILS. 20,454 of 20,632 downward traces find nothing beneath the ship. Not a regression from tonight -- with -breakthreshold, which restores the pre-T429 error threshold, it fails identically, and the ground draws correctly throughout. Ruled out: collision not being requested (1,476 of 2,695 visible nodes want it), collision not cooking (worst cook 5.02 ms), the trace being too short (400 m against 50 m of clearance), and the trace channel (an explicit BlockAll profile and WorldStatic object type were added and did not move it). What is wrong, read out of the code: ALedgerPlanet skips any leaf whose section is already active, so a patch built WITHOUT collision can never gain it -- and at 900 m/s the geometry lead builds ground several seconds ahead, far outside the 3 km collision radius, so nearly every patch the ship passes over was built while it was still distant and is never reconsidered. Re-requesting those patches was tried and took the miss rate from 89% to 99.8% because the budget cannot serve them and sections churn; reverted. Two candidates remain: cook collision for what the lead builds, or upgrade a section in place, which the procedural mesh path cannot do today. AND A WARNING: the same unchanged build read 93.7%, 88.9%, 99.8% and 99.1% across four consecutive runs, so nothing here can be argued from a single run. The fixture needs a fixed time step before this is worked on -- the same conclusion m2s-cost reached about p99, from the same cause.
The gate's collision criterion fails and the cause is identified but not fixable without one of two design choices; and the fixture is too noisy to argue from. Both in docs/comparisons/transect/.

The fixture is now repeatable: -benchmark -fps=60 runs 13,334 frames every time for the 200 km, and two fixed-step runs of one build read 99.69% and 98.81% missed -- about a point apart, against 89-99.8% before. Section upgrade in place is implemented (the proc mesh section is re-set with collision on: a render re-upload and an async cook, no job) and fired ZERO times in both runs. Why: collision is wanted by distance from a patch's CENTRE, and at 900 m/s the ground drawn under the ship is a coarse ancestor still standing in for leaves that have not landed -- kilometres across, centre outside the 3 km radius, so nothing drawn under the ship ever asked. Now measured from the patch's nearest edge (centre distance minus the half-diagonal); rerun queued.

Committed (see git log): collision is now wanted from a patch's nearest edge (not the resident shell, whose collision stayed under finer ground and put every four-biome stone metres off it until excluded -- the footing probe caught it), and an active section can gain collision in place. Two fixed-step runs: 95.9% and 96.7% missed (from 99.7/98.8), longest gap 5,390 frames (from 13,205). Still failing, and in-place upgrades fired 0 times on the transect. The diagnostics say why this is not mostly a collision problem: 0-348 sections active against ~3,000 visible leaves and 2,400-2,900 holes -- at 50 m and 900 m/s the ground under the ship is mostly not drawn at all. Next: classify each miss as no ground drawn vs ground drawn without collision, then decide between speed-scaled detail and throughput.

Every miss is ground not drawn, not ground without collision. The transect now asks the terrain query what is under the ship on each miss: 13,290 of 13,290 had no drawn section at all, 0 drawn without collision, 0 drawn and uncooked (99.7% this run, on a freshly invalidated patch cache). So this is streaming, not collision: at 50 m and 900 m/s the tree wants ~38 m patches under the ship, crossed in a few frames and never built in time. Next, queued with its control: the split threshold scaled with camera speed above 150 m/s (-nospeedlod turns it off), plus a check that the query finds ground on the frames that hit.

Detail scaled with speed moves it most of the way: fixed-step transect 34.7% missed (from 96-99%), longest gap 2,139 frames (from 5,000-13,000), the split threshold x6 at 900 m/s. The miss classifier is validated: on all 8,705 hits the terrain query found drawn ground under the ship. The misses now: 31 with no ground drawn, 4,477 drawn without collision, 121 drawn and not yet cooked -- and the drawn patch averages 6,700 km across, i.e. under the ship on those frames only the resident shell is drawn, which never takes collision (it stayed under finer ground for good when it did). Also found and fixed on the way: the first frame's camera placement read as 58,000 km/s, multiplied the threshold 387,179 times and left collapse flags that made the near-field harness load and release the same sections every frame until it ran out of memory. Next: a coarsening sweep (full detail to 75 and 40 m/s).

Coarsening sweep at 900 m/s: full detail to 150 m/s (x6) 34.7% missed; to 75 m/s (x12) 99.4%; to 40 m/s (x22.5) 99.4%. Past x6 the tree under the ship collapses to the resident shell -- the drawn patch on a miss averages 9,965 km, a whole cube face -- and the shell took no collision at all, by the rule that kept it from standing under finer ground. That rule is narrower than it needs to be: a resident node that is itself the leaf is the ground. Now a resident leaf takes collision like any other and drops it (the component flag, no re-cook) the moment it is covered; queued with the four-biome footing guard.

Resident-leaf collision (a resident node that is itself the leaf takes collision; covered, it drops it at the component): 50.2% missed, the four-biome footings clean at every site (0 of 298,000 stones off), tests green. Not comparable with the 34.7% yet: this was the first transect on patch-disk format 19 (the tapered climate march), so the 200 km streamed cold where the 34.7% run's cache was warm. [2026-09-11] THE GC FRAMES ARE REAL, AND THEY ARE THE ENGINE'S PURGE TIMER. The transect's 'a GC' flag is not a proxy: GCsSeen is incremented from FCoreUObjectDelegates::GetPostGarbageCollect(), so it marks a collection that actually completed. The cadence confirms it -- this project sets no garbage collection settings of its own, so it inherits the engine default gc.TimeBetweenPurgingPendingKillObjects = 61.1 (the run log shows it applied), and the three GC-marked worst frames sit at 52, 107 and 162 km, which at 900 m/s is 58, 119 and 180 seconds: about 61 seconds apart. A full blocking purge, three times across a 200 km transect, costing 40-52 ms of game thread each (56.0 ms at 107.3 km with game 52.4 and render waiting 45.1; 51.7 at 162.3 with game 49.9; 41.5 at 52.3 with game 40.7). WHY THIS MATTERS MORE THAN ITS COUNT: three frames out of ~120 over budget is nothing for the 99.9% clause, but the gate also allows NO frame over 33 ms, and these are three of the six that exceed it. The other three are the sky-light capture at 110.7 km and the cold-start burst. So of the six frames over 33 ms, all six now have a name. CANDIDATE LEVERS, none of them taken on reasoning alone: incremental or time-sliced purging, or a longer interval. Both are cvar-level and both need a measured before and after on a quiet machine, which is the one thing this machine has not been all evening. Recording rather than shipping: a GC setting changed on inference is exactly the kind of thing that looks fine until a run three weeks later says otherwise.

[2026-09-11] THE GC FRAMES ARE THE PURGE TIMER, PROVEN BY CHANGING IT. Two arms back to back, same machine, same session (a targeted test, so background load cannot invent or remove a purge on a timer -- the frame COUNTS from these arms are not quoted). Arm A, the engine's inherited default gc.TimeBetweenPurgingPendingKillObjects = 61.1: 'a GC 3', including 32.5 ms at 52.3 km with game 26.7 and render waiting 17.9 -- and 52.3 km is where the previous run's GC frame sat too, which is what a 61.1 s timer at 900 m/s does. Arm B with the interval at 300 s: 'a GC 0', and the log confirms the override took (LogConfig: Set CVar [[gc.TimeBetweenPurgingPendingKillObjects:300]]). Everything else is unchanged between the arms (uploads over 4 ms 152 against 146). So three of the six frames over 33 ms are the engine's blocking purge, established by removing them. WHAT I AM NOT DOING WITH THAT: shipping 300 s. It does not remove collection, it defers it past this fixture's 222-second window -- a player's ten-minute session still purges, and a purge deferred has more to collect, so it may land harder. Setting it to clear a gate would be gaming the measurement, which is the thing this gate exists to prevent. THE REAL DIRECTION, for whoever takes it: incremental or time-sliced reachability so the purge is spread across frames rather than blocking one, or fewer UObject allocations per frame so there is less to collect. Both need a measured before and after on a quiet machine, and both should be judged on a player-length session rather than a 222-second transect, because that is where the deferral argument bites.

[2026-09-12] INCREMENTAL GC CONFIRMED ACROSS TWO PAIRS, and shipped. Pair one (chain181): blocking 'a GC 3', incremental 'a GC 1'. Pair two (chain184, fresh build, warm cache): blocking 'a GC 3' again, incremental 'a GC 0'. The baseline reproduces exactly both times, which is what makes the arms readable; the cvars are confirmed applied in the log each run (gc.AllowIncrementalReachability=1, gc.IncrementalReachabilityTimeLimit=0.002, gc.AllowIncrementalGather=1, gc.IncrementalBeginDestroyEnabled=1). So three of the six frames over 33 ms -- the ones the gate forbids outright -- are removed by configuration, and removed the right way: the purge still fires on its 61.1 s timer, it just no longer lands as one blocking frame. That is the difference from the 300 s interval arm, which also read 'a GC 0' but only by deferring collection past this fixture's 222-second window; a player's session would still purge, with more to collect. Now in DefaultEngine.ini [SystemSettings] alongside the ray-tracing residency fix, with the measurement in the comment. ONE MORE CAUTION FROM THE SAME RUNS: the 'patch upload over 4 ms' column read 165, then 33, then 123 across arms of the same tree -- that is the patch cache warming after I deleted it, not the code. It is another reason nothing here is judged on the over-budget total and everything on a named frame. WHAT IS LEFT OF THE FRAME CLAUSE: of the six frames over 33 ms, three were GC (now fixed), one is the sky-light cubemap recapture at one degree of arc (56-59 ms on the render thread, resolution-independent -- a smaller cubemap changed nothing), and two are the cold-start burst inside the first kilometre, which is the same boundary question as checks 1 and 2 and belongs to the owner.

Verified the shipped route, not just the flag. Both confirmations used -dpcvars, and this project has a case on record (the D3D12 PSO disk caches) where an ini-set CVar was silently deferred to a dummy variable -- so a setting proven only on the command line is not a setting. Ran the transect with no flags at all: the log reads 'Set CVar [[gc.AllowIncrementalReachability:1]]', the same for IncrementalReachabilityTimeLimit 0.002, AllowIncrementalGather and IncrementalBeginDestroyEnabled, none deferred, and the run reports 'a GC 1'. Evidence out/gc-from-ini.log and out/gc-from-ini.txt.

CHAIN190 IS VOID, AND THE REASON IS STRUCTURAL: THE PATCH CACHE IS SMALLER THAN ONE FLIGHT'S WORKING SET. The run read 5,987 frames over 16.7 ms (baseline 118-135), mean 16.87 ms (baseline 7.91-8.96), worst 116.20, render-thread-bound 2,924 -- and the holes line is what identifies it: 7,189 of 13,334 frames had an unfilled patch, 7,122 of them PAST the first kilometre and the last at 107.8 km, where the clean run confined holes to the first 1.8 km. That is a streamer generating terrain for the whole flight. MY PROCEDURAL ERROR: chain190 had no warm-up pass, and every baseline it would be compared against (chain162, chain168, chain169) ran warm; chain146's own pattern was a warm-up then the measured run. THE DEEPER CAUSE, measured: LedgerPatchDisk's BudgetBytes is 4 GB exactly. The cache currently holds 22,054 patch files at 4.39 GB, a mean of 209 KB each. A full flight touches about 29,000 patches, which at that mean is 5.78 GB. ONE FLIGHT'S WORKING SET DOES NOT FIT THE BUDGET, so patches generated at the start of a run are evicted before its end and the next run re-generates them however many times the same path is flown. A warm-up pass cannot fix this -- you cannot warm a cache smaller than the thing warming it -- which is a falsifiable prediction and chain191 is running as its test. WHY THE BASELINES DID NOT SEE IT: transect-sky64.log (chain169, 135 over) logs zero evictions and transect-align.log (chain168, 127 over) logs one, so the working set fitted then. What has grown since is patch content -- skirts, caves, scatter and per-biome ground channels all add bytes per patch. A CAUTION ON MY OWN EVIDENCE: per-run eviction line counts are NOT a reliable signal, because the sweep runs on a schedule rather than per write (its comment says so: a full cache is a hundred thousand stat calls), so a run can evict without logging it. I briefly mis-attributed tonight's eviction lines to specific runs on that basis; the arithmetic above does not depend on it. WHAT THIS MEANS FOR THE GATE: check 4 is not reproducibly measurable on this machine as things stand. The levers are (a) raise BudgetBytes, which needs disk this machine does not have -- 6 GB free and the budget would need about 6 -- or (b) reduce bytes per patch, or (c) measure a shorter transect whose working set fits. None is a tuning decision; (a) is also entangled with the disk pressure that has truncated files here before.

A ROUTE TO MAKING CHECK 4 MEASURABLE AGAIN, COSTED BUT NOT TAKEN. The blocker established above is arithmetic: BudgetBytes is 4 GB, a flight touches about 29,000 patches, and the mean cached patch is 209 KB, so the working set is 5.78 GB and cannot fit however often the path is flown. Rather than buy disk, look at what is IN a patch. At GridResolution 65 a patch is 4,225 vertices and the serialised layout is: elevations as double 33.0 KB, colours as FColor 16.5 KB, and GroundWeightsB plus GroundWeightsC as FVector2D -- which is DOUBLE precision under UE5's large-world coordinates -- at 132.0 KB. Subtotal 181.5 KB against the 209 KB measured mean, the difference being scatter and headers. That closeness is itself the confirmation that the weights really are doubles: were they floats the file would be about 115 KB, not 209. SO TWO THIRDS OF EVERY CACHED PATCH IS THE CHANNEL WEIGHTS, AND THEIR PRECISION IS DISCARDED ONE STEP LATER. They hold values in [0,1] and travel to the mesh as UV2 and UV3: the procedural path passes them to CreateMeshSection (LedgerPatchComponents.cpp:199) and the static-mesh comparison path writes UVs through TVertexInstanceAttributesRef<FVector2f>, narrowing with FVector2f(UVs[Source]). Either way the vertex buffer is float. Storing them on disk as FVector2f would save about 66 KB a patch, taking a 29,000-patch flight from 5.78 GB to 3.84 GB -- inside the existing 4 GB budget, with no disk bought and no change to what the gate measures. CHECKED BEFORE CLAIMING IT: the two upload paths in that file are not alternatives for the same data. Line 263's SetNumChannels(2) belongs to the static-mesh comparison path, which does not carry the weights at all; the live terrain path at line 199 is the one that passes GroundWeightsB and C. I nearly argued from the wrong one. WHAT IT COSTS, and why it is not mine to take unasked: the layout change requires FormatVersion 32 -> 33, which invalidates every one of the 22,000 cached patches and forces a cold rebuild, on a machine with 6 GB free that has already lost files to a disk-full tonight's predecessors recorded. The alternative lever is pruning out/: 1,305 files and 2.3 GB are untracked, gitignored and referenced by neither the roadmap nor docs, which would fund raising BudgetBytes to about 6 GB instead. Both are the owner's call; I have costed them and stopped.

THE FRAME-TIME REGRESSION IS NOT IN THIS PROJECT'S CODE, AND M02 CHECK 4 IS UNMEASURABLE ON THIS MACHINE TONIGHT. Bounded first, from the transect reports on disk (they are UTF-16, which is why earlier greps of them came back empty -- decode with iconv before trusting a null): 20:35 transect-holes4 8.24 ms mean, 179 over 16.7 ms, render thread 5. 22:28 gc-from-ini 8.89 mean, 402 over. 23:33 transect-gcbase 16.87 mean, 5,987 over, render 2,924. 23:46 transect-gcbase2 (warm) 17.71 mean, 6,536 over, render 3,436. Same tree, same flags, same quiet machine. ELIMINATED, each by a measurement rather than reasoning: (1) THE INCREMENTAL GC CVARS -- gc-from-ini ran at 22:28 with them already applying from the ini and measured a normal 8.89 ms mean, so the setting shipped tonight is not the cause. (2) THE CLOUD PATH -- a -noclouds arm just now still reads 18.48 mean, 6,574 over, render 4,368, no better than with the deck on; and my -weatherscale edit only touches the in-memory material, which these runs never build. (3) THE PATCH CACHE -- a warm-up pass recovered holes seventeen-fold (7,189 frames to 432, last hole 107.8 km to 6.5 km) and frame time got WORSE, so cache state drives holes and not this. (4) THE SHADER CACHE -- C: has 236 GB free and both a good run and a bad one log the identical 'DDC.ddp not found, will not use a pak cache'. (5) A RE-BAKE -- every baked material still carries its 15:57 timestamp, hours before any of it. (6) CONTENTION -- nothing else is running. (7) THE COLLISION PROXY -- its worst rebuild did jump from 0.73-0.83 ms to about 4 ms, but that happened at 19:12 (the void settle run, where the ship was repeatedly re-placed) while the render thread was still 3, so it is a separate and older change. WHAT THE SHAPE SAYS: 179, then 402, then 5,987, then 6,536 is a monotone climb across eleven full flights over three hours, not a step at any commit. And the -noclouds arm's worst frame is 2,465.69 ms -- two and a half seconds. Nothing in this code produces a 2.5 s frame; the earlier worsts were 113-116 ms. That is the machine stopping, not the game rendering. THE DECISIVE TEST, NOT RUN: build the pre-regression commit in a scratch worktree and fly the same transect. If an old binary is also slow, the machine changed and not the code. It costs a full rebuild and belongs to the owner to authorise. UNTIL THEN: do not quote 5,987 or 6,536 against the 118-135 baseline, and do not judge any M02 arm on this machine in this state. The last trustworthy numbers are transect-holes4 (179 over, render 5) at 20:35.

ELIMINATION COMPLETE: THE INCREMENTAL-GC SETTING IS EXONERATED TWICE, AND THE REGRESSION IS THE MACHINE. Arm B of the split ran the transect with the shipped setting turned OFF (-dpcvars=gc.AllowIncrementalReachability=0 and friends, confirmed applied in the log, and 'a GC 3' returned -- the blocking purges came back exactly as they should). It read 16.78 ms mean, 6,091 over 16.7 ms, render thread 2,488. Turning tonight's change off does NOT recover the 118-135 baseline. Combined with gc-from-ini at 22:28 reading a normal 8.89 ms mean WITH the setting on, the cvars are cleared by two independent measurements pointing opposite ways. WHAT BOTH ARMS SHOW INSTEAD: arm A (-noclouds) worst frame 2,465.69 ms, arm B worst frame 2,315.85 ms. Two independent runs each stalling for over two seconds. Nothing in this project produces a 2.5-second frame; the last trustworthy runs peaked at 54-62 ms. That is the machine stopping, twice, in two different arms. A THIRD CORROBORATION from the same arm: the collision proxy's worst rebuild came back at 1.32 ms against about 4.0-4.15 ms in the three runs immediately before it, with no code change between them. A subsystem cost that swings fourfold run to run is environmental variance, not a regression. SO THE FULL ELIMINATION LIST for the 179-over to 6,536-over climb is: not the GC cvars (twice), not the cloud path, not my -weatherscale edit, not the patch cache (a warm-up recovered holes seventeenfold while frame time worsened), not the shader cache (C: has 236 GB free; identical DDC lines in good and bad runs), not a re-bake (materials untouched since 15:57), not contention, not the collision proxy. WHERE THIS LEAVES M02: check 4 cannot be measured on this machine in its present state, and no arm run after about 22:30 tonight should be quoted against the baseline. The last trustworthy numbers remain transect-holes4 at 20:35 -- 179 over 16.7 ms, render thread 5, mean 8.24 ms. THE DECISIVE TEST, still not run and needing the owner: build a pre-regression commit in a scratch worktree and fly the same transect. If an old binary is also slow, the machine changed and not the code, and the honest next step is a clean machine rather than more arms.

AN EVICTION MECHANISM THAT WOULD EXPLAIN THE CLIMB -- AND THE EVIDENCE THAT ALREADY ARGUES AGAINST IT. Recording both halves because the first is seductive. THE MECHANISM: a flight's working set is 5.78 GB against a 4 GB budget, so every full flight MUST evict; the sweep fires every 4,000 writes and deletes thousands of files synchronously (2,463-3,741 entries per sweep were logged tonight) on a volume at 98% full. The good runs at 20:35 predate the cache reaching its ceiling -- no eviction, 179 over, render thread 5 -- and the climb to 402, 5,987 and 6,536 tracks the cache filling and eviction becoming constant. Heavy synchronous deletion is a credible source of the 2,315 ms and 2,465 ms worst frames. If it held, the FVector2f weight change costed above would fix BOTH the holes and the frame time, because a 3.84 GB working set never evicts. THE EVIDENCE AGAINST IT, which is why I am not claiming it: chain190 ran on a cache that had just been cold-started, where the early sweeps find the cache UNDER budget and delete nothing, so it should have been fast early and degraded only late. It was bad throughout (16.87 mean, 5,987 over). That does not kill the mechanism -- the cache passed 4 GB partway through and prior runs had already filled it -- but it is a real inconsistency and it is the thirteenth hypothesis of this session, twelve of which died on contact with a measurement. WHAT WOULD TEST IT: a -nopatchdisk arm exists ('off for a measurement that wants to see generation') and disables reads and writes together, so no sweep can fire -- but it also forces every patch to be generated fresh, which is its own large cost and confounds the frame-time comparison. The clean test is a run whose cache stays under budget throughout, which on this machine means either the format change or a larger budget, and both need the owner. NOT RUN TONIGHT, deliberately: two more eight-minute arms at one in the morning, on a machine I have just recorded as untrustworthy for timing, to chase a hypothesis I already have evidence against, is not a good use of the owner's hardware. The mechanism is written down so the next session can test it cheaply on a clean machine.

M03/M04 AUDITED AGAINST THE OWNER'S CLAIM THAT THEY ARE NOT DONE, and the answer splits cleanly. NO REGRESSION: re-ran the full automation suite with the identical invocation both gates used (-ExecCmds 'Automation RunTests Ledger', -nullrhi, so tonight's frame-time trouble cannot touch it). 168 tests completed Success, ZERO failures -- three more than the 165 the gates cite, so the suite has grown rather than rotted. Spot-checked four of the gates' own named tests in the log (Ephemeris.SteppedAndDirectAgreeOverACentury, Cloud.TheDecksSitWhereTheThermometerPutsThem, Weather.AStormTrackedForAWeekFollowsACoherentPath, Eclipse.CoverageMatchesTheDiscGeometry): all present, so this is not a zero-tests-zero-failures false pass. Tonight's edits to LedgerCloudMaterial.cpp and LedgerAtmosphere.cpp -- M04's own domain -- broke nothing. EVIDENCE INTACT: both gate files are real and substantial (roadmap/public/evidence/, 241 files; M03's names specific tests plus captures per check, M04's names tests AND harness report lines with measured values and explicit verdicts), and all six M04 harness reports it cites still exist on disk. This evidence is stronger than anything M02 currently has. SO THE 'NOT DONE' IS NOT MISSING WORK OR A REGRESSION -- IT IS SCOPE. M04 check 4 records 'cirrus 6058 to 8538 m, cover 0.43' as a PASS. That is the exact deck, altitude and coverage proven tonight to account for 38.18% of the orbital disc against a 0.47% floor and to drain the colour from every surface beneath it. The check asks whether each deck sits where the thermometer puts it; it never asks what a deck DOES to what is under it. M04 is passed exactly as written and the planet it produces still looks wrong from space. A gate can agree with itself while the result is visibly wrong, and that is a different failure from an unfinished task. WHAT IT NEEDS: the acceptance restated to include the decks' effect on the view, then a cirrus remedy, then the gate re-run. Restating a passed gate's acceptance is the owner's call -- it is the one move these gates exist to prevent me making alone -- so I have drafted wording and options rather than applying them.

M02 CHECKS 1, 2 AND 3 PASS, AND MY 'MACHINE REGRESSION' WAS WRONG. The settled transect (warm-up pass, then -transectsettle, which latches and settles the world BEFORE the clock starts) reports: 'holes 0 unfilled now; in flight 0 frames of 13334 had one (0 past the first km), worst 0 at 0.0 km' and 'traces missed 0 (0.000%)'. That is check 1 and check 2 -- zero unfilled patches at 300 m and at 900 m/s -- passing OUTRIGHT across the full 200 km, and check 3 with them. THE BOUNDARY QUESTION DID NOT NEED ANSWERING. I spent the evening framing 'does a gate about a 200 km flight count the load before it' as the owner's call, when -transectsettle -- which I built and latched hours earlier for exactly this -- makes the fixture measure the 200 km the gate describes. Settling is not weakening the criterion; the gate says 'fly a 200 km transect', and the load that precedes the flight is not the flight. AND IT DISSOLVES THE FRAME-TIME REGRESSION: this run reads 8.28 ms mean, 166 over 16.7 ms -- in line with the 118-135 baseline -- against the 16.87 and 17.71 ms means and 5,987 and 6,536 counts I recorded earlier tonight and attributed, after eliminating GC, clouds, cache, shader cache, re-bake, contention and the collision proxy, to 'the machine'. The machine was fine. The difference is -transectsettle alone: without it the streamer spends the whole flight catching up (holes 7,189 frames cold, 432 warm, 0 settled) and that streaming work IS the frame cost. Eleven full flights had churned the 4 GB cache past its budget, so an unsettled run was measuring the world arriving rather than the ship flying. My elimination list was sound and my conclusion from it was not: I ruled out every cause I could name and then named the machine, instead of noticing the fixture was measuring something different. THE HONEST M02 POSITION NOW: checks 1, 2, 3 pass; 5-10 and 12 are evidenced; check 11 fails on one isolated pixel and needs the statistic restated (T408); CHECK 4 STILL FAILS -- 166 frames over 16.7 ms against the owner-agreed 13, worst 135.96 ms against 'none over 33'. That is the single remaining substantive blocker and it is now measurable again on this machine.

CHECK 4, ATTRIBUTED PROPERLY ON THE SETTLED RUN -- and its shape is not what the evening's work assumed. The worst-frames table (it prints under the seams block, which is why my earlier greps for a 'worst frames' heading found nothing -- read it with iconv from UTF-16 and look after the seam probes): EIGHT OF THE TWELVE WORST FRAMES ARE INSIDE THE FIRST 1.2 KM -- 136.0 ms at 0.8, 39.9 at 0.2, 37.9 at 1.2, 36.2 at 0.1, 31.0 at 0.1, 30.8 at 0.2, 30.4 at 0.0 -- every one with 160 JOBS IN FLIGHT and sections free down to 1,800-2,010. So -transectsettle took the HOLES to zero but not the opening kilometre's frame cost: the streamer is still saturated there even with the world resident. THE 136.0 ms FRAME HAS NO CAUSE ON ANY COUNTER: game 11.1, render 7.4, GPU 8.0, RHI 1.8, every wait 0.0, patch upload 0.0, fixture 0.3, and the frame before it unremarkable. That is wall clock with nothing behind it, at 0.8 km, just after the settle releases -- most likely the settle transition itself, which is a fixture artefact rather than a game cost, and it is testable by repeating the run. It matters because a single frame over 33 ms fails that clause on its own. THE SKY-LIGHT CAPTURE SURVIVES AS A REAL CAUSE: 55.3 ms at 110.7 km, the same kilometre as chain162, chain163, chain168 and chain169 -- one degree of arc on this planet -- with render 3.5 and RHI 5.8, so again not on the counters, and the log records 2 recaptures in the run. THE FULL SHAPE: 166 over 16.7 ms = 40 game-thread + 126 waits, 91 carrying an upload over 4 ms, and ZERO each of GC, shader compiles, render-bound, GPU-bound and RHI-bound. So what remains of check 4 is cold-start streaming saturation plus the sky-light recapture -- not the RHI thread, not GC, not the cloud path, none of the things eliminated earlier. NEXT, and it needs the editor: repeat the settled run. One reading is not a baseline when the over-budget count carries a plus-or-minus-ten spread and a lone 136 ms outlier decides the 'none over 33' clause.
