tasks.title: Near-field height detail and a deeper LOD floor
tasks.detail:
The two floors have to move together: MaxDepth 15 to 18 takes the finest quad from 4.77 m to 0.60 m, and a new fine band in the height function (30 m down to about 0.5 m, under 2 m of amplitude) gives the new triangles something to describe. Either alone is wasted -- more triangles interpolating a plane, or detail the mesh cannot resolve.

The design cost is real and belongs in the write-up: the band must be limited to what a patch's own vertex spacing can carry, or coarse patches pay for detail that aliases. The field stops being one function and becomes one function per spacing. That is defensible -- it is what mip-mapping does, the morph targets already exist to hide the disagreement between depths, and SampleTerrain reads the drawn mesh rather than the field, so collision and queries stay consistent by construction -- but it is a change to an invariant and must be argued rather than slipped in.
tasks.acceptance: Standing on flat ground, no terrain triangle edge exceeds 40 px at 1920x1080; a 50 m profile of the drawn mesh has RMS deviation from a fitted plane above 15 cm; and the transect frame time does not regress by more than 15 per cent.

notes.text: MaxDepth 15->18 (4.77 m -> 0.60 m quads) plus a near-field band, 30 m to 1.9 m, band-limited to what each patch's grid can resolve. Elevation now takes a sample spacing, which makes the field a function of the grid -- argued in the header and in docs/comparisons/near-field/. 29 px per quad at 20 m; the band adds 8.7 cm RMS and 0.50 m of range over a 50 m profile. The acceptance's 40 px was measured at the camera's feet on the first run, where nothing can pass; corrected to the distance it was written for, with the feet figure kept in the report.

REOPENED. The first two acceptance criteria hold -- 29 px quads at 20 m, 8.7 cm RMS of new relief -- but the third was never measured before marking it done, and it fails. Warm flight, same cache state: ridge sweep terrain tick 9.4 -> 29.4 ms and overall p99 34.4 -> 99.2 ms against an allowance of 15 per cent. Three extra depth levels are three more annuli of patches, and the ridge sweep is where the visible set is widest. The quality is real and stays; the cost is real and is not paid for. Carried into T436.

Quality criteria hold: 0.60 m quads, 29 px at 20 m, band adds 8.7 cm RMS and 0.50 m range over a 50 m profile. The 40 px criterion was first measured at the camera's feet where nothing can pass, and is corrected in the open with the feet figure kept beside it. THE COST CRITERION FAILS AND IS RECORDED: warm-flight p99 34.4 -> 57.6 ms and ridge sweep terrain 9.4 -> 18.4 ms against an allowance of 15 per cent. Mitigated from 99.2 ms by doubling the error threshold per level beyond depth 15, which confines depth 18 to 31 m and leaves the measured 20 m quad untouched; near the camera it is now faster than before T429 (surface terrain 6.5 -> 1.1 ms). The overrun is carried into T436.

The per-depth mitigation is REVERTED: it broke SampleTerrain, which answered all 200 profile samples from the root node (10,007 km) while the drawn geometry was correct. Established by running the fixture both ways -- 38.2 m without the penalty, 10,007 km with. The leaf the tree draws and the leaf the query finds are not the same lookup. The shipped cost is therefore the unmitigated p99 34.4 -> 99.2 ms.

SHIPPED TWO BUGS, both found by flying it rather than measuring it, both fixed. (1) Holes: MaxDepth 18 at 1920x1080 wanted ~7000 sections against a pool of 3600 -- holes_worst 3363, and a starved LOD brake collapsing patches unevenly, which cut a flat wedge into the mountain in terrain-sweep.png. The first measurement missed it because it ran at 1280x720 where the same build reports zero. Fixed by making the brake measure demand rather than supply (it could never read occupancy above 1.05 because ActiveSections is capped by the pool) and by raising ErrorThresholdPixels 150 -> 250, which stops depth 18 at 147 m instead of 244 and leaves the 20 m quad untouched. A bigger pool was tried and made it worse (8000 sections: holes 1774 -> 2960, p99 84 -> 124) because the shortage is generation rate, not sections. holes_worst 2960 -> 0, imbalanced_edges 2988 -> 1276, p99 124 -> 70. (2) Sliding: the near-field band faded all five octaves as one unit, so adjacent LOD rings differed by 43% of the band and the ground re-formed as the rings swept past. Morphing cannot hide that -- a morph target is the bilinear average of the patch's own samples, which is only the parent's surface if the parent is a smoothed copy. Per-octave fading now; worst single-depth step 9.4 cm, measured by Ledger.NearField.AdjacentDepthsAgree.

evidence.caption: 0.60 m quads (was 4.77), 29 px at 20 m, and 8.7 cm RMS of new relief over a 50 m profile.
Eye height, two kilometres east of the town. The ground undulates and has no visible facets; the black cones are placeholder scatter and are what T434 is for.
The cost, measured after the fact: ridge sweep terrain tick 9.4 -> 29.4 ms warm, p99 34.4 -> 99.2 ms. T429's own acceptance allowed 15 per cent.

After doubling the error threshold per level beyond 15: ridge sweep terrain 29.4 -> 18.4 ms, p99 99.2 -> 57.6. Surface terrain 6.5 -> 1.1 ms, better than before T429. Still +67% against an allowance of +15%.
After the fix: holes_worst 0 (was 3363), imbalanced edges halved, p99 124 -> 70 ms.

tasks.title: Parallax occlusion mapping on close ground
tasks.detail:
Every scan ships a height map, the material samples all of them, and they are used only to decide which layer wins. Nothing is displaced. This is the single largest gap between the ground as rendered and the ground as photographed: a normal map relights a flat surface but never occludes, so pebbles have no silhouette against each other and the surface slides under a moving camera instead of parallaxing.

POM in the material, faded out with distance (the cost is per-pixel ray marching and it is invisible past a few metres), with silhouette clipping left off -- it costs more than it returns on ground seen from above.
tasks.acceptance: A raking-light capture at 2 m shows gravel occluding gravel, and the occlusion moves correctly as the camera translates; measured by differencing two captures a metre apart, where a normal-mapped surface produces no parallax and a displaced one does.

notes.text: Parallax OFFSET mapping landed and measured; parallax OCCLUSION mapping, which the acceptance asks for, has not. Offset is applied to the world position all three triplanar projections derive from rather than to a UV, so the projections move together and the seams do not swim; one extra triplanar sample, faded out from 3 m to 15 m. The view-dependence is proven against a -noparallax control arm: difference by image row, which on a ground plane is difference by distance, runs 0.66 -> 3.33 of 255 from far to near. Occlusion needs a per-pixel ray march and is priced before it is taken. Separately and usefully negative: this does NOT fix the near-ground softness. At two degrees the footprint ratio is ~30:1 against anisotropy's maximum of 16, so parallax on a blurred sample gives blurred parallax -- the fix is displacing geometry, not the sample position.

Half delivered and committed: parallax offset mapping, measured. The remaining half is the per-pixel ray march the acceptance asks for, and its cost lands on every ground pixel -- priced in T436 before it is taken, not after.

The per-pixel march is in: 16 steps through the scan's height field along the view ray, three triplanar samples each at mip 0, inside the 15 m parallax fade, interpolated between the last two samples -- a Custom node over the same camera-relative coordinate the triplanar sampling uses, with -nopom (and -livematerials) as the control. Measured the way the acceptance asks, by differencing captures a metre apart, against a control build with parallax off so perspective and relief cancel (tools/parallax_spread.py): the march moves the ground 28.6 px RMS more than the control, the one-step offset 12.3 px. The first pair was aimed at a point on the height function and looked at the horizon on this relief; it is re-aimed by direction, 45 degrees down, and the raking-light half of the acceptance is still to be framed.

The raking-light pair was unmeasurable, not unconvincing: a 1 m step 2 m over the ground moved it ~570 px, the tool searched +-48 px, and the 17-24 px 'differences' were noise. Fixed both ends: the tool matches coarse to fine (self-test recovers a known 130/-310 px shift exactly), the pair steps 25 cm, and exposure adapts instantly (the old frames were still climbing toward the bias, means 9 and 12). Re-shoot pending.

Pair re-shot with the terrain held and exposure settled (all six frames 20-27 of 255, consistent). The stone moves (78, -82) px between shots, and the tool, seeded there, recovers (72, -70) on the ground -- but only ~40 tiles pass, and march-minus-flat (median 1.44 px) and onestep-minus-flat (1.26 px) are indistinguishable, at the noise floor. The framing is the problem: straight down is where parallax is smallest by construction (the offset goes as tan of the view angle). Same-view march-vs-flat displacement straight down is 0.5-0.9 px, about 2 mm at 2 m. Next: the acceptance's raking view -- 40-45 degrees down from 2 m -- where the 3 cm depth should move texture several pixels.

Found and fixed a defect the pair was hiding (1752b82): the terrain material sampled every texture at the camera-relative position, so the ground's texture travelled with the camera. After a high-pass, 27 of 40 ground tiles in the old pair matched best within 25 px of zero shift while the stone moved 110 px -- the gravel was stuck to the screen, which no parallax measure could survive. The planet now hands the material the camera's world position modulo 3.6 km (a whole number of every tiling), and after a re-bake 0 of 40 tiles stick to the screen. Remaining for this task: the raking 40-45 degree view, where the 3 cm depth should move texture several pixels.

Raking view measured (40 degrees down from 2 m, 25 cm step, terrain held, textures world-locked, exposure settled: frames 96-105 of 255, 312 tiles matched). Same camera, march against flat: tiles correlate at a median NCC of 0.956 -- the offset does distort the gravel, about 5% -- but the one-step control correlates at 0.954, so the 16-step march adds nothing measurable. That follows from the code: the march returns the height where the ray goes under, the one-step the height at the pixel, and on a smooth gravel height map at 3 cm depth those agree except where one pebble hides another. Per-texel parallax at this step is ~0.8 px, and tile averages cancel it because the height is centred. Evidenced: offset mapping. Not evidenced: occlusion -- needs a rougher height map or a larger depth, and a per-texel measure rather than tile shifts.

Measured per pixel (tools/occlusion_fb.py): dense flow forward and back between the two raking captures 25 cm apart, counting pixels whose round trip fails -- which is what disocclusion does and a smooth offset does not (self-test: plain shift 0.00%, moving occluder 1.62%). On the world-locked pair: march 7.7% off by more than 1 px, one-step 8.3%, flat ground 8.6%. The ~8% floor is the scattered stones and the light; the march adds nothing above it. So occlusion is not there at a 3 cm depth on a smooth gravel height map, now measured rather than argued. Next: deepen or sharpen the gravel's height and re-measure the same way.

At 8 cm (-parallaxdepth=8, after the near-field harness stopped running out of memory) the per-pixel round trip does not separate occlusion from the scene. Whole ground: flat 16.6%, one-step 17.6%, march 18.1% off by more than 1 px -- the order occlusion predicts. Near ground only (bottom 40%): flat 20.8%, one-step 18.3%, march 15.7% -- the reverse; and at 3 cm the same crop puts the one-step control highest of all (20.9%). An ordering that flips with the crop is the stones and the light, not parallax. So occlusion remains unevidenced at 3 and at 8 cm, and this measure on this scan cannot evidence it. What could: a controlled fixture -- a synthetic height map with sharp relief (a checker of steps) under raking light, where a pixel hidden behind a step can be predicted and checked -- rather than a natural scan whose relief is smooth and small.

A controlled fixture: -pomchecker makes the relief a checker of sharp 8 cm steps (the texture seen is still the scan). The march frame on it shows what the gravel never did -- step walls, the raised blocks' sides drawn as short vertical streaks where the ray meets them, which is a near block hiding the ground behind it -- and the one-step frame does not. The round-trip flow measure is blind to it (march 22.1%, one-step 23.6%, flat 22.4%): dense flow smooths across a wall a few pixels thick. So a measure built for the fixture instead: -channel=pomheight shows which height each pixel ends up sampling, and at a raking view occlusion makes the raised tops cover more than their geometric half of the near ground, where an offset that cannot occlude leaves them at half. Queued for march, one-step and flat, both shots of the pair.

The checker fixture, measured three ways. Frames (attached): the march draws coherent raised squares with hatched side walls where the ray meets a block -- a near block hiding the ground behind it -- and the one-step offset tears the same squares into slivers at every step edge. That is the mechanism, evidenced. No scalar separates them robustly: the shown-height fraction with an Otsu threshold is flat 59.2%, one-step 56.7%, march 54.7% (the channel is unlit, hazed and graded, not two-tone); fragment counts are flat ~160 pieces (median 180 px), one-step ~310 (40 px), march ~310 (5 px, the wall hatching). The acceptance asks for gravel occluding gravel, and the gravel scan's own relief is too smooth and shallow to occlude anything at 3 or at 8 cm -- the march on it reads the same as the offset. What would meet it: a gravel height map with sharp relief (a different free scan with real pebble heights; ADR-0005 rules out purchased ones). That is a content choice and is left open.

[2026-09-11] The content T430's last note asks for is already downloaded and CC0, and it is measurably deeper than what the shader samples now. incoming/polyhaven holds two Poly Haven sets (CC0 1.0, Amal Kumar), both already described in client/Config/surfaces.json since ba3fd53. Their displacement maps, read at their true 16-bit depth: gravel_stones std 0.088, p1-p99 range 0.416, Laplacian sharpness 0.0182; dry_river_pebbles std 0.138, range 0.630, sharpness 0.0061; against the height the shader samples today (out/channel-height.png) std 0.044, range 0.161, sharpness 0.0106. So gravel_stones is the candidate -- 2.6x the depth AND 1.7x the high-frequency sharpness, which is what 'gravel occluding gravel' needs; dry_river_pebbles is deeper still but smoother (big rounded stones). Indicative, not conclusive: the comparison frame is a render capture of the sampled height, not the raw texture, so the render measure (tools/occlusion_fb.py, flat vs one-step vs march) remains the test. TWO OBSTACLES, both in tools/import_surfaces.py, neither fixed yet: (1) it cannot see these sets -- classify() anchors on the LAST underscore-separated piece of the stem (deliberately, after an asset id ending in 'ao' broke it), and Poly Haven names are dry_river_pebbles_diff_2k.png, whose last piece is '2k', so is_a_texture_set finds no base colour and the run reports 'no texture sets found'. (2) A LATENT BUG that would silently ruin exactly this task: import_one packs the height channel with Image.open(...).convert('L'), and Poly Haven displacement is 16-bit (mode I;16), which that call saturates to white -- the same clipping that made my first measurement read std 0.3, p1-p99 255-255. Imported through that path the height would be FLAT, and the POM march would measure nothing, looking like another negative result. Megascans maps are 8-bit JPG, so this has never shown. Also: import_one requires Megascans metadata for an asset id and hard-codes the Fab licence and 'Quixel Megascans via Fab' as the source, so a rename-into-Megascans-names shortcut would stamp CC0 assets with the wrong licence -- which is the one thing the manifest exists to prevent. What a fix looks like: a Poly Haven path (id from the folder, CC0 licence/source, their suffixes in classify with its self-check extended) plus a 16-bit-safe greyscale conversion; then point a biome's surfaceSet at gravel_stones_polyhaven and re-shoot -nearfield -pomprobe. Left for after M02, on the owner's stated order.

[2026-09-11] CORRECTION to my own note above, and the importer now handles these sets. The earlier comparison ('2.6x the depth, 1.7x the sharpness') was measured against out/channel-height.png, which is a RENDER CAPTURE of the sampled height across a frame, not the current scan's texture -- not a like-for-like comparison and I should not have quoted it. Measured properly, packed height against packed height: the current scree scan gravel_ground_vi0maebg reads std 0.1029, p1-p99 range 0.486, Laplacian sharpness 0.01386; gravel_stones_polyhaven reads std 0.0882, range 0.416, sharpness 0.01940; dry_river_pebbles_polyhaven reads std 0.1380, range 0.631, sharpness 0.00878. So the honest case is SHARPNESS, not depth: gravel_stones carries about 40% more high-frequency relief than what the ground uses now, at slightly LESS total depth; dry_river is 30% deeper and 37% smoother. Whether 40% more sharpness is enough to make occlusion measurable where the current scan showed none is exactly the open question, and it is weaker than the case I first wrote down. IMPORTER: tools/import_surfaces.py now reads Poly Haven sets (classify strips their trailing resolution and reads their role names -- diff, nor_gl, rough, ao, disp -- with nor_dx dropped so it cannot race the OpenGL normal; a set with no metadata that looks like theirs gets the id 'polyhaven' and the CC0 licence rather than the Fab one; the manifest merge keeps a person's provenance, since the author and page are on the website and not in the files). And the 16-bit bug is fixed and proven end to end: the packed height now matches the source disp exactly (std 0.0882 -> 0.0882, range 0.416 -> 0.416), where convert('L') would have delivered flat white. Both sets are staged in surfaces/ (gitignored intermediates); next is the Unreal import, then a biome pointed at gravel_stones_polyhaven and -nearfield -pomprobe re-shot.

[2026-09-11] FIRST CROP-STABLE POSITIVE, measured like for like -- and it also corrects what I wrote an hour ago. Three arms (march, one-step offset, parallax off) shot at the same camera, same 11.9 degree raking sun, same build, once on the CC0 gravel_stones_polyhaven scan and once on the scree scan the ground uses now (gravel_ground_vi0maebg); round-trip flow failure (tools/occlusion_fb.py, self-test: plain shift 0.00%, real occluder 1.62%). WHOLE FRAME -- old scan flat 8.60, one-step 8.79, march 9.80; pebbles flat 7.87, one-step 8.78, march 9.72. So BOTH scans separate the march on the whole frame, and my earlier framing that the old scan shows nothing was wrong; worse, today's old-scan numbers do not match the ones recorded for it before (march was LOWEST there, 7.7 against flat 8.6), which is the measure's documented sensitivity to build, sun and camera showing itself again. NEAR GROUND (bottom 40%, the crop that broke every earlier claim) -- old scan flat 5.27, one-step 4.90, march 5.48: the ordering flips (one-step under flat) and march-minus-flat is +0.21, noise. Pebbles flat 4.86, one-step 5.48, march 6.49: monotonic, march-minus-flat +1.63, and the march's p99 detail 7.93 px against flat's 4.92. THAT is the difference that matters: the pebble scan's ordering survives the crop and the old scan's does not, which is exactly the test that exposed the previous results as stones and light. Attributable to relief: measured packed height to packed height, gravel_stones carries 40% more high-frequency sharpness than the current scree scan (0.01940 against 0.01386) at slightly less total depth (range 0.416 against 0.486). STILL OPEN, and not mine to decide: the game does not use this scan -- the biome files were pointed at it only for the measurement and are reverted. Adopting it is a look decision (which biome, or the scree slot the material hard-codes) for the owner. Also open: a repeat, because one run per arm is thin for a measure this sensitive; running now.

[2026-09-11] THE REPEAT DOES NOT REPRODUCE IT -- retracting the 'first crop-stable positive' I wrote above. Same scan, same flags, same camera, same 11.9 degree sun, one run later. Near ground (bottom 40%), round-trip failure: run 1 flat 4.86, one-step 5.48, march 6.49 (march-minus-flat +1.63, monotonic); run 2 flat 5.62, one-step 5.45, march 5.86 (march-minus-flat +0.24, and one-step BELOW flat -- the same non-monotonic pattern that condemned the old scan). Whole frame: run 1 7.87/8.78/9.72 (+1.85), run 2 8.42/8.88/9.41 (+0.99), old scan 8.60/8.79/9.80 (+1.20) -- overlapping, so the whole-frame separation does not distinguish the scans either. THE NUMBER THAT SETTLES IT: the flat arm, an identical configuration run twice, moved 4.86 to 5.62 -- 0.76 points of run-to-run noise, and the march arm moved 6.49 to 5.86, 0.63 points. The between-scan effect I was reading (+1.63) is the same size as the noise in the instrument measuring it, so one run per arm could never have supported the claim and I should not have written it before repeating. WHERE THIS LEAVES T430: the per-pixel march is implemented and correct (the checker fixture shows the mechanism plainly -- step walls, a near block hiding the ground behind it, which the one-step offset tears into slivers), but no scalar measure this project has -- tile shifts, dense-flow round trip, shown-height fractions -- separates it on natural ground, on the old scan or on a sharper CC0 one. The acceptance asks for a raking capture that SHOWS gravel occluding gravel, which is a person's judgement, and that is the honest remaining route: put the frames in front of the owner, as T437, T442 and T444 already are. The CC0 scans stay imported and available (the importer fix and the 16-bit repair are worth having regardless); the biome files were only ever pointed at them for measurement and are reverted.

evidence.caption: Parallax offset in, measured by difference-by-row against a -noparallax control: 0.66/255 at the far edge rising monotonically to 3.33 at the near one.
Checker relief (8 cm steps), shown height, the march: coherent raised squares with hatched side walls where the ray meets the side of a block -- a block hiding the ground behind it.
Same camera, the one-step offset: the raised squares slide as flat sheets and tear into slivers at every step edge -- what an offset that cannot occlude does.

tasks.title: Break the tiling repetition
tasks.detail:
A 2 m tile over a 305 m patch is 152 repeats each way, unrotated and unoffset. The eye finds that grid immediately, and it is the most recognisable tell of procedural ground.

Stochastic sampling -- three hex-grid taps per texture, each with a noise-driven offset and rotation, blended by barycentric weight. Three times the samples on the ground layers, which is why it needs measuring rather than assuming.
tasks.acceptance: An overhead 200 m capture has no visible grid, and the autocorrelation of its albedo shows no peak at the tiling period above the noise floor. The before capture shows that peak.

notes.text: Closed by measurement, no code. The premise -- a 2 m tile repeated 152 times across a patch, unrotated -- is true of the texture and false of the render. High-passed autocorrelation of an overhead capture at 120 px/m puts the tiling period 0.9 sd BELOW the surrounding noise floor; there is no peak at 2 m or at its harmonic. Four things already break it and none were put there for this: triplanar's three out-of-phase projections, three ground slots with different tiling metadata, the 90 m and 1.2 km macro bands, and the vertex colour. Stochastic sampling would have tripled the texture samples on the most-shaded surface in the game to fix something that is not happening. The autocorrelation is the deliverable -- re-run it if the material ever loses triplanar or drops to one slot.

evidence.caption: Overhead from 8 m, 120 px per metre, scatter off. High-passed autocorrelation puts the 2 m tiling period at -0.0151, which is 0.9 sd BELOW the noise floor. No repeat to break.

tasks.title: Multi-scale detail, blended by distance
tasks.detail: One tiling scale cannot serve one metre and one kilometre. Close up the 2 m tile is right; at 200 m it averages to a flat colour, and past that it aliases. Three scales: a macro variation layer at 20-50 m that breaks up large-scale flatness, the scan's own tile, and a detail normal at around 0.25 m that survives being stood on -- crossfaded by distance so exactly one pair is ever active.
tasks.acceptance: Texel density measured at 1 m, 10 m, 100 m and 1 km stays inside one octave of the target; captures at those four distances show neither smearing up close nor a flat average far away.

notes.text: The three bands (2 m scan tile, 90 m macro, 1.2 km macro) already existed and are untouched; what was wrong was when each was switched off. The fade was saturate(Depth/600 m), a ramp starting at the camera -- a quarter gone at 150 m, half at 300 -- and the 90 m macro, which exists to carry variation once the fine detail goes, was faded on the same curve. Now set from where each band stops resolving: a tile of size S is two pixels across at S/2 x 960 metres, so 2 m -> 960 m (held to 400, gone by 1.2 km) and 90 m -> 43 km (held to 20 km). No new samples or textures. Texel-density-at-four-distances measurement not done; the grazing-angle smear near the camera is anisotropy and parallax, which is T430.

evidence.caption: After the fade fix: ground texture legible to the hillside instead of collapsing to a flat tint a hundred metres out. Stones from T434 visible in the same frame.

tasks.title: Audit what the shading model actually receives
tasks.detail:
Before adding anything further: confirm every channel the scans provide reaches the output and means what the shading model thinks it means. AO reaching base colour rather than the AO input, a normal map sampled as sRGB, roughness that was authored as gloss -- each is a one-line bug that costs the whole surface its realism, and none of them announce themselves.

Includes specular occlusion from AO, which is free once AO is wired and is most of why crevices read as crevices.
tasks.acceptance: A checklist capture per channel: each of albedo, normal, roughness, AO and height isolated in a debug view and shown to be the map the manifest names, in the colour space the manifest names.

notes.text: All five channels isolated behind -channel= and checked. Three scalars (roughness 0.77, AO 0.83, height 0.47 linear) arrive grey to within 3 of 255, which is the check that they are not being read from the wrong channel of the packed map. Albedo arrives coloured at a plausible sandy value. The normal was WRONG: FGraph::Triplanar weights and adds three projections, which is right for a scalar and wrong for a normal because each projection is in its own tangent frame -- and on a sphere the weights come from the radial direction, so all three always carry weight and the incoherent sum is the common case. Now swizzled into world space, blended, normalised, with bTangentSpaceNormal false and the fade going to the vertex normal rather than +Z. Verified against something known: the channel decodes to (0.53,0.76,0.35) against the site's actual radial (0.55,0.75,0.37). Two earlier versions of this table were wrong and are documented -- auto exposure, then AEM_Manual which passed every check on five black images.

tasks.title: Rocks with silhouettes, generated by rule
tasks.detail:
Ground detail that a heightfield cannot hold: boulders, cobbles and slabs as real geometry, placed by the same slope and biome rules the material blends by, so a gravel surface has gravel standing proud of it and a scree slope has stones with edges. ADR-0005 applies -- these are generated (noise-deformed convex hulls, eroded), not bought.

This is also where the cone trees start being replaced, but rocks first: they are generatable to a convincing standard by rule, which vegetation is not, and they are what makes ground read as ground.
tasks.acceptance: A capture at 3 m shows stones whose silhouettes break the horizon line of the surface behind them, at a density that matches the material underneath; and the transect frame time holds.

notes.text: Mesh done and tested: 320-face noise-displaced icosahedron, three variants, flat shaded, clast sizes 0.15+u^2*0.85. Instance variant was masked to one bit so a third mesh could never be placed. Winding was inside out -- the geometry test passed anyway because it only checked normals, and now checks both. Open: a handful of instances render as black squares from directly overhead only; geometry, winding, distance fields and the ground material each ruled out.

Generated stone: 320-face noise-displaced icosahedron, three variants, flat shaded, clast sizes 0.15+u^2*0.85, replacing the 18 m cone tree the scatter had been using as gravel. Geometry test covers solidity, bounds, degenerate faces, outward normals AND winding -- its first version passed on an inside-out mesh because it only checked normals. The black squares that held this open were a stale baked material: -bakematerials after a material change is part of the loop. Remaining: stones cluster along the collision-ring boundary rather than at a density matching the ground, which is where scatter is allowed to exist at all -- T059, not this.

Reopened by T437 and fixed. Two defects that one photograph of one grassland site had not shown: the stones were white, because an instanced static mesh does not deliver the mesh's vertex colours to the shader and Tint x (absent colour) is the tint -- darkening the bake changed nothing, which is what identified it, and the colour now lives in the tint at 0.16 linear. And they were on a lattice, because a cell fills when a uniform draw falls under the biome density, so density 1.0 fills every cell and the jitter that has always been inside each cell is jitter inside a full grid; capped at 0.55. Per-stone colour variation is lost until per-instance custom data or one material per variant. Stones still band along the collision-ring boundary, which is T059.

evidence.caption: Eye height after the change: clean ground, no cone forest. The scatter had been placing an 18 m tree at full size as its rock.
Straight down from 8 m. The stones still render as a few hard black squares from directly above -- unresolved, documented in docs/comparisons/rocks/.
After re-baking the material: stones render as stones and break the horizon line of the hillside behind them. The black squares were a stale baked material asset, not geometry.
Savanna after the fill cap and the tint: dark rock at a plausible density, not white blobs on a lattice.

tasks.title: Reference comparison against photographs
tasks.detail:
The measuring stick, and the reason this milestone can be failed. Freely licensed photographs of real ground -- arid gravel, scree, forest floor, snow -- put beside the render at matched focal length, exposure and sun angle, at 2 m, 20 m and 200 m. The existing capture comparison harness does the framing; what is new is the reference plates and the honest verdict.

The write-up names where the render still loses. A comparison page that concludes everything is fine is a comparison page nobody ran.
tasks.acceptance: Twelve side-by-side pairs published, each with a written verdict, and at least three naming a specific remaining deficiency.

notes.text: Sourcing decided 2026-09-10: CC0 / public-domain landscape photography, downloaded by me, with every source and licence recorded in a manifest the way surfaces/manifest.json already does. Keeps ADR-0005 intact -- nothing purchased, and non-commercial personal use is covered. The alternative considered and not taken was the user supplying the photographs; CC0 was chosen so the comparison set can be regenerated from its manifest rather than depending on files only one machine has. This removes the last decision in front of the task; what remains is work.

Render side under way (4385d6f): -surfacestudy -reference renders 2/20/200 m at a chosen -studyat site; sites logged for desert gravel 3.0,123.0, rainforest floor 2.0,154.0, cliff apron scree -2.3968,120.0014, winter snow -52.0,43.0 at season 0.25. First pass was white (exposure pinned) and rolled 90 degrees at the equator; both fixed. Photographs need the user's permission to download.

Scree re-rendered where the site actually is, with -studyasis so the study does not walk to the flattest ground: at 2 m it is still sand with a scatter of pebbles and scree only on the upper slope, so the scree deficiency stands (no clast field on the talus itself). Contact sheet at out/reference-sheet.jpg covers gravel, rainforest, scree, sky and snow. The verdicts against CC0 reference photographs wait on permission to download them.

Twelve pairs published in docs/comparisons/reference-photographs/: desert gravel, scree, forest floor and snow at 2, 20 and 200 m, each render beside a CC0 or public-domain photograph from Wikimedia Commons (fourteen downloaded, author and source recorded in surfaces/reference/manifest.json), each with a written verdict. Distance and ground are matched; focal length, sun and exposure are not, so they compare what the ground is rather than how it is lit. Eleven of twelve lose and every one of those names its deficiency. In order of cost to the picture: no clasts where the ground is stone (gravel and scree render as sand at every distance -- a close stone scatter, talus block geometry, and the right scan winning at those sites), dark skies at the reference sites (every 20 m and 200 m frame near black against bright photographs), no vegetation or litter in the forest, and snow without grain at 2 m. The one that holds, snow at 20 m, holds on shape alone. These are what the rest of M2S has to fix.

evidence.caption: Gravel at 2 m: the render is smooth sand, the photograph desert pavement -- no clasts where the ground is stone
Scree at 2 m: sand against a talus of angular blocks -- scree needs block geometry, not a texture
Forest at 20 m: green marble hills with no tree against trunks and leaf litter
Snow at 20 m, the closest pair: wind-shaped drifts against sastrugi; the sky is dark where it should be bright

tasks.title: The cost of all of it, measured
tasks.detail: Every task above adds per-pixel or per-vertex work to the thing that already dominates the frame. Measured together, on the transect, against the budget -- and if it does not fit, the write-up says which of these is being turned down and to what.
tasks.acceptance: A frame time breakdown before and after the whole milestone at 300 m and at 900 m/s, with the terrain's share attributed to geometry, material and scatter separately.

notes.text: Four flights, one control arm each, same cache state. The milestone's material work is inside the noise floor: -noscatter moves the overall mean 0.2 ms in the WRONG direction, -noparallax likewise, and the world-space normal blend is the same three samples with a swizzle. The whole bill is the CPU terrain tick from T429's three extra depth levels: ridge sweep 9.4 -> 20.5 ms, while the surface phase got FASTER (6.5 -> 1.22) because the disk cache serves the fine patches. -flatterrain is not a valid control arm here and the report's own cache line proves it -- 20% served from disk against 99% everywhere else, because dropping the biome set changes the content key and the flight regenerates; its 41 ms terrain tick is generation, not material. Also recorded: p99 on this flight has read 34.4, 57.6, 61.5, 65.9 and 72.7 across the session and is too noisy to attribute a few ms to a cause. Mean is the number to reason about: 19.7 -> 21.7 across the milestone.

tasks.title: Playable proof: stand still and look at the ground
tasks.detail: Rule 6 applied to a surface. Walk to four different biomes, stop, and look down, then out to the horizon.
tasks.acceptance: Four captures at eye height in four biomes, each of which a person shown it without context does not identify as a video game heightfield -- and the four look like four different places.

notes.text: RUN, AND IT FAILS. The measurable half passes: four biomes found at weights 1.00/1.00/1.00/0.99, and the four grounds are measurably different places -- closest pair 27.0 of 255. The half that matters does not. Nobody shown the rainforest capture would fail to identify it as a video game: the scatter places one stone per cell of a 20x20 grid and in the mid-distance that lattice is plain, and the stones are a light grey tinted white so they blow out to featureless blobs and take no colour from the ground they sit on. Both were signed off in T434 on one photograph of one biome, which is exactly what this fixture exists to catch. T434 reopened.
Blocked on T434: the stones are on a visible lattice and are white. Re-run when they are fixed.
unblocked

Re-run now that T434 is fixed and the sun actually lights surfaces. The measurable half passes again and more clearly: the four grounds differ pairwise by a mean of 24.7 to 73.9 of 255 (closest pair desert/savanna). The two defects T434 was reopened for are gone -- the stones are brown and there is no lattice. The half that matters still fails, on new and specific defects rather than on the old ones: (1) the boulders are visibly faceted, because T434 flat-shaded a 320-face hull and at 3-10 m that reads as low-poly; (2) crisp-edged white patches sit on the ground in the desert and grassland frames -- a surface blend with a hard edge; (3) the savanna frame has a vertical column of stacked boulders in the middle distance, a scatter placement defect, probably a slope test at cell spacing that cannot see a face narrower than a cell on a coarse patch; (4) the daytime skies are nearly black overhead. No longer blocked -- open work with named defects.

Two of the three defects fixed and one narrowed. Faceted rocks: normals blended 45/55 between the face and the direction to the face centre, baked, and the stones now read as rounded boulders. White patches: the terrain material's blend depth 0.2 -> 0.5, and scree/rock exposures now meet the ground with a gritty edge instead of a cut-out. The savanna boulder column is still in frame, but it is not floating: ALedgerPlanet::MeasureScatterFootings traced every stone within 400 m of all four cameras against the drawn ground -- 59,489 + 5,175 + 52,631 + 41,003 stones, none more than 1.5 m off it. So the column stands on real ground, most likely a face steeper than the placement's slope limit, which is measured on the height function a cell away rather than on the surface the stone lands on. The next run records the drawn slope under every stone out to 1.5 km.

Savanna column isolated (b7f4848): hiding every scatter component removes it, and taking every instance out and putting it back leaves it pixel-identical -- so it is scatter, and the renderer draws what the components hold. But 3,074 stones project into the column rectangle, all traced onto live, drawn terrain within centimetres, and none projects above y 459 while the drawn column climbs to 415. Next: every instance at any range by where its mesh is drawn, plus the mesh bounds.

The savanna column is not a defect. The four stones in it are ~1 m boulders 32-37 m from the camera (scale 0.89-0.97, pivots 0.4 m under their drawn centres, meshes 1 m with base at z=0), each traced onto drawn, live terrain within 1 cm. View rays down the column (x 1045) hit ground at 31-35 m from y 440 downward and find nothing nearer above y 430: a mound 35 m off, and the stones sit on its crest. The frame reads them as climbing the hill 250 m behind because the mound's grass matches that hill and nothing in the image separates 35 m from 250 m. The acceptance -- that someone shown these without context would not call them a game heightfield -- is a human judgement and is left for review.

tasks.title: Body definition: mass, radius, rotation, tilt, orbit
tasks.detail: One description a planet, moon, station or asteroid is built from, in double precision, deterministic from seed.
tasks.acceptance: A system description round-trips through serialisation and rebuilds identically.

notes.text: FLedgerBody, FLedgerOrbit and FLedgerSystem in LedgerCore, with JSON serialisation, validation and seeded generation. Three green tests. Round-trips EXACTLY -- bit equality, not a tolerance, because at one astronomical unit the fifteenth significant digit of a double is about a hundred metres and a tolerance would let a planet drift every time the file was written. That is why doubles are written at %.17g and read back with FDefaultValueHelper rather than through FJsonSerializer, whose number path does not promise the last bit. Re-serialising the parsed system is byte-identical too, which is what makes a system description diffable in version control. Validate is separate from parsing on purpose: a file can be valid JSON describing an impossible system, and saying which of those went wrong is the difference between a five-minute fix and an afternoon. It rejects no bodies, zero mass or radius, eccentricity outside [0,1), a body orbiting itself, a parent that does not exist, more or fewer than one primary, and cycles -- the last by walking to the root with a step limit, because a cycle would otherwise hang whatever computes positions rather than reporting anything. SI throughout: kilogrammes, metres, seconds, radians. Centimetres are a rendering unit and belong at the boundary.

tasks.title: Keplerian ephemeris
tasks.detail: Position and velocity of every body at any time, from orbital elements. Analytic rather than integrated, so there is no drift and no need to simulate the solar system to know where a moon was last Tuesday.
tasks.acceptance: Positions at t agree whether computed forward from zero or directly, to sub-metre over a simulated century.

notes.text: Analytic Kepler ephemeris in LedgerCore: mean motion, eccentric anomaly, state relative to a parent, and states for a whole system in the primary's frame by walking the parent chain. Four green tests. The acceptance -- stepped from zero against asked-for directly, sub-metre over a century -- reads 0.000000 m worst over 36,525 accumulated day-steps, which for a function of time is close to a tautology and is exactly the point: an integrator would fail it, and this test is what stops one quietly replacing this. THE SOLVER SHIPPED A DIVERGENCE AND A TEST CAUGHT IT. The first starting guess was the third-order seed M + e sin M / (1 - sin(M+e) + sin M), whose denominator passes through zero; at e=0.95 and M=-18002 it did, Newton launched off the root, and Kepler's equation came back with a residual of 6.5 MILLION radians. Danby's seed cannot blow up -- M displaced towards periapsis by at most 0.85e, always inside the interval containing the root -- and the worst residual is now 4.4e-16. A table of expected values would not have caught it, because the answer was not wrong in a way anybody would have thought to tabulate; checking by substitution into the equation being solved would catch any solver that returns a plausible-looking number. Three other properties are pinned: a body returns to where it started after one period and after a hundred, and the analytically-written velocity agrees with a central difference of the position it claims to describe to 1.5e-10 relative.

tasks.title: Reference frame hierarchy
tasks.detail: System, body, surface and vehicle frames with transforms between them. Everything positional in the project ends up expressed in one of these, and getting it wrong later is unaffordable.
tasks.acceptance: A point on a rotating planet's surface transformed to system frame and back is unchanged to the millimetre.

notes.text: Four frames -- system, body, surface, vehicle -- as separate types in LedgerCore with no implicit conversion between them, because a position that forgets which frame it is in is wrong by up to a planet's circumference and by a different amount every second. Three green tests. ACCEPTANCE: worst round trip 0.015052 mm at a system-frame distance of order 1.5e11 m, against a 1 mm bound. That scale is the difficulty: a millimetre out of 1.5e11 is 7e-15 relative, about a hundred times the double floor, which is enough room to be right and none to be sloppy. Surface frames are anchored by a unit DIRECTION rather than a latitude and longitude, so there is no pole singularity to special-case at the call site; the one place it is unavoidable -- north is undefined on the axis -- falls back to a fixed reference, and EastNorthUpIsRightHandedEverywhere checks orthonormality and east x north = up at 200 anchors including both poles. Tilt is applied before spin, which is what makes axial tilt mean what it says and is what T073's seasons come out of. THIS TASK FOUND THAT UNREAL'S PI IS A FLOAT. TheBodyFrameActuallyRotates turned the planet through one full rotation and it landed 1105.057985 mm from where it started. 1.1 m over a 6.4e6 m radius is 1.7e-7 relative -- single precision, in code that is double everywhere else. '2.0 * PI' evaluates to 6.2831854820251465 against a true 6.283185307179586, because PI is a float constant and float-to-double is the widening conversion that is normally safe, so no compiler warns. It now reads 0.000001 mm. My first diagnosis was wrong and worth recording: the failing test differenced two vectors of order 1.5e11 m to recover one of 6.4e6, so the obvious suspect was the test measuring its own cancellation. Rewriting it to compare the rotations directly -- no large magnitudes anywhere -- still read 1105 mm, which ruled the test out in one build. Taking the measurement a different way beat arguing about it. Swept every double-precision use of PI in the project into LedgerPi/LedgerTwoPi in a new LedgerMath.h: 13 files, of which three are generation inputs (the seasonal term in LedgerClimate, the scatter yaw, the shelf shaping in LedgerTerrainMath), so patch-disk FormatVersion is now 8 -- the correction moves the terrain by an amount nobody can see and by an amount every cached patch disagrees about. Rule written into docs/coding-standards.md under Precision. 60 tests pass, 52 of them Ledger.*, module layering legal.

evidence.caption: Frames, ephemeris and body, all green: worst round trip 0.015052 mm against a 1 mm bound; one rotation returns to 0.000001 mm, was 1105.057985 mm before the float pi was found

tasks.title: Rotation, day and night from the real rotation rate
tasks.detail: Sun position derived from the body's rotation and orbit, not from a time-of-day slider.
tasks.acceptance: Local noon happens when the ephemeris says the sun is at its highest, at any latitude and any date.

notes.text: Sun position from the body's rotation and orbit. LedgerSky in LedgerCore: sun direction in the body frame, in east-north-up at an anchor, solar altitude, hour angle, and NextLocalNoon solved rather than sampled. Two green tests. ACCEPTANCE: at 9 latitudes from -85 to +85, 3 longitudes, 5 dates across a year and on both the planet and its moon, the altitude at the solved noon is within 1.054e-05 rad of the highest the sun gets all day -- 0.0006 degrees, about one per cent of the width of the sun -- and the hour angle there is 1.256e-12 rad. THE MOON FORCED TWO THINGS. First, the solver: the hour angle does not advance at the rotation rate but at the rotation rate minus the rate the star's own direction moves, which on the planet is a third of a per cent and on a tidally locked moon is several, so eight Newton steps with an assumed slope left the hour angle at 2.283e-9 against a 1e-9 bound. Secant instead: one extra evaluation, and it does not care what orbits what. Second, the bound: the altitude peak is genuinely NOT at the meridian crossing, because the star keeps moving in declination while the body turns, and the displacement goes as the declination rate over the SQUARE of the rotation rate. At latitude 85 on the moon that is 7054 s -- two hours -- and it is physics, not error. So the assertion is on whether the sun is at its highest, which is what the acceptance says, plus a scale-free bound that noon is within one per cent of the body's own day of the peak; the drift uses 0.3% of it. THE WORLD NO LONGER HAS A HARDCODED SUN. LedgerWorld's (0.55, 0.35, 0.78) is gone; the sun is LedgerSky::SunDirectionInBody at a time set by -when=, with the system generated from -systemseed=. A hand-picked vector was a fourth independent variable next to the orbit, the rotation and the season, and a sky that can disagree with the ephemeris is not evidence of anything. New -daysweep fixture: one site, one camera, eight frames across one rotation, nothing changing but the time. Solar altitude runs -63.43, -38.18, 2.26, 44.04, 75.09, 44.01, 2.22, -38.29 -- symmetric about noon, peak at the step the ephemeris named before anything rendered. Sky brightness tracks it: 8.7, 0.0, 145.0, 200.9, 152.7, 127.0, 69.0, 4.3 out of 255, with step 1 fully black. FOUND A SEPARATE AND LARGER BUG WHILE PHOTOGRAPHING THIS: the terrain takes no direct light at all. At noon with the sun 75 degrees up, the unlit base colour reads 128.90 and the lit frame with fog and atmosphere off reads 0.00. Every normal frame is in-scattered air in front of a black surface. Shadows off changes 6.96 to 6.95; re-baking materials changes nothing; the terrain query and the height field agree on the ground to 0.0 m; standing the flight harness down changed no measurement. Fixed a real defect on the way -- the triplanar normal swizzle put the out-of-surface channel on +x, +y, +z unconditionally, so half a sphere had normals pointing into the ground -- and the frames came back bit-identical, which is the finding: if changing the surface normal changes no pixel, the surface is not being shaded. Written up in docs/comparisons/day-sweep with the numbers. 62 tests pass, 54 of them Ledger.*.

CORRECTION to the note above and to the commit message. The claim that 'the terrain takes no direct light' is WRONG and is withdrawn. The foreground band that read 0-7 out of 255 was the day-sweep camera's framing, not the ground: the fixture stands 40 m up looking at the horizon, so the bottom of the frame is a slope seen edge-on. Running the same sweep at the pre-T072 site gives 0.00 at all eight steps -- darker -- while the scripted flight at that same site photographs ground at 97 and 102 out of 255 on the same build. The ground is lit. Three errors produced the wrong claim, all mine: (1) several comparisons ran with two Unreal processes at once, and one of them never wrote fresh captures, so a before/after was measured against leftover PNGs from another commit and reported a difference that did not exist -- the exact stale-output trap already recorded in this project's notes; (2) every measurement came from the one site T072 happens to choose, and nowhere else was checked until much later; (3) the triplanar normal-sign fix was validated only in those frames, where the foreground was dark for an unrelated reason, and wrongly pronounced inert. The normal-sign fix is a real defect fix and is kept. WHAT T072 ACTUALLY CHANGED BESIDES THE SUN: the landing site moved, because ChooseSite follows the sun and a different sun qualifies a different band of the sphere. Old hardcoded sun put the site on a 660 m lowland; the ephemeris sun at t=0 puts it on a 2.4 km mountain. Flight captures, old site against new: terrain-surface 97.05 vs 23.30, terrain-town 102.36 vs 12.89, terrain-coast 19.57 vs 0.50. That is not a regression, it is a different place -- but every committed reference capture is of the OLD site, so the reference set is now measuring two different locations. Needs a decision: regenerate the references against the site the world now chooses, or pin the site independently of the sun. Flagged here rather than settled. One measurement from the investigation survives on its own: SetAtmosphereSunLight(false) reads 177.20 against 3.87 at the new site, so atmospheric transmittance is taking most of the light there -- an M04 question, not this task's.

evidence.caption: Eight frames across one rotation: solar altitude peaks at step 4, the step the ephemeris named as noon before anything rendered
Noon: the sun 75 degrees up. The site, camera and ground are identical in all eight frames
Sunset, the same camera: the sun 2.22 degrees up, a quarter of a rotation later

tasks.title: Axial tilt and seasons
tasks.detail: Tilt drives insolation, which drives the climate field from M02 and the snow line with it.
tasks.acceptance: A high-latitude site has a measurably shorter day in winter and its snow line moves across a simulated year.

notes.text: Tilt drives insolation, insolation drives the climate field, and the snow line moves. Both halves of the acceptance measured. DAY LENGTH: on the generated planet (tilt 17.18 deg, year 30597692 s, solar day 77914 s), latitude 60 gets 14.86 h at one solstice and 6.79 h at the other, a swing of 8.08 h; latitude 75 is inside the polar circle -- 21.64 h against 0.00 h. The equator reads 10.82 h at both, which is half of this planet's 21.6-hour day, because a twelve-hour day is Earth's number and not a law. The closed form cos(H0) = -tan(lat)tan(dec) is checked against sampling the solar altitude 20000 times and counting the lit fraction: worst disagreement 0.0001 of a day, about 8 seconds, over every latitude and both solstices. SNOW LINE: at latitude 55 the line runs from sea level in deep winter to 1230 m at the height of summer and returns to where it started after one year. THE DRAWN CURVE IS GONE. The climate's seasonal term was SeasonalSwingC * sin(latitude) * sin(2*pi*phase) -- right shape, no cause, and THE TILT DOES NOT APPEAR IN IT. It gave a planet with no tilt a full set of seasons and gave planets tilted 10 and 40 degrees identical ones, and no test written against it could notice, because the quantity it was wrong about was not one of its inputs. It is now the difference between today's insolation at a latitude and that latitude's annual mean, normalised against a REFERENCE tilt rather than the body's own -- dividing by its own tilt divides out the season and reproduces the original bug exactly. At 60 degrees in midsummer: +2.87 C with a 5 degree tilt, +22.27 C with 35, and identically zero at every latitude and phase when the tilt is zero. TWO ARTEFACTS OF THE OLD MODEL SURFACED AND BOTH WERE REAL FINDINGS. (1) The annual mean is not the midpoint of the two solstices. The first version used that midpoint and the pole caught it: the star sits on the horizon at an equinox and below it all winter, so insolation is zero at both, while the midpoint reads half the summer value -- an equinox came out 20 C below its own annual mean. Now integrated over eight points of the year, which is eight sines against a climate that already marches forty steps upwind resampling the height field per point. (2) The seasonal offset is not antisymmetric in latitude; the SWING is. sin(lat)sin(2 pi phase) is antisymmetric by construction and a test asserted it. Sunlight is not: at 10 degrees the two hemispheres read +1.65 and -3.51, because a latitude's annual mean is not halfway between its solstices. What is exactly equal and opposite is the distance between the two solstices, since I(-lat,dec) = I(lat,-dec) and it is the same year. The test now asserts that instead. Ledger.Climate.SeaLevelTemperatureIsMonotonicPoleToEquator now asks its question of a zero-tilt planet, which is what it always meant -- the claim is about the latitude band, and under the old sine a phase of zero made the seasonal term vanish, while under insolation a phase of zero is an equinox and a real moment. IN THE WORLD: the season is no longer a switch. The world reads phase 0.6903 and declination -6.01 deg from the orbit at begin play, and that agrees with the sun's own direction (asin(-0.105) = -6.03 deg) because both come from the same ephemeris rather than two settings kept in step by hand. -season= still overrides, because the fixtures that photograph a summer and a winter side by side must be able to ask for one. Patch-disk FormatVersion is 9 and the tilt is mixed into the content key. 66 tests pass, module layering legal.

evidence.caption: Day length 14.86 h against 6.79 h at latitude 60, polar night at 75, closed form agreeing with sampling to 0.0001 of a day, and the snow line running 0 to 1230 m across the year

tasks.title: Multi-body rendering with correct illumination
tasks.detail: Other planets and moons visible in the sky, at the right place, with the right phase and the right apparent size.
tasks.acceptance: A moon's phase matches the sun-moon-observer geometry at any time and from any body in the system.

notes.text: A moon's phase matches the geometry, checked as a computation and as a photograph, because those fail separately. THE COMPUTATION: (1 + cos alpha)/2 against counting -- 200,000 points spread over the target's sphere, each marked lit if it faces the star and visible if it faces the observer and weighted by how square-on it is, with no phase angle anywhere in it. Twenty combinations, every non-star body seen from every other, at eight points around a month plus two much later times. Worst disagreement 0.003751, on the planet seen from its own moon at a 125.3 degree phase angle. That residual is not error: the formula is the far-field one and assumes a hemisphere, and a finite distance sees slightly less, which is largest exactly where it showed. Across a month the moon runs 0.0003 to 0.9996 lit. THE PHOTOGRAPH: new -moonshot fixture, a 10 degree lens on the ground, eight frames around the month, forwarding at each point to the moment the body is highest. Nothing draws a phase -- the body is a sphere lit by the same directional light as the ground, so the terminator is where the geometry puts it and there is no second implementation to disagree. That makes counting lit pixels an independent check on both: against what the computed fraction and angular diameter predict, the frames land within about ten per cent everywhere the disc is more than a sliver (99.7% lit 0.0%, 80.3% -5.8%, 61.0% -3.6%, 44.5% -8.8%, 14.6% +0.1%), and badly out only at 0.7% where a twenty-pixel crescent is measuring antialiasing. The angular diameter breathes 0.581 to 0.669 degrees around one month because the orbit is eccentric, which nothing was written to produce. THREE BUGS FOUND BY LOOKING, ALL WITH THE TESTS GREEN, each producing eight frames of empty sky while the log insisted the moon was overhead. (1) A degenerate camera basis: the fixture forwards to the moment the body is HIGHEST, which puts it near the zenith, where the look direction and local up are the same vector and MakeFromXZ has no basis to build. Falls back to east when overhead. (2) A one-step-stale sky: the spheres are placed by ULedgerSkyBodies on its own tick, so setting the clock and photographing in the same frame photographs the sky as it was one step ago. Aiming and capturing are two ticks now. (3) A clock that moved the moon but not the sun: SetWhenSeconds set the number while the directional light kept the direction it was given at begin play, so a body the ephemeris called 99.7% lit was photographed as a thin crescent -- lit correctly, for the wrong moment. The clock now moves the sun. ALSO FIXED A TEST THAT PASSED BY LUCK: an assertion that the star dominates the sky passed only because the moon happened to be 0.5% lit at the timestamp chosen. The moon is the LARGER disc from this planet -- 0.58 degrees against 0.49 -- so a full one sorts first, and the assertion would have been true then and false a fortnight later, which is worse than no assertion. It now checks the ordering is self-consistent and says plainly that real brightness needs T076. That larger disc also means this system can have total eclipses: the moon subtends 1.184 of the star. T075 starts from there. STILL WRONG AND NOT THIS TASK'S: with the atmosphere on the moon is invisible. These frames needed showflag.Atmosphere 0. The aerial perspective is strong enough to erase a body on a 500 km sky shell -- the same over-dense atmosphere measured in docs/comparisons/day-sweep where ground two kilometres away is already flat blue. Belongs with atmosphere calibration in M04, and the number is recorded so that work starts from one. 69 tests pass, module layering legal.

80.3% lit: a gibbous moon with a real elliptical terminator, lit by the same directional light as the ground
