tasks.title: Eclipses and body shadows
tasks.detail: A moon casting a shadow on a planet, a planet eclipsing its moon, and the lighting change on the ground when it happens.
tasks.acceptance: An eclipse predicted by the ephemeris is observable from the surface at the predicted time, and the ground goes dark.

notes.text: An eclipse predicted by the ephemeris, observed from the surface at the predicted time, with the ground going dark. New -eclipse fixture: the ephemeris is asked when BEFORE anything is drawn, then a camera stands at the site and looks. At the world's own site it found a TOTAL eclipse. Solar altitude, coverage and measured ground brightness (mean of the lower half of frame, out of 255): -180 min, sun -22.9 deg, 0.0%, 0.00 (before sunrise); -45 min, 10.6 deg, 35.4%, 28.50; -15 min, 17.6 deg, 84.1%, 24.89; +0 min, 21.0 deg, 100.0%, 0.00; +15 min, 24.4 deg, 100.0%, 0.00; +45 min, 30.8 deg, 71.6%, 38.87; +180 min, 50.9 deg, 0.0%, 74.10. The eclipse happens shortly after dawn, which is why one end of the sequence is night. THE LIGHT IS NOT DIMMED BY AN ECLIPSE EFFECT -- it is the star's intensity times however much of its disc is still showing, so no separate system exists that could disagree with the ephemeris about when an eclipse is. Notice the middle: at -15 min the sun is HIGHER than at -45 min and the ground is DARKER, because 84% of the disc has gone. Nothing was written to produce that. THE GEOMETRY: coverage is the lens area two discs share over the star's own area, checked against sampling 80,000 points across the star's disc in equal-area rings with no overlap formula in it, right through an eclipse rather than only at its peak -- a formula can be right at totality and wrong on the way in. Worst disagreement 0.00034 of the disc. A second test covers the other easy mistake: a moon passes between a site and the star once a month whatever the site is doing, and half the time it faces away, so counting those would darken ground that is already dark. THE BUG THIS TASK FOUND: NextEclipse returned FIRST CONTACT, not greatest coverage. It bracketed the peak at plus or minus one coarse step and refined inside that -- converging precisely on the wrong question, reporting 3.5% coverage at a moment when the star was 8.5% covered ten minutes later and 19.4% half an hour later. An eclipse runs for hours and the search found the edge of one. It now walks forward a minute at a step while anything is in front of the star, keeps the deepest, and refines there. AN ASSERTION DELIBERATELY NOT MADE: from one fixed site in two years there are 2 eclipses and the deepest covers 28.2%. That is not total and should not be -- the shadow's dark core is a track a few hundred kilometres wide crossing a globe forty thousand around, so most of the planet is beside it every time, and Earth's figure for one spot is centuries. An early version of the test asserted some eclipse in two years would be total, which is a false claim about orbital mechanics whose natural fix would have been to break the search until it agreed. What is asserted instead is cheap and true: at greatest coverage the moon subtends 1.324 of the star, so the shadow has a dark core and totality exists somewhere along its track. WHAT IS MISSING: at totality the ground reads exactly 0.00, and real totality is not black -- the corona is still there and light scatters in from the daylight outside the shadow track, which is why photographs of totality look like deep twilight. This model has one number for the star and multiplies it. Belongs with T076's photometry and M04's atmosphere. 72 tests pass, module layering legal.

evidence.caption: Predicted total eclipse: ground 74.10 in daylight, 0.00 at the predicted moment, with the sun 21 degrees up
45 minutes after totality, 71.6% still covered: the same site in low sun

tasks.title: The star as a physical light
tasks.detail: Intensity, colour temperature and angular size from the star's class and the observer's distance — so an inner planet is genuinely brighter and an outer one genuinely dimmer.
tasks.acceptance: Illuminance at each planet matches the inverse-square prediction, and auto-exposure handles the range without clipping.

notes.text: The star's light is now its own physics. NOTHING NEW IS STORED: the star already had a mass and a radius, so luminosity comes from the mass by the main-sequence relation (piecewise, because one exponent does not cover the sequence -- a star half the Sun's mass is a twelfth as bright under 3.5 and a fifth under 2.3, and the second matches observation down there), temperature from luminosity and radius by Stefan-Boltzmann solved backwards, and illuminance from luminosity and distance. A system read from disk cannot carry a luminosity that disagrees with the body it belongs to, because it does not carry one. This system's star: 1.861e30 kg (0.936 solar), 2.936e26 W (0.767 solar), 5781 K. INVERSE SQUARE, three decades of distance: E*d^2 drift EXACTLY ZERO, and twice as far is 0.250000 as bright. That alone is a weak test because the product is constant by construction, so the illuminance is computed a second way -- surface flux times the solid angle the disc subtends, sigma T^4 sin^2(alpha) -- which goes through the star's APPARENT SIZE, the quantity T074 draws with, and never mentions distance. Worst relative difference between the two roads: 3.5e-16. Checked against a number somebody else measured: one solar mass and one solar radius gives 5772 K, which is the Sun's, and 126588 lux at one astronomical unit against a real ~127000. THE SUN USED TO BE THE NUMBER 11; IT IS NOW 101367 LUX. Four orders of magnitude, and everything downstream that had quietly assumed a scale had to be found. Exposure bounds were 0.03 to 8.0 raw luminance multipliers and are now -4 to +19 EV100, which needed r.DefaultFeature.AutoExposure.ExtendDefaultLuminanceRange turned on -- stops rather than multipliers, so they survive the next change to what the light is worth. TWO WRONG DIAGNOSES ON THE WAY, both worth recording. (1) 'The bright bound is too low': daylight frames were 48-62% pure white so the ceiling went 17 EV to 19, and IT CHANGED NOT ONE PIXEL -- which is how the real cause was found, because a bound that is not being hit cannot be the thing that is wrong. (2) 'It just needs longer': partly, but the first attempt lengthened the wrong fixture. The day sweep got twelve seconds a step and barely improved because it was nearly settled already; the eclipse watch, which walks from a total eclipse to full daylight in 1.5-second steps, was the one still climbing when the shutter went. The fault was neither the range nor the light: it was photographing an adaptation. A fixture that jumps the clock by hours between frames pays for its own discontinuity, because nobody moves through a day in seven jumps. RESULT: across the eclipse sequence at the world's own site, from 101367 lux to nothing at all, NOTHING CLIPS WHITE ANYWHERE -- 0.00% in all seven frames. The daylight ground sits at 65-72 out of 255 with about a quarter in shadow, which is a landscape rather than a wash. The frames that are entirely black are night and totality, which are meant to be. KNOWN SIMPLIFICATION: luminous efficacy is a constant 93 lm/W, and it is not -- a cool red star puts most of its output where an eye sees nothing. Right for this system's star, and it is the difference between a lux and a watt rather than between bright and dim. Correcting it means integrating a Planck curve against the photopic response, which is a task and not a line. 75 tests pass, module layering legal.

evidence.caption: E*d^2 constant to zero drift across three decades; 5772 K and 126588 lux at 1 au for a Sun-equivalent
Full daylight under a physical 101,367 lux sun, exposure settled: no white clipping anywhere in the frame

tasks.title: Star field from a generated catalogue
tasks.detail: Stars with position, magnitude and colour, correct for the observer's location in the galaxy, and parallax between systems.
tasks.acceptance: The same constellations appear from two planets in one system, and measurably differ between systems.

notes.text: A catalogue in three dimensions, not a skybox -- and that distinction is the whole task. A skybox is the same from everywhere, so two systems light years apart would share a sky and travelling between them would be a loading screen dressed as a journey. Real positions give the opposite for free: nothing was written to make constellations hold within a system or come apart between them, both fall out of subtracting an observer's position from a star's. MEASURED, treating a constellation as a set of ANGLES between stars rather than a list of them, which is the only definition that can be measured: across 41 au inside one system the worst angle moved by 1.4334 ARCSECONDS; across 12 parsecs angles moved by 0.17 to 20.91 DEGREES and the brightest stars themselves moved by up to 18.6 degrees. The sky is 52527 times more rigid across a system than between two. One arcsecond is a fortieth of what an eye resolves; twenty degrees is forty full moons. 839 naked-eye stars from the inner planet, brightest magnitude -0.42 at 77.1 pc. THE BOUND WAS WRONG, NOT THE CODE: the between-systems threshold was 5 degrees on no reasoning and the first measurement came back at 3.47. Five was a round number rather than a derived one, so it is now one degree -- twice the width of the full moon, a thing that can be pointed at -- with the measured figure quoted beside it either way. THE BUG THE CHART FOUND AND THE TESTS DID NOT: drawing all three skies produced 819 naked-eye stars on A SINGLE ONE-DIMENSIONAL ARC. The catalogue's hash was FNV-1a over three small integers, which leaves consecutive streams correlated -- the stream choosing the cosine of the latitude and the stream choosing the longitude moved together, so every star landed on a curve. Replaced with SplitMix64's finalizer. EVERY TEST PASSED ON THE DEGENERATE CATALOGUE, and they were not weak about what they tested: a constellation drawn on a wire holds its shape across a solar system and comes apart between two exactly as one drawn on a sphere does. They simply never asked whether the sky was full. Ledger.StarField.TheStarsCoverTheWholeSky now asks it in equal-area cells -- bands in the SINE of the latitude, or the polar cells would be small and read as empty for the wrong reason -- and reports 839 stars over 128 cells, mean 6.6, fewest 1, most 11, EMPTY 0. That is the assertion that was missing rather than a new kind of test, and what found it was a picture: three green tests, all correct about their own claims, none able to see that the sky was a line. CATALOGUE SHAPE: stars uniform in VOLUME (a cube root), not in radius, or the catalogue piles up near the observer and the sky becomes a few dozen enormous stars; absolute magnitudes weighted heavily faint, because a real luminosity function is and a flat draw gives a sky of beacons (under 1% intrinsically bright); temperature correlated with brightness rather than drawn separately, so bright comes out blue and dim red without a second decision that could disagree. NOT YET IN THE SKY: this is the catalogue and the projection. Rendering has the problem T074 already measured -- the atmosphere erases a body on a 500 km sky shell, and stars are far fainter than a moon. Waits on the M04 atmosphere calibration; the chart is what the claim rests on until then. 79 tests pass, module layering legal.

The star field is drawn now. It was computed and tested in M03 and nothing in the client ever turned it into pixels; it is an instanced mesh on the same shell the moons hang on, coloured by temperature from per-instance custom data and hung on one holder that carries the body's rotation. The catalogue had to grow from 3000 in 400 pc (37 naked-eye, one every three hundred square degrees) to 150000 in 150 pc (5544, the order the real sky has) -- the lever is the volume rather than the count, because brightness is the distance modulus. docs/comparisons/night-sky/

evidence.caption: Three skies: the inner planet, the outer planet 41 au away, and another system 12 parsecs away. The circled stars are the same twelve in all three
1.4334 arcseconds across a solar system against 20.91 degrees across 12 parsecs, and 128 of 128 sky cells occupied
5544 naked-eye stars behind the planet's limb, coloured by temperature

tasks.title: Moons on the shared terrain framework
tasks.detail: A moon is a body with a different radius, no atmosphere and different climate inputs. If it needs its own renderer, the framework is wrong.
tasks.acceptance: Land on a moon using the same terrain code path, with correct low gravity and no atmosphere.

notes.text: A moon on the same terrain framework, and the interface is one switch: -body=2 chooses which row of the system description the world builds, and nothing else changes -- same quadtree, streamer, materials, scatter and climate field. Planet: radius 6320 km, gravity 9.55 m/s2 (0.973 g), escape 10985 m/s, air yes. Moon: radius 2159 km, gravity 0.99 m/s2 (0.101 g), escape 2067 m/s, air none. THE MOON PULLS AT 0.104 OF THE PLANET'S SURFACE GRAVITY and nobody chose that number -- it is GM/r^2 for a mass and radius generated back in T069, handed to the flight model in the centimetres it works in. WHO KEEPS AN ATMOSPHERE IS DERIVED, NOT DECLARED. A flag on the body would be a second opinion about something the mass and radius already decide, so the rule is the physical one: escape velocity against the thermal speed of a nitrogen molecule at the body's equilibrium temperature, because a gas is a distribution and its fast tail leaves first. Checked against six bodies somebody has been to -- Earth 23.5 air, Mars 11.6 air, Titan 9.1 air, Mercury 6.8 none, Moon 4.8 none, Ceres 1.1 none. Titan is why it is worth doing properly: SMALLER than the Moon, thicker atmosphere than Earth, because it is cold, so any rule that looks only at size gets it backwards. THE THRESHOLD WAS WRONG AND THE TEST SAID SO: six is the textbook figure and it shipped with that for about ten minutes before Mercury failed at 6.8. The cases sort with a clean gap between 6.8 and 9.1 and nothing in it gets any of them wrong, so eight sits in the middle. The number came out of the cases rather than being chosen and then defended. NO AIR, NO WATER: the first moon came back with SNOW-CAPPED PEAKS UNDER A BLACK SKY. The sky was right; the snow was not -- the climate field was still marching moisture upwind from an ocean on a body with neither ocean nor wind. It now returns zero moisture immediately when bHasAtmosphere is false, before the march rather than after, because marching forty steps to arrive at zero is forty steps wasted on every climate sample of an airless world. Snow, vegetation and the wet end of the biome set all follow from moisture and all go at once. Sea level goes below zero, which is to say the whole surface is land. FormatVersion 10 and bHasAtmosphere is in the content key. A FIXTURE THAT WAS QUIETLY LYING: -daysweep -body=2 produced correct pictures of the moon under a report quoting the PLANET's rotation period and axial tilt, because the fixture had constexpr int32 DaySweepBody = 1. It now asks the world which body it built, and reads 724.67 hours and 0.0 degrees -- what a tidally locked moon should. STILL THE PLANET'S: the settlement spawns on the moon too, which is a base rather than a town and is not obviously wrong but nothing decided it; and the surface reads as pale rock on a tan plain, which is the shared material's height blend rather than snow, since moisture is zero by construction. Whether an airless body wants its own surface composition is T053's, and T053 waits on a texture-array decision. 82 tests pass, module layering legal.

evidence.caption: 0.104 g on the moon and no atmosphere, with the retention rule checked against Earth, Mars, Titan, Mercury, the Moon and Ceres
Noon on the moon: black sky, no atmosphere, same terrain code path as the planet

tasks.title: Gas giants
tasks.detail: Volumetric banding, storms, and a surface you can descend into until pressure ends the attempt.
tasks.acceptance: Descend into a gas giant: bands resolve, pressure rises, and the ship is destroyed at the depth the atmosphere model predicts.

notes.text: HALF DELIVERED AND COMMITTED; the other half is named below. The generator now makes a gas giant beyond the frost line (4.5 to 7 au), because that is where they can form -- past the distance at which water is ice rather than vapour, so there is enough solid material to build a core big enough to hold hydrogen. A gas giant has no surface, so altitude needs a datum that is not one: the one-bar level, which is the convention a giant's quoted radius already uses, so RadiusMetres keeps meaning the same thing whether or not anything is solid underneath. PRESSURE: predicted crush depth 135.8 km, and a descent stepping down a metre at a time failed at 135.8 km -- two computations, a logarithm and a loop, agreeing to under a metre. The pressure law is checked against the differential equation it solves: stepping dP = rho g dh in five-metre slices over 150 km with rho recomputed each slice, worst disagreement 3.1e-4, which is the first-order integrator's own error rather than the model's. AGAINST JUPITER, two findings. (1) THE EQUATORIAL RADIUS IS NOT A DETAIL: Jupiter's quoted 24.79 m/s2 is GM over its EQUATORIAL radius of 71492 km; asked with the volumetric mean radius of 69911 km -- which is what the generator uses, reasonably -- it gives 25.92, and the test failed until it was asked with the radius that number was quoted at. Two right answers to two different questions. (2) The scale height comes out 24.1 km against a measured 27, 11% low, because this model carries one mean molecular mass of 2.3 for every giant while Jupiter's is nearer 2.22, and because an isothermal profile is not Jupiter's. Both push the same way. Stated with the reason rather than opened until it passes quietly. The model errs SHALLOW -- it kills the ship sooner than a real atmosphere would -- which is the safe direction. BANDS ARE A FIELD, NOT A TEXTURE: a function of latitude, longitude and time anything can sample, which is what lets them be checked rather than admired. The jets alternate with quiet poles; the field carries more than twice the variance across the bands as along one, which is the difference between a gas giant and a marble; storms cover 3.64% and drift the way their own band blows. THE BUG THE DRIFT TEST FOUND: storms were placed EXACTLY on the jet boundaries, on the reasoning that a shear line is where a storm lives. A jet boundary is where the wind reverses, which is where it is zero -- so all nine sat in perfectly still air for ever and the drift test could not find one moving. They now sit a third of a jet's width off the boundary, embedded in one of the two jets and carried by it, which is also why they are lenses rather than circles. NOT DELIVERED: you cannot fly into it. The giant is five astronomical units away, the world builds one body's terrain at a time, and a body with no surface needs a volumetric renderer rather than a cube-sphere -- the framework T078 showed is body-agnostic is agnostic about SURFACES, and this has none. The acceptance's 'descend into' is unmet. What exists is the model it would descend through, measured, and the bands it would descend past, drawn. 88 tests pass, module layering legal.

The physics and the banding are done and measured; the descent is not. A body with no surface needs a volumetric interior rather than the cube-sphere, which belongs with T226's volumetrics and needs the atmosphere calibration that T074, T075, T077 and T079 are now all waiting on.

[2026-09-11] DONE, measured. -giant builds the system's first gas giant from the core's own fields (LedgerGiant bands, storms and zonal flow; LedgerGas pressure; LedgerRings) and descends from 20 km above the one-bar level in 100 m steps: 1.0 bar at 0 km, 2.2 at 30, 4.9 at 60, 11.0 at 90, 24.4 at 120, and the hull (built for 50 bar) fails at 147.00 km against the 146.99 km the pressure law predicts for 113 K -- within the step. BANDS RESOLVE: from orbit the globe shows belts, zones and storms; on the way down the field was flat below about two degrees (five octaves), so a descent over a band boundary saw one soft gradient. SurfaceAt now takes the caller's sample spacing and adds flatter-spectrum octaves (gain 0.7) only where four samples span a wavelength -- the globe and the tests see the field they always did, the descent's cap sees the eddies. Below ~60 km the cloud deck is the volumetric layer's (T094), and at 20 km the frame is still smooth.

evidence.caption: The band field drawn: alternating belts and zones with wobbling boundaries, and storm ovals sitting inside them
Crush depth predicted 135.8 km, reached at 135.8 km; Jupiter's gravity to 0.01 m/s2; storms drifting with their wind
The giant, its rings and the descent: pressure from 1.0 bar at the cloud tops to 50 bar, the hull failing at 147.00 km against a predicted 146.99 km.
3,000 km above a band boundary: the eddies inside the band resolve -- turbulence the field adds only where the sample spacing can resolve it.
From four radii on the star's side: belts, zones and storms, and the ring lit on its sunward face.

tasks.title: Ring systems
tasks.detail: Particle rings with self-shadowing and a shadow cast on the planet, flyable through rather than a texture on a disc.
tasks.acceptance: Fly through a ring plane: density resolves into particles and the ring's shadow moves across the planet correctly.

notes.text: HALF DELIVERED AND COMMITTED. The ring's geometry and its shadow are built and measured; flying through it is not. THE SHADOW SWEEPS A YEAR, and three things fall out of the table that nobody wrote: the shadow is always in the hemisphere the star is NOT over (declination negative, shadow north, and the reverse), because the ring shades the winter side -- that is the side the light has to cross it to reach; it VANISHES ENTIRELY at the equinox, where the star is 0.25 degrees out of the ring plane and the ring throws a line of zero width, which is what Saturn does every fifteen years; and its width tracks the declination, 23 degrees across when the star is 16 degrees out of the plane and 5 degrees when it is 3.7. There is no shadow code that knows about seasons -- there is a line from a point on the surface towards the star and a question about whether it crosses the annulus. WHERE A RING CAN BE: the outer edge is the Roche limit for icy rubble, computed rather than chosen -- 158530 km, or 1.96 body radii, against Saturn's rings ending at about 2.3 of its own. THE REASONING THIS TASK GOT WRONG: the first version refused rings to rocky bodies on the grounds that a rocky body's Roche limit sits barely outside its surface so there is nowhere to put them. That is BACKWARDS and the test said so with both numbers side by side -- the rocky planet's limit is 4.40 radii against the giant's 1.96, because the limit scales with the cube root of THE PRIMARY'S density and a dense body has MORE room for icy rings than a puffy one. Earth's Roche limit for ice is over four Earth radii. The real reason the inner planets have none is supply: ring material is ice, ice is not solid inside the frost line, and what little arrives is swept up or dragged down. So the condition is now about where a body formed, and the Roche limit does the job it actually does, which is setting the outer edge. GAPS ARE RESONANCES: a particle whose period is a simple ratio of a shepherd moon's gets the same nudge at the same place every few orbits and ends up elsewhere. Five gaps covering 23.94% of the ring's width, landing where the moon puts them since a period ratio of N is a radius ratio of N to the two-thirds -- and the converse is checked, because with no moon the ring has ZERO gap samples. They come from the moon rather than from a stripe pattern. NOT DELIVERED: you cannot fly through it. Density resolving into particles at close range needs the same volumetric machinery T079's descent needs, behind the same atmosphere calibration. 91 tests pass, module layering legal.

The ring geometry and its shadow are done and measured; flying through the plane and resolving density into particles is not. Same volumetric dependency as T079, behind the same M04 atmosphere calibration.

[2026-09-11] DONE. Flown through and photographed (-giant). FROM OUTSIDE the ring is an annulus from 1.20 to 2.22 radii, brightness from its optical depth, each face lit only when the star is on its side (one shared normal had lit both faces from above and neither from below, so with the star 22 degrees under the plane the whole ring rendered black). This giant has no shepherd moon inside its rings, so the only open bands are the tapers at the edges (67,286-69,614 and 122,269-124,597 km); the resonance gaps T080's core tests measure need a moon and none is there. IN THE PLANE the ring resolves into rubble: a lattice of 15 m cells around the camera, 60 m either side of the plane, filled at min(0.8, tau/2) with the baked rock -- 9,119 pieces within 300 m at tau 1.2 -- and the sheet, which has no thickness, is not drawn inside it. THE SHADOW moves: the star 22.0 degrees below the plane puts it on latitudes 5.8 to 32.5 north; half a year later, 20.3 degrees above, on -28.8 to -5.2 -- always the winter hemisphere, as the core's year sweep predicted, and it is the same ShadowAt the globe is painted with. Exposure is metered on the brightest tenth of the frame (the disc, or the rubble), not the black around it. Not done here: particles shadowing each other (the rubble casts none -- a lattice-footprint black square otherwise).

evidence.caption: A year in twelfths: the ring shadow sweeps from +27 to -27 degrees and vanishes at the equinox
Roche limit 1.96 body radii, shadow always in the hemisphere the star is not over, zero width at equinox
The star 22 degrees below the ring plane: the ring's shadow is the dark band across the northern (winter) hemisphere, latitudes 5.8 to 32.5; the ring's own unlit face is black against space.
Half a year later, the star 20.3 degrees above: the shadow has moved to the southern hemisphere, -28.8 to -5.2.
150 m above the densest ring (optical depth 1.2), looking 60 degrees down into it: the sheet resolves into rubble, 9,119 pieces within 300 m.
In the ring plane: rubble on every side, 2,913 pieces ahead of the camera.

tasks.title: Asteroid fields and small irregular bodies
tasks.detail: Non-spherical bodies need a different mesh path from the cube-sphere, and orbits that are individually tracked rather than instanced.
tasks.acceptance: Land on an irregular asteroid with correct local gravity direction at every point on its surface.

notes.text: Gravity on an irregular body from a sum over its actual mass, not a formula about its centre. 'Correct' is the load-bearing word in the acceptance: the cheap answer -- straight at the centre -- is exactly right on a sphere, wrong on everything else, and looks right in a screenshot either way. THE CHECK THAT THE SUM IS A GRAVITY FIELD: set irregularity to zero and the shell theorem says the answer must be GM/r^2 at the centre. Integrated mass 0.060% out; at 10 radii the magnitude is 0.06% out and the direction 0.0000 degrees off. A fifty-thousand-term sum that cannot do the one case anybody can do by hand is not doing the others either. THE LEAN: across 400 surface points gravity leans 3.09 degrees off radial on average and 7.64 at worst, against the same integrator's 1.0242 degrees on a sphere -- so 7.5 times its own floor. THE FLOOR IS MEASURED, NOT ASSUMED, AND THE CLAIM IS STATED AGAINST IT. Evaluating gravity exactly ON a surface is the integrator's worst case, since the point sits amid the cells it is summing, so a perfect sphere still reads about a degree of false lean there; that is real and will not go without a much finer grid. An earlier version asserted the floor was under half a degree. It is not. Comparing signal to a measured floor is a better test than comparing it to a number somebody picked. EVERY POINT, which is what the acceptance says: 2000 surface points, ZERO with gravity pointing outwards, worst local slope 34.79 degrees, and surface gravity running 0.002546 to 0.002765 m/s2 -- you weigh nine per cent more at one end than the other because the near end of a lumpy body is nearer its own mass. THE SHAPE WAS WALKED DOWN, NOT THE BOUND WALKED UP: at irregularity 0.32 the body carried 50-degree slopes and at 0.22 it carried 40. Loose material sits at an angle of repose near 35 and slumps past it, so faces that steep would have rearranged themselves long before anybody landed. It is 0.18 now and its slopes are ones a real asteroid is observed to hold. A TRAP WORTH NAMING: the first run reported gravity 90.0000 degrees off at ten radii while the magnitudes were right to a fifth of a per cent all the way out. GetSafeNormal tests the SQUARED length against a default 1e-8; an asteroid pulls at thousandths of a metre per second squared, and ten radii out it is 2.8e-5, whose square is 7.8e-10 -- under the threshold. The default normalise returned a zero vector and every angle taken from it came out a right angle. Documented on GravityAt, because any caller normalising a micro-gravity vector meets the same wall. NOT HERE: the drawn mesh. The shape is a displaced sphere -- defined everywhere, askable in any direction, and the same function that gives the surface gives the mass distribution -- and turning it into geometry reuses the icosahedron path T434 built for stones. That is a rendering job and not what decides whether the gravity is right. 94 tests pass, module layering legal.

evidence.caption: Shape and gravity lean over the surface: radius 0.90 to 1.12 of mean, lean up to 7.64 degrees off radial
Shell theorem to 0.0000 degrees at 10 radii; 7.64 degree lean against a 1.02 degree floor; zero of 2000 points pointing outwards

tasks.title: Orbital stations and platforms
tasks.detail: Structures on rails around a body, with their own local frame that things can dock to and stand in.
tasks.acceptance: A station's position matches its orbit over a simulated month, and a docked ship stays docked.

notes.text: A station is a body: parent, orbit, and the ephemeris puts it where it belongs. Nothing new was needed for the first half of the acceptance except a fourth row in the system description. ON RAILS: station at 556 km altitude, 96.7 minute orbit, 28.4 degrees inclination. Over 30 days in 20000 steps the two routes to its position -- the whole-system walk summing a parent chain, and the direct 'parent's place plus its own orbit' -- differ by at most 0.000000 m, and one orbit returns it to within 0.000000 m. A station is two orbits deep, so the sum has to come out the same either way. THE FRAME IS THE ORBIT'S, NOT THE STARS': up away from the parent, forward along the track, third axis from those -- the local-vertical local-horizontal frame every real spacecraft uses, costing nothing extra because both vectors are already in the state the ephemeris returns. Up is 1.479e-06 degrees off outward and the basis is right-handed to 1.453e-10. Forward is NOT exactly the velocity and should not be: on an eccentric orbit the velocity has a radial part -- the station climbing and falling -- which belongs to up, and the 0.0939 degree angle between them is this orbit's eccentricity of 0.00164 showing itself. STAYING DOCKED: the dock stays 41.665 m out to within 3.333e-05 m over a month, and its local coordinates return to within 3.487e-05 m, while being carried 44143 km in a quarter orbit. BOTH BOUNDS STARTED TIGHTER THAN THE ARITHMETIC CAN REACH: the station is 1.5e11 m from the primary and the dock 42 m from the station, so recovering the second from the first throws away eleven digits -- a double's last bit at 1.5e11 is about 20 microns and both figures are a couple of those. The first bound written was a micron, finer than any correct implementation could have met. Same mistake in a second place: the frame axes were probed with a one-metre lever arm, putting 20 microns of subtraction noise on a 1 m vector and reporting a thousandth of a degree of false lean; a hundred-kilometre arm reads the same direction with the noise divided by a hundred thousand. WHAT THE STATION BROKE, AND WHY THAT IS THE POINT: adding a fourth body IMMEDIATELY FAILED a test green for two tasks. Ledger.SkyBody.PhaseMatchesTheSunTargetObserverGeometry walks every pair, and the station is 556 km above a 6320 km planet -- the formula said 0.38102 of it was lit where sampling its surface said 0.05268. The formula was never wrong; (1 + cos a)/2 assumes the observer sees a hemisphere, and nothing in the system had previously been close enough to anything to leave that domain. So the domain was measured rather than assumed: out by 0.314 at 1.05 radii, 0.036 at 5, 0.017 at 10, 0.004 at 40. A PER CENT WANTS ABOUT FORTY RADII. Five was the figure guessed before measuring -- and written into the exclusion before the table existed -- and it is out by nearly an order of magnitude. The documented domain is now the measured one, with a test that walks an observer in and records the breakdown so nobody removes the restriction on the grounds that it seemed to work. Every real pair clears it easily; the closest is a planet seen from its own moon at sixty-seven radii, and the only thing that trips it is something in low orbit, which is exactly what a station is. 98 tests pass, module layering legal.

evidence.caption: Position exact over 30 days, dock held to 33 microns, and the far-field phase formula's domain measured at forty radii for a per cent

tasks.title: Gravity field from real masses
tasks.detail: Inverse-square from every significant body rather than one hardcoded constant, including the transition between spheres of influence.
tasks.acceptance: A ship coasting between two bodies follows the trajectory the two-body model predicts, and the dominant body switches cleanly.

notes.text: A coast under the pull of every body, checked against the two-body prediction. THE COAST: a circular orbit 2000 km up (6770 m/s, 128.7 minutes) integrated with RK4 under every body and compared against a rotation -- with no perturbation the ship traces a circle at a constant rate, so the prediction at time t is the starting offset turned by 2*pi*t/T, computed from nothing the integrator touches. Worst departure 1273.0 m in 52277 km of arc, which is 2.44e-05 of the orbit. THREE NUMBERS, BECAUSE ONE WOULD NOT HAVE MEANT ANYTHING. A non-zero drift proves nothing by itself: an integrator accumulates error too, and a field that had quietly dropped every body but the planet would still wander. (1) Halving the step gives 1273.0 m against 1273.0 m, a change of 0.00% -- the integration has converged and the residue is physics. (2) Taking the other bodies out of the FIELD drifts 166 km against 185 km predicted from half-a-t-squared on the planet's own 6.20e-03 m/s2 fall around the star. THAT CAME OUT THE OPPOSITE WAY ROUND FROM WHAT I EXPECTED AND IS THE BETTER RESULT: the planet-only field is not slightly worse, it is a hundred and thirty times worse, because the frame is not inertial -- the planet is falling around the star, so a ship that does not feel the star does not accelerate with it and falls out of the frame. The star is not a small correction to a coast near a planet; it is what keeps the ship WITH the planet at all. A MISTAKE ON THE WAY THERE: the first attempt to isolate the field zeroed the other bodies' MASSES, which also stops the planet's own orbit since its mean motion is computed from its parent's mass. The planet stood still while the ship kept the velocity it had been given, and the test reported a drift of 1.4e11 m and blamed the integrator. Only the field may be cut down; where the bodies ARE is not the variable. THE SWITCH: spheres of influence are 893795 km for the planet, 69022 for the moon, 41998298 for the gas giant and 0 for the station -- correct, since a hundred tonnes has no gravitational reach. Walking the 388515 km from planet to moon in 200000 steps gives EXACTLY ONE change, at 69020 km against a 69022 km boundary, which is one step of the walk. A boundary that chattered would make a trajectory planner switch reference frames dozens of times in a row and every switch is a chance to lose a digit. INSIDE A BODY the field falls linearly to zero at the centre rather than dividing by nothing: nothing should ever be down there, but a trajectory that ends up inside a planet should produce a wrong answer rather than an infinity that poisons every step after it. At the surface the summed field is 9.549345 m/s2 against the planet's own 9.545979 -- everything else in the system is three parts in ten thousand. 101 tests pass, module layering legal.

evidence.caption: 1273 m from the two-body circle over one orbit, converged; 166 km without the star; the dominant body switching once at the sphere of influence

tasks.title: System generation from seed
tasks.detail: Star class, planet count, orbits, compositions and moons, generated to be plausible rather than uniform — hot rocks close in, gas giants further out, habitable zones where the star puts them.
tasks.acceptance: Twenty generated systems are all physically plausible and none is a rearrangement of another.

notes.text: Twenty systems, all plausible, none a rearrangement of another. PLAUSIBLE IS NOT AN OPINION: every rule was built and measured by an earlier task in this milestone -- frost line from T079, Roche limit from T080, Hill sphere from T083, mass-luminosity from T076. This is where they stop describing one system and become constraints on all of them. THE TWENTY: 8 to 19 bodies, stars 0.63 to 1.45 solar which is a luminosity range of 0.153 to 4.376, 1 to 5 giants, 2 to 11 moons. THE HABITABLE ZONE FOLLOWS THE STAR AND NOTHING SAYS SO ANYWHERE: the dim star's world sits at 0.495 au and the bright one's at 2.926, because the zone goes as the square root of the luminosity and the luminosity as a power of the mass. Across all 190 pairs: 0 identical, 0 rearrangements (compared on the sorted multiset, since the acceptance says rearrangement and not merely difference). THE CHECKER EARNS ITS KEEP BY REFUSING, and by refusing for the RIGHT reason -- checking only that a broken system is rejected lets a case pass on somebody else's rule, and two did: moving the home world out to four au was meant to test the habitable zone and was refused for landing next to a gas giant; moving it in to a tenth of an au was refused because a Hill sphere scales with the orbit, so its companion ended up outside a sphere that had shrunk by seven. Breaking one thing means breaking exactly one thing, and each case now asserts the reason it names. WHAT THE CHECKER FOUND IN THE GENERATOR: the first run rejected SIXTEEN OF TWENTY and every rejection was real. (1) 'The planets are not in order of distance' was the CHECKER's fault -- a rule about the array rather than the system, refusing any description that listed the home world before an inner planet. Where a body sits in the description is nobody's business but the description's; planets are sorted by distance before spacing is checked. (2) MOONS HAD MOONS: the giant's index was computed inside the moon loop as Num()-1, which is the giant only until the first moon is added, so eighteen systems had a moon orbiting a moon. (3) Pairs seven or eight mutual Hill radii apart, because a geometric walk outwards does not know how heavy the next planet is -- the mass is chosen first now and the orbit pushed out until there is room. (4) SMALL GAS GIANTS LIGHTER THAN BALSA: radius-as-mass-to-the-0.08 says a small giant is nearly as wide as a large one and therefore far less dense, and a 0.12-Jupiter body came out at 265 kg/m3. Real small giants are DENSER -- Neptune is a sixteenth of Jupiter's mass, a third of its radius and half again its density. Two segments fitted through Neptune, Saturn and Jupiter: 0.52 below a third of a Jupiter mass, 0.14 above where degeneracy holds the radius flat. TWO INDICES, NOT FIVE: Generate used to produce exactly five bodies and seven test files had learned that body 3 was the gas giant and body 4 the station. A system with four planets and one with seven cannot both put a giant at index 3. Only body 0 (star) and body 1 (home world) are fixed now; everything else is asked for by role, and two of the seven converted files were then found to be looking at the wrong body entirely -- an eclipse test measuring something nowhere near the sun, and a noon test whose 'moon' had become an inner planet with a months-long day. The mass-luminosity relation moved to LedgerBodies in the same pass, because the generator needs it before anything has a sky. 104 tests pass, module layering legal.

tasks.title: Time acceleration for testing
tasks.detail: Run the ephemeris and climate at a thousand times normal so a year can be inspected in minutes, without the renderer trying to keep up.
tasks.acceptance: A simulated year runs in under a minute and ends in the state the analytic model predicts.

notes.text: A year of 29,013,065 s stepped hourly in 12 ms, ending on the analytic answer to the bit (0.000e+00 s out, 0.000000 m). Skipping a century and placing every body: 3 microseconds, because the ephemeris is a function of time rather than an integration. Advance was rewritten to measure every step from the interval's start -- accumulating SecondsFromEpoch eight thousand times is an integration of the clock itself, and it drifts. docs/comparisons/time-acceleration/

tasks.title: Ephemeris determinism and agreement tests
tasks.detail: Two processes, one seed, identical positions; and the sky agrees with the ephemeris at a hundred random times and places.
tasks.acceptance: Sky and ephemeris agree to the arcminute in every sample.

notes.text: Sky and ephemeris agree to 6.4705 arcseconds at 100 random times and places, against an arcminute asked. The residual is parallax -- 6.4802 arcsec predicted from radius over distance, worst case with the sun 0.6 degrees up -- and is asserted with a floor as well as a ceiling. The first draft (navigator's identity vs SolarAltitude) agreed to zero because both come from the same SunDirectionInBody vector; it was replaced with a route that goes the other way round the frames. Determinism: 44 rows across two processes, 0.0000 m. docs/comparisons/determinism/

tasks.title: System map and query API
tasks.detail: What is where, how far, how long to get there. The Command lens in M22 is a view over this and so is every travel decision before it.
tasks.acceptance: Travel time between any two sites is queryable and matches what actually flying it takes.

notes.text: A quote of 6.80 days flies in 7.34 -- +7.5% to +10.4% across three departures, arriving 1 km out at 133.6 m/s against the 132.9 that stops in that distance. The overrun is accounted for: 2.7% is the 10% steering margin by arithmetic, the rest is 1,154 km/s of the 6,140 burned going sideways to match a destination that moves across the route. Four pilots were tried; three unrelated ones all came out at exactly +21%, which was the clue that it was never the steering -- the curve and the brake were drawn at the same throttle, so a ship above the curve could never come back. Ruled out: integration error (20x finer steps moved it 0.05 points). docs/comparisons/travel-time/

tasks.title: Playable proof: watch a moon transit and then fly to it
tasks.detail: Rule 6. The gate, run and recorded.
tasks.acceptance: A moon rises, transits and sets on schedule; then it is flown to and landed on, in one session.

notes.text: The schedule is right and the photographs do not show it. Rise, transit and set are computed from the ephemeris and the renderer places the moon at the predicted altitude to 0.000 arcminutes; the frames are night sky with nothing above the horizon, cloud edge to edge at transit, and a washed-out white sky at set. A 0.72 degree moon is 69 pixels in a 20 degree frame at 1080p, so this is not a size problem -- it is the over-dense atmosphere and the cloud layer, the same blocker as T074, T075 and T077. Unblocks with M04 T089 and T094. docs/comparisons/moon-passage/

Re-run after T089. Half the blocker is gone: the atmosphere is no longer washing the sky out -- the home world's sky is blue and the deck is broken cumulus at 1.2-5.2 km rather than solid overcast at 2-8. What remains is purely cloud placement: the transit frame is now a broken deck with black gaps in it, and the moon is behind a patch. That is a weather problem (where the clouds are), not a sky problem, so the block moves from T089 to T092 and T094.

Blocker moved again. The passage frames are no longer behind a solid overcast -- after T094 the moon transits at 79 degrees through 43 per cent cirrus. They are black because it is night and nothing renders a night sky at this exposure yet, which is the star field and exposure rather than the clouds.

Half unblocked: the moon rises, transits and sets and all three are now photographed. The night was black for three reasons and none was the ephemeris -- an exposure floor at -4 EV100 that clamped every night, a star field that was computed in T077 and never drawn, and a 1.5 s settle photographing the middle of a twenty-seven-stop adaptation. What remains is the second clause: flown to and landed on IN ONE SESSION. The world builds one body's terrain at startup and the sky places bodies for an observer on the home surface, so the crossing is still two processes. docs/comparisons/night-sky/

The machinery for the second clause exists: SwitchToBody tears the world down and BuildWorldFor builds it again around another body, one frame apart. The crossing runs -- watch, departure, cruise, arrival, with the world genuinely changing bodies mid-session -- and then the process takes an access violation on the render thread about fourteen seconds later, during the landed step. Four real defects were found and fixed on the way there and none of them was the cause: a failed asset load retried every frame (147 ms stalls, in T093's wind subsystem, affecting every run); the ship caching a planet pointer and re-fetching only when null rather than when invalid; the sky renderer keeping the old body's sphere set; and the planet being spawned non-deferred, so on a rebuild it woke before its surface material was assigned and fell back to an engine vertex-colour debug material. Ruled out as the cause: the destination being airless (same crash to a body with air), the teardown and rebuild sharing a frame (split, no change), the view target being destroyed (kept alive, no change), and a level-of-detail jump from orbit to the ground (graded descent, no change). The same body is completely stable when built at startup with -body=.
unblocked

Both clauses, in one session. The crash was a function-static TMap of raw UTexture2D* in LedgerBiomeSurfaces.cpp with nothing rooting it: the first world's materials died, the collector took the textures, and the second world built its palettes on freed memory. -forcelogflush is what found it -- the last line before the fault was 'LogUObjectBase: Warning: Object is not registered' right after a palette was created. Rooted with TStrongObjectPtr, with an IsValid check so a stale entry reloads and says so. Then three of the six frames came back black or blown out, and that was a second real defect rather than framing: SunFacing is the star's direction in the ACTIVE BODY's rotating frame and the switch never recomputed it, so the moon's landing site was chosen against the planet's sun vector -- sun.site 0.946 and solar altitude -80 degrees for the same place. The town was built in the dark. One line after SetActiveBody and they agree at 0.946 and 71.1 degrees. Also: the stand-off is measured in the radii of whichever body is underneath (the arrival is above a moon a third the size), the clock is clamped at arrival so the landing is minutes after it rather than five hours, and with no air the exposure meter moves to the 70th-96th percentile because a frame that is half sunlit ground and half pure black has no meaningful average. Terrain stats now print process memory: a saturated 3600-section pool costs 10.8 GB against 2.5 at startup, 2.3 MB a patch, and a warning fires when commit headroom drops under 2 GB. Landed in b00fe76. docs/comparisons/crossing/

tasks.title: Atmosphere profile per body
tasks.detail: Composition, surface pressure, scale height and lapse rate as data. Earth's numbers become one row rather than the only row.
tasks.acceptance: Three bodies with different atmospheres render correctly from ground and orbit from data alone.

notes.text: Composition, pressure, scale height, lapse rate, Rayleigh coefficients, ozone and cloud deck now computed per body. Five real atmospheres through the same function: Earth 8428 m against 8500, Mars 10856 against 11100, Venus 15940 against 15900, Titan 20638 against 21000, Jupiter 24061 against 27000. Rayleigh from refractivity and number density, not a slider; blue/red ratio exact at 5.70. Grey greenhouse turns 255 K into 288.1 on Earth and 232 into 721.6 on Venus from the same two lines. Surface pressure and free oxygen are stated as generated/assumed rather than derived. Three bodies captured from ground and orbit. docs/comparisons/atmosphere-profile/

tasks.title: Scattering for non-Earth compositions
tasks.detail: Rayleigh and Mie coefficients derived from composition, so a CO2 sky is the colour physics says and not the colour someone liked.
tasks.acceptance: A thin CO2 atmosphere produces a butterscotch sky and a blue sunset, from composition alone.

notes.text: Half delivered, half not expressible. The butterscotch sky is there from composition alone: CO2 scatters blue 2.86x harder than air, so a clean CO2 sky would be DEEPER blue than Earth's, and what turns it is the dust -- iron oxide with a single-scattering albedo of 0.63 blue against 0.94 red. Predicted before rendering (Mars R 1.000 G 0.928 B 0.681; the same air with the dust removed R 0.176 B 1.000) and confirmed by capture. The blue sunset is not: it is a diffraction effect needing a per-channel phase function, because the forward lobe narrows as wavelength over particle size. Unreal's Sky Atmosphere has one MieAnisotropy for all three channels, so the aureole takes the colour of MieScattering, which for dust is red. Needs a custom sky shader or a separate aureole element -- M11. docs/comparisons/sky-colour/

Blocker found while fixing the black town: the engine's sun transmittance for fog, forward, Lumen and RT lighting is ONE global value computed as if the viewer stood at the planet top along world +Z (FAtmosphereSetup::GetTransmittanceAtGroundLevel, engine TODO). Per-pixel transmittance fixes deferred opaque only; the elevation floor is now driven each tick from the viewer's true solar elevation (SetTransmittanceMinLightElevationAngle), which fixes the colour at and above the true angle but cannot redden below it. A true blue sunset needs a world frame whose +Z is the viewer's up (rotate the world, not the sun).

[2026-09-11] THE BLUE SUNSET: the aureole, from composition. Unreal's sky gives the aerosol one Henyey-Greenstein lobe for all three channels; a particle much bigger than the wavelength scatters about half of what it removes by diffraction, into a peak round the sun whose width goes as lambda/r (two over the size parameter), narrower and so brighter-centred in the blue. LedgerAir now carries the aerosol's radius (Martian dust 1.5 um, sulphate haze 0.3) and gives, per channel, the peak's width and its share of the sky's scattering (half the extinction over the albedo -- an absorbing dust puts more of its blue in the peak -- times the aerosol's share against the gas, faded in between size parameters 4 and 10). A post-process pass (M_Aureole, linear light, sky pixels only) multiplies each channel by (1 - F) + F * peak / HG: both integrate to one, so it moves light towards the sun and adds none. Test: on Mars's numbers the blue share is 0.78 against red 0.53 and Earth's haze gets 0.000. MEASURED in one run, one weather, the pass switched between two frames (two runs of a world do not share their weather -- the first comparison had snow in one and not the other): blue over red within 60 px of the sun 0.36 off, 0.76 on; 420-600 px out 0.57 and 0.58. So the redistribution is there and nothing far from the sun moves. On this world the core is cream, not blue: it holds 55,666 Pa of carbon dioxide and its gas takes half the blue from the dust (share 0.45 blue against 0.49 red). Queued: the same frames under Mars's own air (-marsair: 610 Pa, 210 K, 3.71 m/s^2), where the arithmetic gives 3.2x the blue boost instead of 2x. The sun-transmittance blocker (one global value evaluated as if at the pole) is unchanged: the aureole is the sky's colour near the sun, not the sun's.

[2026-09-11] DONE: a butterscotch sky and a blue sunset from composition alone. Under Mars's own numbers (-marsair: carbon dioxide at 610 Pa and 210 K under 3.71 m/s^2, through the same LedgerAir arithmetic as every generated world -- the one carbon-dioxide world the fixtures had holds 55,666 Pa, ninety Martian atmospheres, and its gas takes half the blue from the dust): by day the sky away from the sun is butterscotch (blue over red 0.49 in the ground view, 0.38 at the zenith); with the sun two degrees up, the sky within 60 px of it reads blue over red 1.03 with the aureole pass and 0.76 without, measured in one run and one weather with the pass switched between two frames, and 0.90 against 0.88 at 420-600 px -- the blue concentrates towards the sun and the rest of the sky stays put. The aureole is the dust's diffraction peak, per channel, from the aerosol radius the composition gives (Martian dust 1.5 um: peak widths 0.093/0.117/0.144 rad at 440/550/680 nm, shares of the sky's scattering 0.78/0.57/0.53), applied as the ratio of the phase function with the peak to Unreal's one lobe, which conserves energy. Not solved here and still on record: the engine's single global sun transmittance (evaluated as if at the planet's pole) for fog, translucency and Lumen -- that is the sun's colour on the ground, not the sky's, and it needs the world frame rotated to the viewer's up.

Control: the carbon-dioxide world (seed 20260900, body 2), the sun 2 degrees up, the aureole pass off. Blue over red 0.36 within 60 px of the sun.

The same run, the same weather, the pass on: blue over red 0.76 within 60 px of the sun, 0.58 at 420-600 px (0.57 with it off). The dust's diffraction peak, narrower in the blue, concentrates blue towards the sun.
Mars's own air (-marsair: carbon dioxide at 610 Pa, 210 K, 3.71 m/s^2), the sun 2 degrees up, the aureole pass off: the one-lobe sky, blue over red 0.76 next to the sun.
Same run, same frame, pass on: blue over red 1.03 within 60 px of the sun -- blue exceeding red, the blue sunset -- and 0.90 at 420-600 px (0.88 off).
The same air by day, away from the sun: butterscotch, blue over red 0.49 (0.38 at the zenith).

tasks.title: Volumetric fog that is not planar
tasks.detail: Exponential height fog fills space from orbit because it has no notion of a sphere. Ground fog, valley inversion and haze need a volumetric layer bound to the body.
tasks.acceptance: Fog fills a valley at dawn, is absent on the ridge above it, and is invisible from orbit.

notes.text: The model is right and the renderer only shows it close up. Delivered: a nocturnal cooling model from surface thermal inertia (2 F sqrt(t) / (I sqrt(pi))) calibrated against Earth 18.0 K, Venus 0.00 K and Mars 73.5 K against a measured ~70; a cold pool depth from turbulent diffusion, 86 m by dawn; a dew-point threshold that makes fog appear in the second half of the night; and a grid of local fog volumes filled to a LEVEL, so 21 of 36 cells fill and the ridge stands 3096 m clear by arithmetic. Invisible from orbit. Not delivered: from a ridge 12 km away the frame is indistinguishable from the -fogoff control -- the pale field filling the valleys there is T089's aerial perspective, not this fog, and only running the control revealed that. Ruled out: a per-view volume budget (144 one-km cells vs 36 two-km ones changed nothing) and density (the component's extinction is per unit sphere, so it wants tau = k*d; corrected, it is visible from inside and still not at 12 km). A bank that reads across a landscape wants the volumetric cloud system with a low layer -- T094. docs/comparisons/ground-fog/

Correction: the fog is not visible from the ridge either. The grey sheet over the valley in the ridge frame is there with -fogoff too -- it is shadowed low ground -- and the ridge frame differs from its control by 35% of pixels for other reasons. Diagnosed with switches on the one volume: a hundredfold height density (visibility 4 m by the model) changes nothing in any view (valley 1.0 of 255 from the control); the radial term at 100 per unit radius changes every pixel in the valley and ridge frames (72 and 65 of 255) and nothing from orbit. So the volume draws and the tile culling assigns it everywhere (r.LocalFogVolume.TileDebug), and it is the height term alone that contributes nothing. Also found: the engine scales HeightFogFalloff by 0.01 before packing, so 400 was 4 in the shader and the sharp top this was designed around never existed. Running: the engine's own height defaults with and without the rotation, to say whether the height term renders at all here and whether the rotation breaks it.

State after a day on the engine side (fog code uncommitted, diagnostics in LedgerGroundFog.cpp). Established from LocalFogVolumeCommon.ush / LocalFogVolumeRendering.cpp and measured: (1) radial and height coverage multiply, so the radial term must be on -- with it at 0 nothing ever drew; (2) densities are per metre (the unit-sphere optical depth is scaled by the radius in metres); (3) HeightFogFalloff is scaled by 0.01 before packing; (4) the volume is placed exactly as intended (centre 11,360 m above the fill level on the axis, radius 14,200 m), both cameras inside; (5) with a flat falloff the pool renders as sensible graded haze, near ground clear and distance fading; (6) any steep falloff (engine value >= 20) turns every view into a uniform saturated wall, identical at 1x, 0.01x and 0.001x density and at offsets -0.8 and -0.95 -- which the shader's own formula does not predict; (7) the same volume turned upside down (-fogflip) draws almost nothing. Unexplained: (6). Next: reproduce it in a minimal scene (small sphere, camera inside, engine-default falloff) to separate engine behaviour from this setup; or give the pool its top another way (two volumes, or a flat falloff inside a sphere sized to the pool).

Finding (6) explained from LocalFogVolumeCommon.ush, and it is this setup, not the engine. The height density is Extinction * exp(-Falloff * (z - Offset)) EVERYWHERE in the sphere, and with the offset at the fill level it grows by e every 36 m below the top -- not only over the sampled valley but over all ground inside the sphere's lower cap, 2.84 km deep and 8.5 km across: the four unsampled segments outside the 6x6 grid, gorges narrower than its 2 km spacing, lower valleys, the sea bed under translucent water. Ground 260 m below the fill level meets the fog at e^7 its top density, which is opaque at 0.001x. The terms then combine as T = 1 - (1-TR)(1-TH) in unit space, so wherever the height term saturates the pixel's opacity is the radial term's -- a saturating mask here -- which is why density scaling moved nothing. Why the local fog volume cannot hold this pool at all: the three terms are packed R11G11B10F (radial capped near 65,000); a low top in a big sphere gives the exploding cap; a top near the rim of a huge sphere puts the pool where the radial density (1-d^2) goes to zero. A wide, shallow, flat-topped pool is not a shape it can express. Next: a volume-domain material on a box, voxelised into volumetric fog (a flat, bounded top; absent from orbit beyond the volumetric fog distance), with the global height fog kept at zero density.

The pool, as a box of volume material in volumetric fog, measured against a -fogoff control on the same build: the valley frame differs in 84% of pixels (a fog of ~360 m visibility, the model's), the ridge frame in 24% -- the shadowed lowland that shows dunes and stones in the control is a flat pale sheet with the ridge clear above it, the top level because the box's density stops at 1,379 m. Orbit is wrong: turning on the height fog that volumetric fog needs makes the view from orbit a white disc under an orange sky (mean 115 against 24), and zeroing its own volumetric extinction did not change that. Now volumetric fog is on only while the camera is within 60 km of the pool; queued with its control.

All three criteria evidenced against a -fogoff control on the same build. Fills the valley at dawn: the valley frame differs from its control in 84.5% of pixels, a fog of ~360 m visibility, the model's. Absent on the ridge: the ridge frame differs in 23.8% -- the shadowed lowland that shows dunes and stones in the control is a flat pale sheet, the ridge standing 1,821 m clear of the 1,379 m fill level. Invisible from orbit: 0.0% of the orbit frame changes (mean 24.2 against 24.1), because volumetric fog is on only within 60 km of the pool. The mechanism is a box of volume material voxelised into volumetric fog; why a local fog volume cannot hold a wide shallow pool is in the notes above.
