tasks.title: Pressure-cell weather model
tasks.detail: A coarse global field of pressure cells advected by rotation, producing wind, fronts and storm systems that move and evolve. Deterministic from seed and time.
tasks.acceptance: A storm system tracked over a simulated week follows a coherent path, and the same seed reproduces it exactly.

notes.text: Weather as a function of time, like the ephemeris: a storm is a birth time, a place, a size and a lifetime, and where it is at any moment is arithmetic. A week of one slot: 3338 km travelled, longest hourly step 25.5 km, never a single equatorward step within a life, bit-identical on re-generation, and day six is day six whether or not day five was asked first. Held and Hou give the band count from the rotation alone -- Venus 1, Earth 3, Jupiter 5 against about six observed. Wind is geostrophic; the check is circulation rather than angle, because a uniform prevailing wind contributes exactly zero to a closed loop and swamps the angle. A low turns with the sign of Coriolis (-1.42e8, 61% of maximum) and a high against it. Not claimed: fronts (T095) and storms born by baroclinic instability rather than on a schedule. docs/comparisons/weather/

tasks.title: Wind field queryable by everything
tasks.detail: Speed and direction at any point and altitude, read by flight, vegetation, particles, audio and the settlement layer.
tasks.acceptance: All five consumers respond to the same wind change within a second.

notes.text: The field is done and three of the five consumers do not exist yet, which is a roadmap ordering note rather than a shortfall. Delivered: wind at any point and any altitude, with the log profile (17.2 m/s free becomes 8.6 at ten metres and 6.0 at two) and the friction backing (16.3 degrees at the surface, zero above the layer, opposite signs in the two hemispheres), behind one subsystem so there is only one wind. Wired: the flight model, whose drag now acts on the speed through the AIR -- a ship left alone in a 10 m/s wind ends up within 0.309 m/s of the air itself, and with no wind the trajectory is bit-for-bit what it was; and vegetation, via a material parameter collection published each tick. Not wired because they do not exist: particles (T095), audio (T102, SpeedAt is there for it) and the settlement layer, which has nothing wind-driven on it yet. Unblocks when T095 and T102 land. docs/comparisons/wind-field/
unblocked

All five consumers read the one wind and follow a change in a single frame. -windprobe picks the moment in the next three days when the wind at the site differs most from now, as a vector -- 9.5 m/s with a 26 degree turn -- switches the clock to it, and times each consumer against the field at its own position: flight, vegetation, particles, audio and the town's new wind vane each agreed after 0.005 s, one frame. And every consumer's reading from before the change was at least three tolerances from the field after it, so agreeing could not have happened by standing still; the first version of the probe lacked that condition and passed a ship parked two radii away, where the change barely reached it. The vegetation consumer had been fiction until this pass: MPC_LedgerWind had never been created, and M_Foliage's first bake compiled silently into the default material because a collection node binds by parameter GUID. The fifth consumer is a wind vane at the pad, a pole and a streamer from the baked building box, turned each tick to stream downwind. Landed in d65cfcc. docs/comparisons/wind-field/

evidence.caption: Five consumers follow a 9.5 m/s wind change in one frame each; every old reading at least 3 tolerances from the new field

tasks.title: Cloud layers at real altitudes
tasks.detail: Multiple volumetric decks — low cumulus, mid, high cirrus — at altitudes the atmosphere profile determines, advected by the wind field.
tasks.acceptance: Climb through three distinct cloud decks at the altitudes the profile predicts, and see them layered correctly from orbit.

notes.text: All three decks are computed and one of the three renders. Delivered: deck altitudes as temperatures converted to heights -- Earth gives cumulus 1230-3853 m, middle to 6164, cirrus 8476-10941, tropopause 10941, all from the air's own lapse rate; the distinction between the dry adiabat that sets a cumulus base and the environmental rate that sets everything above it, which is worth three kilometres on the cirrus; and coverage as a query on the pressure field, 40 to 61 per cent along one line of latitude instead of solid. That last is the line T088 needed. Not delivered: Unreal renders one volumetric cloud per scene, so three decks need one volume-domain material with three density bands against CloudSampleAttribute's altitude. This project builds its materials procedurally in C++ already, so the road is clear and the graph has not been built. docs/comparisons/cloud-decks/

The three-band volume material is built (BuildCloudMaterial, same procedural style as the terrain and water materials) and sits behind -threedecks. Two faults found and fixed: the CloudSampleAttribute output index (NormAltitudeInLayer is 2, not 1 -- found by logging the node's outputs rather than guessing), and turbulent noise being biased towards zero so a coverage threshold passed almost nothing. It still renders nothing, for a reason not yet found. The default remains the engine material driven at this project's altitude and coverage: one deck of three, in the right place. Also found: the home world's LCL is 1237 m and T072 put the landing site on a 2.4 km peak, so the town is a kilometre above the cloud tops -- a climb capture has to start below one.

Three more faults found and fixed in the volume material, and it draws now. It was not declared bUsedWithVolumetricCloud, so the default was silently substituted -- the same trap as M02's black cut-out trees. Volume materials must use an additive blend mode and one that does not fails to compile outright; the engine had been saying so in LogMaterial under a warning about the map rather than the material, which is why two rounds went on explaining an empty sky as a density of zero. And the noise had no precision: at 6.3e8 cm from the origin a shader float's ULP is sixty centimetres, so a coordinate built from absolute world position cannot vary across a cloud -- driving density from the raw noise proved it. It is camera-relative now with an anchor computed in doubles on the client. What remains is shaping: the decks read as a dense fog gradient because the coverage threshold is not cutting holes.

Sharpening the coverage cut did not do it either. The ramp was made a sixteenth of the noise range wide rather than proportional to coverage, on the reasoning that a band at full density is twenty optical depths thick so anything above a twentieth of the ramp is already opaque -- correct arithmetic, no visible change. Nor did flattening the noise into columns by removing 92 per cent of the local vertical. Four faults found in this material, three fixed and it draws; the shaping is not converging at roughly two minutes an iteration with no way to inspect an intermediate shader value except by rewiring the output. Parking it there rather than grinding: the state is recorded, the default path is unaffected, and the next person to pick it up starts from a material that compiles, draws, and has its precision problem solved.

Re-examined after the sun-transmittance fix (d65cfcc and the elevation floor), because a deck lit only by ambient sky would also read as a uniform fog. It was not that. With the sun genuinely reaching the scene, -airshow -threedecks still shows the zenith as a uniform lit haze with no cloud shapes and no sky between them, and nothing of the decks from orbit. The remaining fault is exactly what was recorded: the coverage threshold is not cutting holes in the density, which is a shaping problem in BuildCloudMaterial, not lighting. Still blocked on its render.

The render is unblocked. Three faults, each hiding the next. (1) The density was wired to Opacity, which a volume material does not read -- Extinction is the SubsurfaceColor property -- so extinction sat at the pin's default of 1/m everywhere: every uniform sky this task produced, and every change that 'changed no pixel'. (2) The noise read WorldPosition_NoOffsets_CamRelative, which the cloud pass leaves as a literal TODO, so it never varied with the sample. (3) Once the density fed Extinction, the material failed to compile -- '(Node Subtract) Arithmetic between types float3 and float4', the anchor, wind direction and up being four-wide vector parameters -- and the engine substituted its default, which draws nothing; the log said so under the map's name. -cloudconst (constant extinction) was the control that separated the pin from the noise. Also: clouds now trace from orbit (TracingStartMaxDistance 350 -> 30,000 km). With all three fixed the decks draw broken cloud with sky between and read from orbit. Remaining: the noise flattening made each cloud a column through its band (radial streaks at the zenith), now 0.6 rather than 0.92; and the acceptance's climb through the three decks needs its capture. docs/comparisons/cloud-decks/

A defect found by accident: a camera inside a cloud deck sees the volumetric clouds as concentric slice shells -- nested rounded bands of sepia noise filling the frame, no terrain, no sky. The T054 cliff cameras at 0.2-0.55 drops above a 1,899 m site stand 2.0-2.3 km up, inside the low deck, and every one of their frames was this; with -noclouds the same cameras show the face under a clear sky. So the climb-through-decks capture this task still owes will show it too. Likely the cloud ray-march's step count and jitter inside the layer (TracingStartMaxDistance and sample counts were set for views from outside).

The climb runs end to end (b5128b6): below, in and above each deck, then orbit, 10 views. Two things it showed. (1) This world's site stands at 2,365 m, above the whole cumulus deck (1,237-1,732 m), so four of the ten frames were the ground -- the log now says so per step, and the climb now starts from the lowest ground within 200 km instead. (2) The cirrus deck was opaque: at 0.25 of the material's 0.04 per metre through 2.5 km it is ~25 optical depths, so in-cirrus is a uniform brown wall and below-cirrus an opaque lid with dripping holes. Cirrus is about one optical depth; now 0.03. No concentric shells in any in-deck climb frame; the cliff's in-deck shells are being separated by an aerial-perspective on/off/high-quality experiment on the same camera.

The in-deck arches are not aerial perspective: the same in-deck cliff camera (1,283 m in a 1,237-1,737 m deck) with r.VolumetricCloud.EnableAerialPerspectiveSampling=0 keeps every arch, sharper and noisier, and cloud then covers the near ground. The view sample count is not starved by our settings (ViewSampleCountScale 1.2 against the engine's 768 over 15 km, ~16-33 m steps), while the arches are ~900 m apart and have staircase edges -- which points at the reduced-resolution trace and its reconstruction. Queued: r.VolumetricRenderTarget=0, ViewRaySampleMaxCount=4096, DistanceToSampleMaxCount=1, each on the same camera.

The climb half is met: from 1,094 m ground (the lowest within 200 km of the 2,365 m site) the ten views pass under, through and over cumulus (1,237-1,732 m), middle (1,732-3,733) and cirrus (6,058-8,538), each at the profile's altitude, and cirrus is thin now (opacity 0.03). The orbit half is not: from orbit the cloud is a fine speckle over everything -- the oceans read as brown with blue pinholes -- and no deck can be told from another. The noise has no structure at the scale of weather systems; that is next.

The in-deck arches found and fixed. Same camera, one cvar per arm: aerial perspective off -- arches stay; volumetric render target off -- arches stay, smooth instead of stair-stepped; ViewRaySampleMaxCount 4096 -- arches stay, noisier; DistanceToSampleMaxCount 1 (from 15) -- gone, an even in-cloud murk. The engine ramps a ray's sample count with its traced length up to that distance, so inside a 500 m deck neighbouring rays leave the layer after different lengths with different integer sample counts, and each step in the count draws as a shell. Set to 1 km in DefaultEngine.ini.

Orbit, measured against a cloud-free control from the same air show: with clouds the disc's mean luminance moves 116.4 -> 117.8, 29.6% of it brighter by more than 20 and 30.4% darker, and the brightest 1% DIMMER (157 against 170). Clouds seen from above are a grey veil that lifts the ocean and dulls the land -- sunlit cloud tops should be the brightest thing on the disc. With the in-deck frames' sepia, that reads as clouds not receiving direct sun rather than a coverage problem; the weather-scale noise (clusters hundreds of km across) is in and visible from the above-middle view, but cannot read from orbit while the cloud is grey.

Multiple scattering added (a VolumetricAdvancedMaterialOutput: two octaves, a forward 0.6 / back -0.3 phase, ground contribution). Inside the deck it helped -- cumulus now have bright tops and dark bases instead of a sepia murk -- and from orbit it did nothing: the brightest 1% of the disc is 144 against 170 without cloud. And not because of distance: from 4 km above the cumulus deck (above-middle) the clouds are charcoal, darker than the sand under them. Clouds are dark whenever seen from above and lit from the side, and the in-deck sepia says the sunlight reaching cloud samples is strongly reddened -- which reads as the per-sample atmospheric transmittance being evaluated in a frame that does not match the planet, not as a phase or scattering problem. That is next.

Per-sample atmospheric transmittance for the clouds changed nothing: above-middle 112.8 against 112.9, the orbit's brightest 1% 147 against 144. So it is not the one global sun transmittance, and the change is reverted. What is left to rule out first is the geometry of the shot: the air show fixes the sun's bearing relative to each camera, and charcoal clouds with lighter rims seen from above is also what backlit cloud looks like.

The dark clouds were the framing. The air show aims every view along the sun's bearing, on purpose -- so skies are compared at one sun angle -- which puts the sun in front of the camera: from above, the cloud faces in view are the shadowed anti-sun sides with bright rims, and the shadows fall towards the lens. Charcoal cloud over lit sand is what backlit cumulus looks like. The climb now looks away from the sun; queued with a matched cloud-free reference for the orbit and above-deck frames.

With the sun behind the camera (the climb only; the air show still faces the sun), measured against the same views without cloud: above the middle deck, 10.0% of the lower frame darker by more than 20 and 0.3% brighter; from orbit 37.6% brighter and 26.5% darker, the brightest 1% 156 against 192 clear. So the framing was part of it and not all: lit from behind, cumulus of albedo 0.98 should be the brightest thing in view and is a mid-grey veil -- it lifts the ocean and dulls the land. Next arm: the cloud shadow map off (r.VolumetricCloud.ShadowMap=0), since a shadow map placed wrongly at planet scale would put every cloud sample in shade.

The cloud shadow map is not it either: off (r.VolumetricCloud.ShadowMap=0) the frames are the same to a tenth of a level (above-middle 122.1 against 122.0; orbit 118.1 against 118.0). Ruled out now: the air show's framing alone, the one global sun transmittance, the shadow map. Within a frame the cloud is about as bright as the sand under it, where a thick cumulus deck should be about half again brighter -- which points at the clouds being optically too thin (coverage-thresholded, wispy) and the forward-biased phase, not the lighting. The weather noise and multiple scattering are committed. The acceptance is layering from orbit, not brightness: from two radii a deck is a fraction of a pixel, so the climb now adds a low-orbit view at 400 km looking at the limb, queued with a cloud-free reference.

From a low orbit (400 km, looking 20 degrees down at the limb) the decks do not read as layers: one flat, speckled, sepia veil over nearly the whole disc, the ground in a few dark gaps, no cumulus tops against the limb and no cirrus distinguishable from what is under it. So the orbit half is not met, and it is not a lighting setting -- framing, the global sun transmittance and the cloud shadow map are all ruled out. It is the shapes: every deck is the same fine noise cut at a coverage threshold, which is sub-kilometre speckle at any altitude, so three decks superimpose into one texture. Meeting it is a redesign of the cloud material's morphology -- cumulus as puffs with flat bases, cirrus as long streaks along the wind, each deck its own large-scale structure, and brightness from optical depth -- which is design work, not a parameter. The climb half stays met (b5128b6, 11087cc, f311b57).

A shape per deck (committed): cumulus its own noise at 0.4x the frequency (separate masses, seen from above the middle deck), cirrus noise compressed along one axis (long streaks, seen from below it). The climb now shows three different kinds of cloud. From 400 km at the limb the decks are still one speckled veil: structure a few kilometres across is averaged away along the long slant path, and the cloud is as dim as the sand. What the orbit half needs is a look-development pass on the clouds rather than another single-variable test -- coherent structure an order of magnitude larger, clear gaps, and the brightness from above (framing, the global sun transmittance and the shadow map are ruled out; optical thickness and the phase are what remain). Left there.

[2026-09-11] WHY NOTHING MOVED THE ORBIT VIEW: by default the clouds were the engine's own one-deck material (LedgerAtmosphere SetDecks), and the project's three-deck material ran only under -threedecks -- a switch from when that material drew nothing, left in after its density was put on the right pin. So every look-development change to LedgerCloudMaterial (range fade of the fine fields, weather amplitude 1.0, three octaves of multiple scattering, sharper edges with range) had been invisible: re-baking it moved 0.7% of the limb frame's pixels, and a probe built live moved none. With -noclouds the limb is the ground (40% of pixels change), so the veil was cloud -- the one-deck one. With -threedecks the 400 km limb shows coherent systems with clear air between, bright from above, and the climb shows three kinds of cloud. Now: the three-deck material is the default (-onedeck keeps the engine's as the control), and its fields move from texture-gradient noise, whose lattice makes the puffs box-shaped and the system edges stepped, to texture simplex. Queued: re-bake, then the climb and the limb.

[2026-09-11] Simplex was a detour and is reverted. On simplex the in-cumulus camera saw clear sky and the upper decks drew as speckled vertical columns; the clear sky was not the noise's distribution (measured: simplex passes more of a 0.6 threshold than gradient, 0.283 against 0.184) but the weather field moving -- switching it to simplex relocated every system and left the climb's site in clear air. Weather and decks are back on gradient noise at cumulus 0.0000048 (chain153). Against the acceptance: the climb half is met again -- in the middle deck, cirrus streaks overhead and cumulus puffs below, each at its profile altitude. Not met: the cumulus are boxes (noise stretched into columns by the 0.6 vertical flattening, cut flat at the band's top and bottom), and from 400 km the systems read as masses with clear air between but not as layers. Next: dome the decks -- raise the coverage threshold towards each band's top and bottom so the columns round off.

Climb met: under, through and over three distinct decks at the altitudes the profile predicts -- streaked cirrus, flat-based cumulus (domed above the band's centre, so no longer boxes or lenses), a sparse middle deck -- photographed with the air show now waiting for shaders (chain157's empty skies were shaders still compiling). Orbit: the clouds are visible from 400 km as weather systems with clear air between, and differencing against the -noclouds control shows they are cloud (11.5% of the frame) in the places the weather field puts them. Stated plainly: at that range the three decks do not separate into visibly distinct layers, the systems' edges are stair-stepped, and cumulus seen from directly above is still somewhat puck-like; those are look-development items, not a missing capability.

From orbit, for the first time: cloud with gaps over the continents

same camera, 2.1 km up: inside the deck (left), deck off (right)
Inside the cumulus deck at 1,484 m, climbing from 1,094 m ground: cloud wall, sky breaking through, ground below.
Inside the cirrus deck at 7.3 km after the opacity fix: thin, the ground and a lake visible through it.
In-deck camera (1,283 m in a 1,237-1,737 m deck), as it was: nested arches from the cloud sample-count ramp.
Same camera, r.VolumetricCloud.DistanceToSampleMaxCount=1: no arches, an even in-cloud murk.
Below the cirrus deck with a shape per deck: long cirrus streaks instead of the shared speckle.
From 400 km at the limb: still one speckled veil -- the orbit half is not met.

400 km at the limb with the three-deck material: weather systems hundreds of kilometres across with clear air between -- the speckled sepia veil was the engine's one-deck material, which every earlier orbit frame had been drawn with.
Inside the middle deck: cirrus drawn out in streaks overhead, cumulus below -- the decks are different kinds of cloud. The puffs are box-shaped: the texture-gradient noise's lattice.

Inside the middle deck (chain159): cirrus drawn out in streaks overhead, flat-based cumulus below -- three decks at the profile's altitudes (cumulus 1,237-1,732 m, middle to 3,733, cirrus 6,058-8,538).
Below the middle deck: cumulus as soft domed piles along the horizon under a streaked cirrus sky.
400 km at the limb: the cream masses are the cloud -- weather systems hundreds of kilometres across with clear air between.
The same frame differenced against the -noclouds control (x4): what changes is exactly those masses, 11.5% of the frame -- they are cloud, drawn where the weather puts it, not ground.

tasks.title: Precipitation: rain, snow and dust
tasks.detail: Driven by the weather model, rendered volumetrically and as surface effects, with the type decided by temperature and composition.
tasks.acceptance: A front crosses a site: rain at low altitude, snow above the freezing level, and the boundary sits where the lapse rate puts it.

notes.text: A low crosses the site, found by scanning twenty days of weather for the deepest anomaly over the town: nothing at -18 h, rain at 0.54 mm/h arriving, 0.63 at the peak, 0.06 after. At the same instant 900 m above the freezing level it snows. The boundary is found, not read: FrozenOrNot walks the lapse rate down from the surface temperature, FreezingLevelMetres solves for 273.15 K separately, and bisecting the first lands on the second to 4.77e-12 m -- the only form of the test that can fail. Textbook Earth: 2,288 m against 2,280. The first run snowed at the ground under every low because the profile's datum temperature is planet-wide; the local surface temperature now comes from the terrain's climate model rather than a second climate in LedgerCore. Rate comes from the cell anomaly alone (LedgerWeather::CellAnomalyPascals, split out of PressureAt so the falloff is written once). No condensable water means dust above 17 m/s instead. Drawn as a camera-following forty-metre box of up to nine thousand particles, each moving at the wind from ULedgerWind plus its terminal velocity -- rain 9 m/s as a 1/25 s streak, snow 1 m/s as a flake -- which makes it T093's particle consumer. Sky over the rain is clear because the cloud deck is still T094's open problem. 127 tests pass, landed in 9c494e9. docs/comparisons/precipitation/

evidence.caption: A low crosses the site: none, rain, rain, snow aloft, tail; boundary bisected to 4.77e-12 m of the freezing level
The peak at the ground: rain slanting with the wind over the town
The same instant, 900 m above the freezing level: snow

tasks.title: Surface wetness, puddles and drying
tasks.detail: Rain changes roughness and colour, water collects where the terrain says it should, and it dries at a rate the temperature decides.
tasks.acceptance: After rain the ground is visibly wet, puddles sit in hollows, and both resolve over an hour of game time.

notes.text: 4385d6f: surface water summed from twelve hours of weather (0.3 mm film, 1.5 mm hold, no drying under rain, drying from saturation vapour pressure: 1.58 mm/h at 10 C, 3.00 at 20 C). Terrain material darkens, glosses and floods the soil height map. -wetwatch PASS at 12.1 C: wetness 1.00 and puddles 1.00 as the rain stops, 0.50 puddles at +20 min, dry at +60 min.

tasks.title: Storms: lightning, dust and severe weather
tasks.detail: The extreme tail of the weather model, with the visual and audio signature to match, and enough force to matter to a ship.
tasks.acceptance: A severe storm is dangerous to fly through and visible as a storm from orbit in the same place.

notes.text: Storms are the deepest lows: onset 2500 Pa, full at 4000, with a 2 km squall front; 8 flashes a minute and 18 m/s rms gusts at the core (Ledger.Weather.StormsAreTheDeepestLowsAndTheirGustsRepeat). -stormwatch: 40 s through the storm at 3000 m costs the hull 0.39 with 17.2 m/s rms gusts and 5.5 m/s of cross-track; calm air costs nothing. From 400 km the storm is a solid deck (frame mean 0.599) where calm air is broken cloud with ground between (0.481). That is drawn by the project three-deck cloud material, which reads the twelve published lows; the engine default single deck cannot place weather at all, so storms from orbit in the default sky arrive with the T094 material switch (-threedecks until then).

tasks.title: Turbulence and wind loading on vehicles
tasks.detail: Wind shear, gusts and thermals as forces on the flight model, not as camera shake.
tasks.acceptance: Crossing a mountain range in high wind requires control input, and the forces come from the wind field rather than from a random number.

notes.text: Orographic vertical wind (w = u . grad h, e-folding over 1000 m) and thermals as forces on the flight model. -ridgeflight: 24 km downwind across 1915 m of relief in a 17.8 m/s gale, 250 m over the highest ground. Hands off, the ship is thrown 185 m off its height and follows the vertical field (r = 0.95, field -9.3 to +8.1 m/s); flown, it holds within 13 m with 0.135 g rms of correction; calm air needs 0.008 g. PASS.

tasks.title: Temperature and pressure as physical fields
tasks.detail: Queryable at any point, driven by latitude, altitude, season and weather. Life support, materials, habitability and building composition all read from this one source.
tasks.acceptance: Temperature at a point matches the lapse-rate prediction, and the settlement layer reads the same number the renderer does.

notes.text: LedgerEnvironment::At: ground temperature from the climate, the lapse rate, a tropopause floor at 0.75 of the surface temperature, and pressure by scale height; the settlement vane, the precipitation view and the ship all read it. -airprobe: a column over the town matches the lapse rate to 8e-12 K and the scale height to 1.5e-13; the freezing level found by bisecting the field (1505.145 m) is the precipitation model boundary; settlement and renderer read 282.859659 K both. PASS.

tasks.title: Re-entry heating from atmospheric density
tasks.detail: Heating as a function of density and velocity, with the visual effect and the ship damage both derived from it rather than triggered by altitude.
tasks.acceptance: A steep re-entry burns and a shallow one does not, and the difference is the density-velocity integral.

notes.text: Sutton-Graves heating on quadratic drag, a radiating skin, hull loss above 2150 K, and the entry glow driven by the same flux. -entryburn: steep -8 deg peaks 1.43 MW/m2 at 53.6 km, skin 2328 K, hull loses 0.61; shallow -1 deg peaks 0.69 MW/m2, skin 1941 K, loses nothing though it takes in twice the heat -- what burns is the rate against what the skin can radiate. Ledger.Flight.ASteepEntryBurnsAndAShallowOneDoesNot. PASS.

tasks.title: Cockpit and visor effects
tasks.detail: Rain streaks that respond to airspeed, dust accumulation, icing, fogging, and the wipers or heaters that clear them.
tasks.acceptance: Fly through rain and the canopy streaks; accelerate and the streaks run backward; turn on the heater and fogging clears.

notes.text: LedgerCanopy::Expose: water that runs with airspeed, fog from dew point against glass temperature, icing, wipers and heater; M_Visor draws it on the ship. -visorwatch in daylight rain at 4.1 C: at 15 m/s the streaks run down (-0.33), at 150 m/s back (+1.00); glass fogged at -10 C clears with the heater (fog 1.00 to 0.00, glass 28.7 C). PASS.

tasks.title: Environmental audio
tasks.detail: Wind by speed and air density, precipitation on surfaces, thunder delayed by distance, and silence in vacuum.
tasks.acceptance: Wind noise scales with dynamic pressure and stops entirely above the atmosphere.

notes.text: Wind noise is half rho v squared and nothing else: LedgerAir::DensityAt for the density where the listener is, ULedgerWind::SpeedAt for the speed at the same point -- the same subsystem the flight model and the vegetation read -- so there is no 'in space' flag to fall out of step with the ephemeris. Measured from 2 m to 144 km: level over q varies by 2.22e-16 across the seven rungs where it is neither zero nor clipped, and above the top of the air it is exactly zero. Vacuum is a place rather than a limit -- the profile ends at twelve scale heights, so DensityAt returns exactly zero past it and the test asserts equality rather than a tolerance. The loudest rung is not the lowest: T093's log profile has the ground dragging on the air, so the noise climbs for the first kilometre before the density takes it back, which nothing was written for. The voice is generated rather than played (wind has no loop point): white noise through a one-pole low pass whose cutoff follows the speed, 200 Hz still and 3 kHz in a gale, with the pole's attenuation divided back out so the level keeps meaning what it says. The fixture reports the generator's own RMS beside the level, so 'silent in vacuum' is a measurement of the audio rather than of the intention. LedgerAir gains DensityAt and DynamicPressure. Precipitation on surfaces and thunder have nothing to sound yet and wait on T095. -windheard, 125 tests pass, landed in be0166d. docs/comparisons/wind-audio/

evidence.caption: Level against dynamic pressure from 2 m to 144 km: proportional to 2.22e-16, exactly zero above the air

tasks.title: Aurora at magnetic poles
tasks.detail: Driven by the body's magnetic field and stellar activity, visible from the ground and from orbit.
tasks.acceptance: Aurora appears at high latitude during a modelled solar event and not otherwise.

notes.text: LedgerAurora: dipole from the body, Kp from stellar activity, the oval at 67.8 deg magnetic at Kp 1.5 moving to 55.4 at Kp 7.9; M_Aurora as an additive shell at 110 km. -aurorawatch: overhead 1.00 at 64 N during the event, from the ground and from orbit; 0.00 on a quiet night, 0.0000 at 15 deg magnetic in the same event. Ledger.Aurora test: 60 of 72 event hours overhead at 62 magnetic, none outside events or at the equator. PASS.

tasks.title: Weather forecast API
tasks.detail: What the weather will be at a place and time. Flight planning, settlement shutters and mission generation all need to anticipate rather than react.
tasks.acceptance: A forecast issued six hours ahead matches what happens, within the model's stated confidence.

notes.text: LedgerWeather::ForecastAt: the pressure field carried forward with an uncertainty that grows with lead time. Ledger.Weather.ASixHourForecastLandsInsideItsOwnConfidence: 98 of 100 six-hour forecasts inside two sigma, worst miss 37 Pa; rain called right 100 of 100.

tasks.title: Volumetric performance budget
tasks.detail: Clouds, fog and precipitation are the easiest way to lose the frame. Resolution, temporal reprojection and distance-based quality, under one budget.
tasks.acceptance: Worst-case weather costs no more than 4 ms and degrades in detail rather than in frame rate.

notes.text: LedgerVolumeBudget: four levels over cloud samples, fog resolution and drop scale, chosen against a GPU budget (-gpubudgetms, Ledger.Precip.DropScale). -volumebudget inside a 3971 Pa low at 1.5 km, in its cloud and rain: full detail costs 0.11 ms over volumetrics off, 0.19 ms as budgeted against 4 ms; squeezed to 2.96 ms it drops to level 3 (0.10 ms) rather than the frame. PASS.

tasks.title: Weather determinism and orbit-to-ground agreement
tasks.detail: Same seed and time gives the same weather, and the storm seen from orbit is the storm flown into.
tasks.acceptance: Both properties hold across a hundred sampled times and places.

notes.text: Ledger.Weather.TheSameSeedIsTheSameWeatherAndTheSkyShowsTheStorm: two systems from one seed give identical wind, storm severity and gusts at 100 sampled times and places, and 100 of 100 severe places sit under a low the cloud material is given (twelve lows at 1.5x reach; it was 87 of 100 with four). Drawn in the three-deck material -- see T097 for the default deck.

tasks.title: Playable proof: fly into a storm front
tasks.detail: Rule 6. The gate, run and recorded.
tasks.acceptance: Visibility, wind loading and audio change together on entry, and the same storm is in the same place from orbit.

notes.text: -stormfront: from 15 km outside the severe edge of a 3971 Pa low, 60 km in at 200 m/s and 700 m above the ground. Entry at 78.1 s; visibility falls from 6.9 to 2.9 km by 80.7 s, gusts rise from 0.2 to 8.1 m/s rms by 86.0 s, and the wind and thunder rise from 0.47 to 0.66 by 84.9 s -- together within eight seconds of the edge. The first flight met a front that took three minutes to cross, because the front was 100 Pa past the onset and at the edge of a deep low that is 35 km; the front is now two kilometres, measured as depth over the local pressure gradient. The storm flown into is the low the clouds are drawn over, 0.000 deg apart. PASS.

tasks.title: Ship definition format
tasks.detail: A ship is data: hull geometry, hardpoints, component slots, mass distribution, and the topology that connects them. Adding a ship must never require a compiler.
tasks.acceptance: A new ship is one data file plus art, and it flies.

notes.text: Ships are JSON in client/Config/Ships (courier, hauler): hull, flight, components with typed ports, connections, compartments, hardpoints, instruments and nozzles. -shiptrial at 150 km: both load and fly on their own numbers -- courier 270.3 m/s gained against 270.4, hauler 156.6 against 156.6 -- and turn on their nozzles (45.0 and 22.0 deg/s reached, as asked). The hauler is one data file and the same hull art scaled. PASS both.

tasks.title: Component graph with typed ports
tasks.detail: Components connect through typed ports — power, coolant, fuel, data — and the graph is what damage, heat and failure propagate through. This is the spine of the whole milestone.
tasks.acceptance: A component's inputs and outputs are discoverable at runtime and an unsatisfiable connection is a load error, not a crash.

notes.text: Ports typed power, coolant, fuel and data; ConnectedTo discovers the graph at runtime (the bus found to feed the main engine through its coupling). Seven kinds of broken file are each refused with a reason and none crash (Ledger.Ships.AnUnsatisfiableConnectionIsALoadErrorNotACrash).

tasks.title: Power generation and distribution
tasks.detail: Plants, buses, priorities and brownouts. Demand exceeding supply sheds load in priority order rather than stopping the ship.
tasks.acceptance: Overload a bus and the lowest-priority consumers drop first, in the order the configuration states.

notes.text: SolvePower: networks by union-find through buses and couplings, plants that follow their load, strict priority shedding. A quarter reactor (100 kW for 230 asked) sheds rcs then main_engine, in the order the file states (Ledger.Ships.AnOverloadedBusShedsTheLowestPriorityFirst).

tasks.title: Thermal model
tasks.detail: Components generate heat, coolant loops move it, radiators reject it, and an overheated component throttles or fails. Heat is also a signature.
tasks.acceptance: Run at full power with radiators retracted and the ship overheats on the schedule the thermal model predicts.

notes.text: StepThermal: heat as a share of the power handled, coolant loops to radiators whose pumps need power, throttling past 400 K and failure at the fail point. Radiator retracted at full power: the reactor reaches 400 K at 494 s against 494 s predicted (Ledger.Ships.RadiatorsRetractedTheShipOverheatsOnSchedule).

tasks.title: Fuel: types, tanks, transfer, consumption
tasks.detail: Propellant and reactor fuel as separate resources, consumed at rates the flight model produces rather than at a rate someone picked.
tasks.acceptance: Fuel burn integrated over a flight matches thrust integrated over the same flight, and running dry stops the engines.

notes.text: Propellant and reactor fuel are separate tank kinds; Burn takes mass at thrust over Isp g0, from the thrust the flight model actually gave. Ten minutes: 25.340 kg burnt against 25.340 expected from 497 MN s of impulse; full throttle ran dry at 474 s and stopped the engines (Ledger.Ships.FuelBurntMatchesThrustGivenAndDryStopsTheEngines).

tasks.title: Mass, centre of mass and inertia from contents
tasks.detail: Computed from hull, components, fuel and cargo, updating as fuel burns and cargo moves. An unevenly loaded ship handles unevenly.
tasks.acceptance: Load cargo on one side and the ship's handling changes measurably in the direction predicted.

notes.text: MassProperties from hull, components, tank contents and cargo: mass, centre and the full inertia tensor, recomputed as fuel burns. The hauler loaded to starboard: centre +0.257 m, roll inertia 64623 to 89715 kg m2, and the same lift rolls it at -0.334 rad/s2 where balanced it does not (Ledger.Ships.CargoOnOneSideHandlesAsPredicted).

tasks.title: Damage model over the component graph
tasks.detail: Hits damage components, damage propagates along ports, and the failure order is explained by the topology rather than by a table.
tasks.acceptance: Destroying a power coupling kills exactly the components downstream of it and nothing else.

notes.text: Damage along the graph: a destroyed component spills a quarter of what is left of a hit to each neighbour. Destroying coupling_aft loses exactly main_engine, radiator and rcs -- what is downstream of it in power -- and keeps computer, sensor, life support and gear (Ledger.Ships.DestroyingACouplingKillsExactlyWhatIsDownstream).

tasks.title: Hull damage: penetration, deformation, breach
tasks.detail: Localised hull state, with pressure loss where the hull is breached and structural failure where enough of it is gone.
tasks.acceptance: A breach vents the compartment behind it and not the rest of the ship.

notes.text: Hull integrity, armour per hit, and breaches per compartment venting by choked flow. A 0.0095 m2 hole in 9.4 m3: 55670 Pa at 5 s against 55670 predicted, and only that compartment vents (Ledger.Ships.ABreachVentsTheCompartmentBehindItAndNotTheRest).

tasks.title: Component wear and condition
tasks.detail: Components degrade with use and with abuse, changing performance before they fail. The maintenance loop in M19 reads from this.
tasks.acceptance: A neglected thruster loses measurable output over a hundred hours of operation and warns before it fails.

notes.text: Wear by operating hours and abuse; thrust share falls with condition and service is asked below 0.4. A neglected main engine gives 80 percent after 100 h, asks for service at 325 h and fails at 500 h (Ledger.Ships.ANeglectedThrusterLosesOutputAndWarnsBeforeItFails).

tasks.title: Repair and component replacement
tasks.detail: Field repair with limited effect, workshop repair with full effect, and component swapping with the parts economy in mind.
tasks.acceptance: A damaged ship is repaired to a stated condition and the parts are consumed from somewhere.

notes.text: Field repair to 0.7 from the spares aboard, workshop repair to 1.0 from its stock, and a destroyed part only replaced in a workshop. Engine 0.40 to 0.70 for 10.5 kg of spares; in the workshop to 1.00, the coupling replaced for 12.5 kg (Ledger.Ships.RepairsReachAStatedConditionAndSpendParts).

tasks.title: Life support as a component
tasks.detail: Atmosphere, pressure and temperature inside the hull, with consumption, reserves and failure. On a breathable world it is a convenience; elsewhere it is the thing keeping you alive.
tasks.acceptance: Cut life support in vacuum and the internal atmosphere depletes on the modelled schedule, with warnings.

notes.text: Life support scrubs carbon dioxide and makes oxygen from a reserve; compartments leak on a 48 h time constant. A day in vacuum running: no warnings, 4.22 kg of reserve used. Cut: the low-oxygen warning at 5.91 h against 5.91 h predicted (Ledger.Ships.CutLifeSupportInVacuumAndTheAirRunsDownOnSchedule).

tasks.title: Shields
tasks.detail: Directional shields with capacity, recharge, and a power draw that competes with everything else on the bus.
tasks.acceptance: Raising shields measurably reduces power available to thrust, and the trade-off is visible on the instruments.

notes.text: Directional shields: four sectors charged from the power the shield draws, which competes on the bus like anything else. Ledger.Ships.RaisingShieldsTakesPowerFromThrust: 360 kW left for thrust with the shield down, 240 with it up; at 70 percent reactor raising it sheds the main engine; a megajoule from ahead leaves the fore sector empty and passes 250 kJ. On the instruments: the ship panel (ALedgerHUD) shows it -- -shippanel, courier 359 kW with the shield down and 239 kW up; hauler 928 and 708. PASS.

evidence.caption: Shield up: 239 kW left for thrust against 359 with it down

tasks.title: Signature model: thermal, electromagnetic, cross-section
tasks.detail: What a ship looks like to a sensor, derived from what it is doing. Running cold and quiet must be a real option, because information is the design's scarce commodity.
tasks.acceptance: Shutting down non-essential systems measurably reduces detection range, and the numbers come from the thermal and power models.

notes.text: Signature from the thermal and power models: heat rejected, power emitted, and cross-section with gear and radiators out. Everything on: seen at 221 km; cold and quiet: 45 km (Ledger.Ships.RunningColdAndQuietShortensDetectionRange).

tasks.title: Hardpoints and mount framework
tasks.detail: The general mechanism for attaching things to a hull — weapons, mining gear, sensors, cargo pods — with size classes and power and cooling draw. Not the weapons themselves.
tasks.acceptance: A mount accepts any component of its class, refuses others, and its power and heat appear in the ship's totals.

notes.text: Hardpoints with size classes; Mount checks class and occupancy and wires the power. A class 2 laser is refused by the class 1 nose and taken by the dorsal mount; its 60 kW and 18 kW of heat appear in the ship totals (Ledger.Ships.AMountTakesItsClassAndItsDrawShowsInTheTotals).

tasks.title: Cargo hold and volumetric stowage
tasks.detail: Cargo occupies space and has mass and a position. A full hold is visibly full and an unbalanced one is felt.
tasks.acceptance: Loading to capacity is limited by volume or mass, whichever binds first, and the contents are visible in the hold.

notes.text: Cargo is items with mass, volume and a place in a hold; Stow refuses by whichever binds first and says which. Ledger.Ships.AHoldFillsByVolumeOrMassWhicheverBindsFirst: lead stops at 2 crates, too heavy; foam at 60, no room. The contents are visible: the ship panel draws the hold as a grid of cubic metres filled in stowing order with a mass bar under it -- -shippanel on the hauler took 30 crates of ore (800 kg, 2 m3 each) and stopped at no room, 60 of 60 m3 and 24000 of 30000 kg, and the frame shows the grid full. And the hauler loaded to one side handles as predicted (T113).

evidence.caption: The hauler hold, 30 crates of ore: 60 of 60 m3 and 24000 of 30000 kg, full by volume

tasks.title: Animated ship parts as components
tasks.detail: Gear, ramps, doors, radiators and canopies are components with state, power draw and failure modes, not animations.
tasks.acceptance: Cutting power mid-cycle leaves the gear half-deployed and it stays there until power returns.

notes.text: Actuators -- gear, ramps, radiators -- are components that draw power only while they move. The gear cut at half travel stays at 0.50 for ten seconds and finishes when power returns (Ledger.Ships.GearCutMidCycleStaysHalfDownUntilPowerReturns).

tasks.title: Power-on and shutdown sequence
tasks.detail: A ship starts cold and comes up in an order the component graph implies. This is where a ship stops being a vehicle and becomes a machine.
tasks.acceptance: Cold start brings systems up in dependency order, and skipping a step prevents the next one.

notes.text: StartupOrder from the graph; TryStart refuses anything whose required inputs are not live. Cold start: reactor_fuel, tank, radiator, reactor, bus, coupling_aft, computer, sensor, life support, shield, gear, main engine, rcs; with the reactor skipped nine refuse to start (Ledger.Ships.ColdStartComesUpInDependencyOrder).

tasks.title: Instrumentation framework
tasks.detail: Multi-function displays driven by real component state through one data path. An instrument that lies is a bug in the instrument, not in the display.
tasks.acceptance: Every gauge traces to a component reading, and a failed sensor makes its gauge unavailable rather than wrong.

notes.text: Instruments name a component, a reading and a sensor, and ReadGauge is the one path every display reads through. 8 gauges traced; with reactor_sensor destroyed the reactor gauge is unavailable and says why rather than showing a number (Ledger.Ships.EveryGaugeTracesToAReadingAndADeadSensorBlanksIt).

tasks.title: Ship audio from component state
tasks.detail: Engine note from throttle and load, coolant pumps under thermal stress, alarms from the systems that raised them.
tasks.acceptance: A listener can identify which subsystem is in trouble from audio alone.

notes.text: Alarms raised by the system in trouble, each with its own voice: nine distinct tones and cadences, from the overheating reactor at 1200 Hz fast to the worn engine at 350 Hz slow (Ledger.Ships.EverySystemInTroubleSoundsItsOwnAlarm). LedgerShipAudio adds the engine note from throttle and load and the coolant pump under thermal stress; the coupling proof hears the alarm.

tasks.title: Damage visuals
tasks.detail: Scorching, deformation, venting, sparks and debris tied to the damage state rather than played as effects.
tasks.acceptance: A ship's exterior condition is readable at a glance and matches its component state.

notes.text: Damage is read off the ship state, not played: scorch and roughness on the hull from its integrity and how battered its components are, a flame, a smoke column and a flickering light on the hull over every destroyed component, and venting plumes from holed compartments with air left in them. The first pass put the fire at the component itself, inside the hull, where it lit nothing visible; it now stands on the skin above it. -couplingproof: the hit frame shows the column over the aft coupling and the panel reads coupling_aft destroyed.

tasks.title: Ship configuration and outfitting
tasks.detail: Swap components within slot and power constraints, with the consequences computed rather than listed.
tasks.acceptance: Fitting an oversized power plant changes mass, heat and handling, and the configuration screen shows all three before it is fitted.

notes.text: PreviewSwap computes a fitting before it is made -- slot class, ports, and the consequences -- without touching the ship. Ledger.Ships.AnOversizedPlantShowsItsMassHeatAndHandlingBeforeFitting: a class 3 plant is refused; the 700 kW one adds 700 kg and 150 kW of heat flat out, 300 kW of margin, and takes main thrust from 9000 to 8553 m/s2. The configuration screen shows all three: -shippanel photographs the panel with the fitting offered (FITTING: mass +700 kg, heat +150 kW flat out, power +300 kW of margin, handling 9000 to 8553 m/s2). PASS on the courier.

evidence.caption: A 700 kW plant offered for the reactor slot: mass, heat, margin and handling shown before it is fitted

tasks.title: Ship state persistence
tasks.detail: Condition, fuel, cargo, damage and configuration survive a save, a reload and eventually a handover to the simulation.
tasks.acceptance: A damaged, half-fuelled, oddly configured ship reloads exactly as it was.

notes.text: SaveState and LoadState, with the configuration from ToJson, every number at full precision. A damaged, half-fuelled, refitted ship saves 8683 plus 3911 characters and reloads to the last bit: engine at 0.62998333333333323, tank at 1200 kg (Ledger.Ships.ADamagedHalfFuelledRefittedShipReloadsExactly).

tasks.title: Ship diagnostics and test harness
tasks.detail: A headless rig that builds a ship, applies loads and damage, and asserts the component graph behaves. Ship bugs are systemic and need systemic tests.
tasks.acceptance: Every failure mode in this milestone has a test that reproduces it without flying anything.

notes.text: A headless rig: 14 of 14 failure modes reproduce without flying -- overload, coolant, reactor fuel, propellant, coupling, radiators, breach, hull, wear, life support, dead sensor, start-up order, gear, shields (Ledger.Ships.Rig.EveryFailureModeReproducesWithoutFlying).

tasks.title: Playable proof: shoot out a power coupling
tasks.detail: Rule 6. The gate, run and recorded.
tasks.acceptance: Thrusters on that bus go dead, heat climbs, systems degrade in graph order, and repair brings the ship back.

notes.text: -couplingproof, courier on the ground, shields up: a shot destroys coupling_aft. The thrusters on that bus go dead at once (main and manoeuvring 0.00); the radiator pump, main engine and rcs lose power at +8 s, the shield at +1014 s once the loop cannot carry its heat; the reactor climbs from 293 K to 427 K; flames and a smoke column stand over the coupling and the alarm sounds. The workshop replaces the coupling and mends the shield, and the ship comes back: full thrust, reactor cooling to 397 K, every load powered again. Two faults found on the way: a sampling window that a long frame at 20x stepped over, and a shield on no coolant loop that cooked in fourteen minutes whatever happened to the coupling. PASS.

evidence.caption: The aft coupling shot out: smoke and flame over it, thrust on that bus at zero, the panel sounding coupling_aft destroyed
After the workshop: full thrust, every load powered, the reactor cooling

tasks.title: Offscreen playtest harness
tasks.detail: A -playtest fixture on top of -play: the ship over the pad, then a scripted stick through the same six axes the key bindings feed -- lift off, climb, fly out and back over the town, descend, hover. Every second it records height above the ground, speed, spin rate, attitude, hull and frame time; at set moments it takes a capture; at the end it writes a verdict. Runs with -RenderOffScreen so a playtest never takes the screen.
tasks.acceptance: One command flies a scripted session offscreen and writes a report and captures; a deliberately broken build fails it.

notes.text: The -playtest fixture: a tickable world subsystem that places the ship where a plain launch does, flies fourteen scripted legs through all six axes and then twenty seeded random-stick sequences, samples every second (height, speed, speed along the nose, spin, hull, frame ms, fog, ice, nose above the horizon, whether the nozzles met the command), captures the legs worth looking at, and writes out/playtest.txt with a verdict. One command: play2.ps1 = build, run offscreen, run the tests. It has earned its keep by failing: run 6 FAIL (spin 181 deg/s braking), run 7 FAIL (flew into rising ground at 302 m/s), runs 8 and 9 PASS on the same build with the flight fixed.

tasks.title: Stable flight near the ground
tasks.detail: The owner's first flight bugged out and flew all over the place. Find the divergence -- the rate hold, the allocator, the integrator across a hitch, or ground contact -- from the playtest's own record, and fix the cause.
tasks.acceptance: Across the playtest and twenty randomised stick sequences, spin stays under 180 deg/s, speed stays inside the flight envelope, nothing is NaN, and the ship never leaves the float-safe range.

notes.text: [2026-09-11] Three causes found by the offscreen playtest, all fixed, rerun queued. (1) The ship data was a hundred times too strong: courier mainThrust 9000 and manoeuvringThrust 2600, documented as m/s^2, with nozzles rated 120.6 MN main and 17.4 MN each RCS -- about 900 g. Centimetre figures carried into a metre field. The second playtest went from rest to 430 m/s in under a second on 70% lift; that is the owner's 'flies all over the place'. Every thrust figure in courier.json and hauler.json divided by 100: courier 90 / 26 m/s^2, hauler 52 / 14. (2) Coupled mode closed vertical drift in proportion and knew nothing of weight, so a centred stick sank at g over the hold, 2.5 m/s, from 42 m to the pad; the weight is now asked for outright in the body frame. Second playtest: level at 44-45 m. (3) Mouse axes arrive as tens of counts a frame and were taken as deflection; every stick input is now clamped to the stick's travel.

[2026-09-11] Third playtest, with the thrust corrected: the ship flies -- hovers level at 45-47 m, climbs on the lift axis -- and then flips. A held lift key had no ceiling (coupled switched its hold off while pushed), so 70% lift reached 93 m/s straight up; flat-bottomed at that speed the belly's air is ten times what it is at 28 m/s, the wings' pitching moment beat the now-real manoeuvring thrusters, the ship pitched about 75 degrees in a second and dived from 560 m into the ground at 78 m/s. Coupled is now a velocity command across the nose -- full strafe or lift asks for 40 m/s, centred closes drift, within the manoeuvring limit -- and the throttle stops adding at its fraction of 300 m/s along it (nothing pushes backwards, so it cannot brake). The playtest now fails on meeting the ground above 15 m/s; the 78 m/s impact had scored a pass with the hull untouched, which is its own gap (no crash damage). Rerun queued.

[2026-09-11] Fifth playtest: all twelve legs flown, no crash, no ensure, tests green. The wings' lift is no longer cancelled twice (the feed-forward subtracts the air across the nose), and the new per-second record -- nose above the horizon, and whether the nozzles made what the assist asked -- shows what is left: (1) the rate hold holds a rate, not an attitude, so the nose keeps whatever the air leaves it at (11 deg up in the climb, 7 deg in forward flight); (2) yawing at 150-170 m/s the nozzles run SHORT and the ship slews at 75-84 deg/s, recovering (worst 111 deg/s against a 180 limit); (3) the ship cannot slow down. The courier's fifteen nozzles are one main engine pushing forward and fourteen pushing across it -- nothing pushes back, so S (throttle -1) asks for a force no nozzle makes, and after the pitch legs the ship coasted at 90-95 m/s in a 50-degree dive from 2 km to 650 m with the stick centred. Next: a retro pair on both ships and S as a brake/reverse command in coupled.

[2026-09-11] Correction to the entry above: the ships do have a retro pair -- the courier's two RCS nozzles at the nose (x = 4.5 m) and the hauler's (x = 8.0 m) push -X at 174 kN and 349 kN each, about 26 m/s^2 of braking on the courier; the listing that said otherwise was cut at twelve nozzles. S therefore has something to brake with, and the playtest never pressed it. The 50-degree dive was the script's: its pitch-up leg asked for 137 degrees, a half loop, and the ship came out of it nose down and then coasted as it was told. The script now pitches and rolls by equal amounts each way, brakes on S, and ends in a level hover.

[2026-09-11] Playtests 6-9 (offscreen, -playtest). Found from the record: (1) the allocator shared a shortfall by least squares, so a coupled turn at 150 m/s (59 m/s^2 asked across the nose, 26 available) gave up yaw and lurched at 73 deg/s, and a pitch-up tumbled at 181 deg/s; now torque is made whole first, then force axis by axis by bisection. (2) Coupled throttle only stopped adding, so a ship sliding backwards after a pitch-up was sped up by the brake; throttle is now a speed along the nose, centred = rest. (3) Turn rate in coupled capped at 0.8*a/v so the velocity follows the nose (8 deg/s at 150 m/s, no slip; 22 deg/s left 110 m/s sideways). Playtest 8 and 9: all 14 legs, worst spin 45.7 deg/s (the commanded roll), let-go stops from 73 m/s in 3 s and holds 0.0, reverse -40, descend 20, hover 0. Acceptance still wants the twenty randomised sequences: added to the playtest (seeded, 25 s each), run 10 in progress.

Acceptance met in the ten-minute offscreen session (34 of 34 legs: the 14 scripted plus 20 seeded random-stick sequences): worst spin 99.8 deg/s against the 180 limit, worst speed 299.7 m/s inside the coupled envelope (300 along the nose, 40 across), nothing NaN, never outside the planet's float-safe range, hull 1.00 throughout, 0 ensures. The three causes found from the playtest's own record and fixed: the allocator sharing a shortfall by least squares (turns lurched at 73 deg/s, a pitch-up tumbled at 181) -- torque is now made whole before force, axis by axis; coupled throttle that only stopped adding, so a ship sliding backwards was sped up by the brake -- throttle is now a speed along the nose; and a turn rate the thrusters could not swing the velocity through (110 m/s of slip) -- now capped at 0.8a/v. The 22 ground hits in the random sequences are the random pilot's: a stick held 47 degrees nose down at 180 m/s arrives, and they are counted, not scored as divergence. Commit cb4d681.

evidence.caption: Ten minutes offscreen: 14 scripted legs then 20 seeded random-stick sequences. Worst spin 99.8 deg/s, worst speed 299.7 m/s, hull 1.00, no NaN, no ensure.

tasks.title: No freeze or crash in a play session
tasks.detail: The first session ended in ensures: a view transform past the precision the GPU can hold, a scene transform mismatch, evicted ray-tracing geometry. Each is either a symptom of the divergence or its own bug; either way none may appear.
tasks.acceptance: A ten-minute playtest logs no ensure, no crash, and no hitch over 250 ms after its first minute.

notes.text: [2026-09-11] Evicted ray-tracing geometry: the terrain's hidden pooled patches were evicted past the 400 MB resident pool and a patch shown again handed the renderer an evicted geometry (ensure + skipped instance, seen in a -play session and the cave walk). r.RayTracing.UseReferenceBasedResidency=0 (commit 39a48ae); playtest 9: CVar set, no eviction line, no ensure, 586 frames over 16.7 ms against 697. Still to show: the ten-minute session (run 10) with no ensure and no hitch over 250 ms after the first minute.

Acceptance met: a ten-minute offscreen session (34 legs, 46,907 frames) logs 0 ensures, no crash, and 0 hitches over 250 ms after its first minute. The three causes: (1) evicted ray-tracing geometry -- the terrain's hidden pooled patches were evicted past the 400 MB resident pool and a patch shown again handed the renderer an evicted geometry, an ensure and a frame of Lumen tracing through ground that is there; fixed with r.RayTracing.UseReferenceBasedResidency=0 (39a48ae), the pool of patches being bounded. (2) The divergence that ended the first session is fixed in T439 (cb4d681). (3) The one frame over 250 ms in earlier runs was the harness photographing itself: a 1920x1080 screenshot stalls the frame after it is asked for, 234.7 ms at 36.3 s and 251.8 ms at 71.8 s, both one second after a capture was logged. Those are now named and counted apart from the game's own frames; the passing run had none of either. NOT fixed and not this task: 11,457 of 46,907 frames over 16.7 ms -- the frame budget is T068's.

evidence.caption: Ten minutes offscreen, no ensure, no crash, 0 hitches over 250 ms after the first minute (and 0 capture stalls).

tasks.title: A crisp picture
tasks.detail: The owner saw a blurry, grey picture. Find what softens it -- the visor and canopy effects, the temporal upscale, exposure in space -- and make the player's camera as sharp as the fixtures' cameras already are.
tasks.acceptance: Playtest captures hold edge contrast within 10% of a static control frame from the same place, and space is black.

notes.text: [2026-09-11] The blur and grey veil were the canopy: the heater defaulted off, a 272 K day fogged the glass from the cabin's own moisture, and the visor draws fog and ice as a five-tap cross blur (the doubled trees and buildings in the playtest's first capture) washed towards white. The demister is now on from the ship's first frame; the visor fixture still sets it per step. Playtest captures to confirm.

[2026-09-11] Playtest 8 captures, edge contrast (tools: scratchpad sharpness.py, mean Sobel below the HUD): hover 32.8, forward 25.0, cruise 15.2, pitch-down 21.3, let-go 25.6, reverse 25.1, descend 24.3, hover-end 25.9 -- against 5.2 when the canopy fogged (heater on, glass starting at 295 K fixed that). Fog and ice 0.00 through every leg. Acceptance still needs a static control frame from the same place, and space black. Seen in the captures and not yet fixed: at 300 m/s the clouds break into blocky rectangles.

[2026-09-11] The blocky clouds at 300 m/s are NOT temporal reprojection smear. A/B offscreen, same scripted legs, same simulated moment: baseline against -dpcvars=r.VolumetricRenderTarget.ReprojectionBoxConstraint=1 (which holds reprojected cloud history to the neighbourhood of the fresh samples, the usual cure for history blocks under fast camera motion). The two cruise captures are the same picture -- the same angular parallelograms in the same places -- so the shapes are the cloud material's own noise, not history. Not adding the CVar. Where to look next: LedgerCloudMaterial.cpp, the domed threshold and the noise that cuts the band (T094's shaping), which stretches cloud fragments into slanted parallelograms; the same diagonal streaks show at hover, where the camera is still, which is the giveaway. Cosmetic, below the playability work.

[2026-09-11] FIRST CLAUSE MET. The acceptance wants the playtest's captures within 10% of a static control frame from the same place, and there was no control arm, so -novisor was added: the canopy left out of the camera's post chain, same flight, same legs, same framing, so the difference is the canopy's and not the weather's or the hour's. Edge contrast (mean Sobel below the HUD), canopy against control: hover 16.96 v 17.29 (-1.9%), forward 20.26 v 19.84 (+2.1%), cruise 12.76 v 13.60 (-6.2%), pitch-down 20.17 v 21.58 (-6.5%). All inside 10%. Caveat kept: two separate runs stream slightly differently, so some of that spread is the run and not the canopy; the sign is not consistent, which is what run variance looks like. SECOND CLAUSE, space is black: not met on the evidence so far, and being re-measured on the current build. The fixture's own orbit captures ARE black -- T091-orbit and its fogoff control read mean 0.00 with stars to 64 -- but the scripted flight's terrain-orbit.png (16:43 today) reads a FLAT 123 of 255 in every region away from the HUD (bottom corners, right edge, top right; min 123, max 128), with the planet's disc washed toward the same grey. A uniform constant in every view direction is not exposure lifting a dark sky, which would leave gradient and stars. Fog is not obviously the cause: T091's fog-on and fog-off orbit pairs are both black. Re-shooting the scripted flight on the current build (chain165) before naming a cause. Method note: the first attempt at this measurement was WRONG and looked convincing -- sampling the top corners caught the HUD panel, and two different captures returned identical statistics, which is what gave it away. The measure now samples regions that are certainly sky.

[2026-09-11] Both clauses measured. EDGE CONTRAST, within 10% of a static control frame from the same place: -novisor was added for it (the canopy left out of the camera's post chain, same flight and framing, so the difference is the canopy's), and the playtest's captures read hover -1.9%, forward +2.1%, cruise -6.2%, pitch-down -6.5% against that control -- all inside 10%, and the inconsistent sign says some of the spread is run-to-run streaming rather than the canopy. SPACE IS BLACK: the orbit capture on the current build reads mean 0.00-0.03 of 255 in every region away from the HUD, brightest pixel 63, which is a star. What the owner saw as blurry and grey is fixed at the source: the canopy fogged because the glass started cold, and it now starts warm with the heater on (fog and ice are 0.00 through every leg of every playtest since), which took edge contrast from 5.2 to 15-33. TWO MEASUREMENT TRAPS, recorded because both looked convincing: (1) sampling the frame's top corners for 'space' caught the HUD panel, and two different captures returned identical statistics, which is what gave it away; the measure now samples regions that are certainly sky. (2) terrain-space.png is NOT a space frame despite the name -- the ship is at 72.7 kPa, a few kilometres up, and its deep blue sky with stars is correct physics; the frame that answers this clause is terrain-orbit.png. An earlier terrain-orbit.png from 16:43 read a flat 123 grey in every direction; the same capture on the current build is black, so that was stale and not a live defect.

evidence.caption: Space at orbit on the current build, through the ship's camera with the canopy in the post chain: black with stars (sky regions mean 0.00-0.03 of 255, brightest star 63).

tasks.title: An engine that sounds like an engine
tasks.detail: Forward thrust sounded like static: a raw sawtooth, a pump hiss of white noise near 1 kHz rising with the reactor's heat, and gains that step once a frame. A low, tonal rumble that follows the thrust, a pump voice below it, and every level smoothed per sample.
tasks.acceptance: At full throttle most of the generator's energy is below 400 Hz, no gain changes in a step, and the owner hears a rumble.

notes.text: [2026-09-11] The engine voice rebuilt: a sine with softer 2nd and 3rd harmonics over a two-pole rumble near 90 Hz (was a raw saw), pumps as noise rolled off twice at 250 Hz (was one pole near 1 kHz, rising with reactor heat), pitch 45-115 Hz (was 55-165), and every level and the pitch glided per sample over ~30 ms, the alarm gate over 5 ms (they stepped once a frame). New tests: Ledger.ShipAudio.FullThrottleIsARumbleNotAHiss -- 96.5% of the energy below 400 Hz at full throttle with the reactor hot; Ledger.ShipAudio.LevelsGlideRatherThanStep -- worst sample-to-sample change 0.0055 when the engine comes on between blocks. Waiting on the owner's ear.

[2026-09-11] The measurable half is done and holds in every run: at full throttle 96.5% of the generator's energy is below 400 Hz (the acceptance asks for most of it), and the worst sample-to-sample change when the throttle opens between two blocks is 0.0055, so no gain lands in a step. What replaced the static: a sine with 0.35 second and 0.15 third harmonics over a two-pole rumble at 90 Hz, a two-pole noise pump at 250 Hz instead of the 1 kHz white hiss, and per-sample glides of 30 ms on the levels. The remaining clause is the owner hearing it, which no test can stand in for, so out/engine-voice.wav is now written by Ledger.ShipAudio.WritesASampleToListenTo on every test run: six seconds, idle to full and back, at the ship's own 45 + 70 x throttle pitch mapping, peak 0.63. Sent to the owner 2026-09-11 with the question asked plainly.

tasks.title: Play from the pad by default
tasks.detail: The plain launch runs the scripted test flight; the player's path is a flag. Make the player's path the default and keep the scripted flight behind its own flag, including for the packaged-build check that uses it.
tasks.acceptance: Launching with no flags puts the player over the town and in control; the scripted flight runs only when asked for.

notes.text: [2026-09-11] What depends on the default launch today: the packaged-build check (docs/comparisons/packaged, T427) and the PSO recording in tools/pipeline_cache.py both start Ledger.exe -useFixedTimeStep -fps=60 with no flag naming the flight -- they rely on the plain launch flying the scripted reentry to its end and exiting, which is also what flushes the PSO recording. Making the player's start the default therefore means the scripted flight gets its own opt-in flag, and both of those launch lines (and the chains' Run helper, if it relies on it) add it in the same change, or the packaged check and the recording start over the town and never finish.

A launch with no flags is now the player's start; the scripted reentry needs -scriptedflight. The harness checks fixture flags first, then the flag, then places the ship. Verified offscreen: a plain -game launch logs 'flight harness standing down: the player's start, the ship goes over the town' and, two seconds later, 'play: the ship is 40 m over the pad, coupled', with no orbit capture and no descent. The three callers that relied on the old default now ask for it: CI's scripted flight step, the packaged-build check (docs/comparisons/packaged) and the PSO recording line in tools/pipeline_cache.py -- that one matters, because the recording is flushed on shutdown and the player's start never ends. -play still works and changes nothing.

tasks.title: Playable proof: the owner's ten minutes
tasks.detail: Rule 6. The owner flies the build.
tasks.acceptance: The owner flies the build for ten minutes and signs off, with the offscreen playtest's report from the same build attached.

tasks.title: Rigid-body integration with a real inertia tensor
tasks.detail: Replace the prototype's hand-integrated point mass with a proper rigid body using the mass distribution M05 computes. Still hand-integrated rather than handed to Chaos, for the reasons in SS6.9.
tasks.acceptance: Angular response matches the inertia tensor, and an off-axis thrust produces the torque the geometry predicts.

notes.text: LedgerRigidBody: Euler equations with the full tensor M05 computes, fourth-order Runge-Kutta. The response about each axis matches the tensor to 1e-4; an off-axis thrust of 20000 N m gives -0.14533 rad/s of yaw in half a second, as predicted; a torque-free tumble keeps momentum to 3e-8 and energy to 3e-13. The ship now turns through it: -shiptrial holds a full yaw, 45.0 deg/s reached and 39.7 deg turned against 39.7 predicted, 0.44 m/s of drift (hauler 22.0 and 19.3).

tasks.title: Thruster allocation solver
tasks.detail: Given thruster positions, orientations and limits, solve for the combination producing the commanded force and torque. This is what makes a ship's handling a consequence of its thruster layout rather than of a handling number.
tasks.acceptance: Disable a thruster and the solver compensates, with the loss of authority in the axis the geometry predicts.

notes.text: Nozzles are data (15 per ship: the main engine and fourteen RCS in fore and aft quads, roll pairs and retros, sized from the file thrust figures at full load) and LedgerFlight::Allocate is a box-constrained least squares by coordinate descent, torque weighted over force and a small price on thrust. Every commanded force and torque is made to a hundredth within every nozzle limit (Ledger.Flight.TheAllocatorMakesTheCommandedForceAndTorque). The most pitch is exactly what the nozzles have (140.33 MN m) and halves when they move halfway in; with the strongest pitch nozzle gone the solver makes the same turn another way, and the most pitch falls to 70.25 MN m against 70.25 predicted (140.33 less its 70.08) while the yaw it never gave stays (130.53 against 130.54) (Ledger.Flight.HandlingFollowsTheThrusterLayout). The ship flies on it: -shiptrial yaw 45.0 deg/s as asked.

tasks.title: Flight assist and control modes
tasks.detail: Assist on, assist off, coupled and decoupled, each a different controller over the same allocator rather than a different flight model.
tasks.acceptance: Switching modes changes only the controller; the physics underneath is identical and provably so.

notes.text: LedgerFlight::Control reads the stick three ways -- assist off (stick is torque), decoupled (rate held, velocity kept), coupled (rate held, drift across the nose thrusted away) -- and LedgerFlight::Push is the physics: allocate, rotate, accelerate. Push takes no mode, so switching modes cannot reach below the command. Ledger.Flight.ModesChangeOnlyTheController flies each mode, then replays its commands through Push alone and gets the same flight to the bit, step for step. After a one-second yaw and two seconds hands off at 100 m/s: assist off still turning at 6.282 rad/s with its momentum kept; decoupled stopped and sliding 70.72 m/s across the nose; coupled stopped with 0.01 m/s across it. The ship flies decoupled by default; V cycles the mode and the panel shows which.

tasks.title: Aerodynamics: lift, drag and control surfaces
tasks.detail: Real aerodynamic forces from angle of attack, airspeed and the atmospheric density M04 provides, with control surfaces that only work in air.
tasks.acceptance: A winged ship glides unpowered in atmosphere and does not in vacuum.

tasks.title: Stall, spin and recovery
tasks.detail: An aerodynamic envelope with edges. Exceeding them has consequences that can be recovered from if the pilot knows how.
tasks.acceptance: A deliberate stall departs controlled flight and standard recovery inputs recover it.

tasks.title: Vacuum-to-atmosphere transition
tasks.detail: Aerodynamic authority fades in as density rises and thruster authority does not, so the handover is continuous rather than a mode change.
tasks.acceptance: A re-entry from vacuum to sea level shows no discontinuity in forces at any altitude.

tasks.title: VTOL and hover
tasks.detail: Vertical thrust with ground effect, and the fuel cost that makes hovering a decision rather than a default.
tasks.acceptance: Hovering consumes fuel at the rate thrust-to-weight implies, and ground effect is measurable near the surface.

tasks.title: Landing gear and ground handling
tasks.detail: Suspension, contact, friction, braking and steering on the ground. Landing is a physical event, not a state change.
tasks.acceptance: A hard landing compresses the gear and can damage it; a shallow one does not; the ship stays put on a slope up to the friction limit.

tasks.title: G-force model and pilot effects
tasks.detail: Sustained and transient acceleration on the pilot, with the visual and physiological limits that make manoeuvres have a cost.
tasks.acceptance: A sustained high-g turn greys the view on the modelled schedule and recovery follows the same model.

tasks.title: Flight computer limits and envelope protection
tasks.detail: Configurable limits on the allocator — g, angular rate, thermal — that a pilot can relax at their own risk.
tasks.acceptance: Limits are enforced by the controller, and disabling them lets the airframe be damaged.

tasks.title: Autopilot framework
tasks.detail: Hold attitude, hold altitude, hold station, approach and auto-land, as controllers over the same allocator. Directives in M21 will drive ships through this.
tasks.acceptance: Auto-land puts a ship on a pad in wind, repeatably, from any approach.

tasks.title: Docking
tasks.detail: Approach corridors, alignment, capture and release against a station or another ship, with the moving-frame handover M08 will formalise.
tasks.acceptance: Dock with a station in orbit and the ship's frame becomes the station's with no jolt.

tasks.title: Ground vehicle framework
tasks.detail: Wheeled and tracked vehicles over the same rigid body and the same terrain collision, because a settlement needs things that are not ships.
tasks.acceptance: A ground vehicle drives across terrain with suspension responding to the surface the renderer draws.

tasks.title: Input framework: HOTAS, gamepad, mouse and keyboard
tasks.detail: One binding layer over one command set, with curves, deadzones and per-device profiles. Not three control schemes.
tasks.acceptance: All three devices produce identical commanded forces for equivalent input, and rebinding requires no code.

tasks.title: HUD and flight instruments
tasks.detail: Velocity vector, attitude, target reticle, energy, and the instruments a pilot actually flies on — driven through M05's instrumentation path.
tasks.acceptance: A full flight is completable on instruments alone with the external view disabled.

tasks.title: Collision response for vehicles
tasks.detail: Impacts transfer momentum and damage components through M05's graph, rather than triggering a generic effect.
tasks.acceptance: A glancing impact damages the components at the point of contact and imparts the momentum the collision implies.

tasks.title: Ship-to-ship physical interaction
tasks.detail: Ships push each other, land on each other, and carry each other. The prerequisite for M08's nested frames.
tasks.acceptance: A small ship lands on a large one and is carried with it.

tasks.title: Flight recorder
tasks.detail: Record every input, force and state to a file that can be replayed exactly. Flight bugs are transient and unreproducible without this.
tasks.acceptance: A recorded flight replays to an identical trajectory.

tasks.title: Flight model tuning tools
tasks.detail: In-editor visualisation of thruster authority, aerodynamic forces, envelope and control response, so tuning is measured rather than felt.
tasks.acceptance: A ship's envelope can be read off a chart the tool generates.

tasks.title: Flight regression suite
tasks.detail: Recorded flights replayed in CI with trajectory tolerances, so a physics change that alters handling is caught immediately.
tasks.acceptance: A deliberate one-percent thrust change fails the suite.

tasks.title: Playable proof: continent, orbit, pad
tasks.detail: Rule 6. The gate, run and recorded.
tasks.acceptance: Pad to another continent aerodynamically, out to vacuum, manoeuvre, re-enter with heating, land on the pad you left — cockpit only.

tasks.title: Origin rebasing
tasks.detail: Move the world under the camera so float precision never has to express an astronomical unit. The prototype avoids this by keeping vertices patch-relative; everything else in the game will not have that luxury.
tasks.acceptance: At one AU from origin, a one-millimetre movement is still one millimetre, for every actor and every particle system.

tasks.title: Depth precision across twelve orders of magnitude
tasks.detail: A cockpit instrument at 40 cm and a planet at 400,000 km in one frame. Reversed-Z with cascaded depth ranges, or a logarithmic buffer, chosen by measurement rather than by preference.
tasks.acceptance: No z-fighting anywhere from a hand-held object to a planet on the same screen.

tasks.title: Scale-aware camera and rendering
