tasks.detail: Near and far rendering passes composited, so distant bodies are drawn at a scale the depth buffer can hold.
tasks.acceptance: A planet, its moon and a ship's own hull are all correctly occluded against each other.

tasks.title: Entity relevance and streaming by distance
tasks.detail: What exists, what is simulated, what is rendered, and what is a dot — with explicit bands and explicit transitions between them.
tasks.acceptance: A ship a thousand kilometres away is a dot; approach it and it becomes a ship with no pop and no state loss.

tasks.title: High-speed travel mode
tasks.detail: The thing that makes a system crossable in minutes rather than weeks: spool time, alignment, a speed that scales with distance, and a real cost.
tasks.acceptance: Cross the system in a few minutes, with every phase interruptible and the ship in a legal physical state at every instant.

tasks.title: Interdiction and interruption
tasks.detail: High-speed travel can be pulled out of, by mass, by another ship, or by failure — otherwise the entire strategic layer has no chokepoints.
tasks.acceptance: A ship in transit is pulled out at the position and velocity the model predicts, and the pursuer arrives with it.

tasks.title: Route planning and navigation
tasks.detail: Plot a route between any two sites, with time, fuel and hazard estimates that match what flying it actually costs.
tasks.acceptance: Estimated and actual travel time agree within five percent over twenty sampled routes.

tasks.title: Interstellar travel
tasks.detail: Between systems: whatever mechanism the fiction settles on, with a duration that keeps information genuinely slow. Design SS8: instant travel means instant information and there is no game left.
tasks.acceptance: An interstellar transit takes a stated time, is interruptible, and leaves the destination system correctly streamed on arrival.

tasks.title: Arrival and approach handling
tasks.detail: Deceleration, traffic separation, approach clearance and the transition into a body's frame — the part where seamlessness usually breaks.
tasks.acceptance: Arrive at a planet from high speed and descend to a pad without a single frame over budget.

tasks.title: Cross-scale physics stability
tasks.detail: Physics at 200 m/s near a rotating planet and at high speed between them, without tunnelling, jitter or integration blow-up.
tasks.acceptance: A twenty-minute transit ends with position error inside tolerance and no jitter at any point.

tasks.title: Bookmarks, waypoints and the navigation UI
tasks.detail: Somewhere to point the ship at, including places the player named and places they were told about.
tasks.acceptance: A waypoint set from the map is flyable to and arrives where it said.

tasks.title: Traffic: other ships going about their business
tasks.detail: Ships on routes, arriving and departing, at a density the streaming budget supports. Placeholder behaviour now; the simulation drives it from M16.
tasks.acceptance: Twenty ships operate in one system without a frame cost that reads on a graph.

tasks.title: Precision and seam regression suite
tasks.detail: Automated traversals at many scales asserting no precision artefact, no hitch over a threshold, and no discontinuity in position or velocity.
tasks.acceptance: A deliberately reintroduced precision bug is caught by CI.

tasks.title: Hitch elimination pass
tasks.detail: Every remaining stall over 4 ms during traversal, found and removed. Seamless is a property that is destroyed by one hitch.
tasks.acceptance: A full system traversal shows no frame over 16 ms and no allocation spike over the budget.

tasks.title: Playable proof: surface to a moon of another planet
tasks.detail: Rule 6. The gate, run and recorded in one continuous shot.
tasks.acceptance: No loading screen, no cut, no precision artefact anywhere on the path.

tasks.title: Spike: three approaches to nested reference frames
tasks.detail: Chaos with a moving kinematic parent, a second physics scene per grid with transform bridging, or a custom solver for grid-local bodies. Build enough of each to measure, then decide in an ADR. Choosing wrong here is a year.
tasks.acceptance: Three prototypes, measured on stability, cost and integration risk, and an ADR that picks one and says why.

tasks.title: Local physics grid framework
tasks.detail: A grid is a moving frame with its own physics content. Bodies inside it are simulated in grid-local coordinates, so a ship at 3,000 m/s is a room at rest.
tasks.acceptance: An object at rest inside a manoeuvring ship stays at rest relative to the ship, at any speed the ship can reach.

tasks.title: Frame entry and exit
tasks.detail: Walking onto a ship, stepping off onto a pad, a ship entering another ship's hold — velocity and angular velocity transferred correctly at every boundary.
tasks.acceptance: Step from a landing pad onto a hovering ship and back with no jolt, no launch, and no lost velocity.

tasks.title: Character controller inside a moving frame
tasks.detail: Walking, standing and falling relative to a frame that is itself accelerating and rotating, with the apparent forces that implies.
tasks.acceptance: Walk the length of a ship while it accelerates and rolls, without sliding and without the controller fighting the frame.

tasks.title: Apparent forces: acceleration, rotation, Coriolis
tasks.detail: Inertia felt inside an accelerating ship, and centrifugal gravity inside a rotating station with the Coriolis effect that comes with it.
tasks.acceptance: A dropped object inside a spinning station lands where the rotating frame predicts, not directly below.

tasks.title: Nested grids
tasks.detail: A vehicle inside a ship inside a station. Depth-limited, but the limit must be a decision rather than an accident.
tasks.acceptance: Two levels of nesting are stable and the limit is enforced with a clear error rather than a failure.

tasks.title: Gravity generation inside grids
tasks.detail: Artificial gravity as a per-grid field with orientation, plus what happens when it fails and everything inside becomes free-floating.
tasks.acceptance: Cutting grid gravity leaves loose objects and characters floating with the velocity they had.

tasks.title: Continuous collision detection at high speed
tasks.detail: Nothing may pass through a hull because it moved far in one step. Sweeps for fast bodies, with a budget.
tasks.acceptance: A projectile at any modelled speed always hits the surface it should, over ten thousand trials.

tasks.title: Collision geometry for large structures
tasks.detail: Ships and stations need collision at a fidelity that supports walking inside them, streamed, without cooking a battleship every time one appears.
tasks.acceptance: A large ship's interior collision streams in ahead of the character and never blocks a frame.

tasks.title: Constraint and joint framework
tasks.detail: Doors, ramps, turrets, elevators, landing gear and cargo clamps as constraints driven by M05's components rather than as animations.
tasks.acceptance: A ramp lowered under load moves at the rate the actuator provides and stops when the power does.

tasks.title: Object handling: pick up, carry, place, throw
tasks.detail: Loose objects with mass that behave inside moving frames, because a cup on a table in a manoeuvring ship is the whole promise of this milestone.
tasks.acceptance: Set a cup on a table, fly a barrel roll, and the cup behaves the way the frame and the friction say it should.

tasks.title: Ragdoll and character physics
tasks.detail: Bodies that fall, are thrown and collide, correctly inside a moving frame.
tasks.acceptance: A ragdoll inside an accelerating ship slides toward the stern at the rate the acceleration implies.

tasks.title: Destruction framework
tasks.detail: Structural damage to ships, buildings and terrain features, with debris that is physical and then is not, on a budget.
tasks.acceptance: A destroyed structure produces debris that settles and is cleaned up without a frame cost that reads on a graph.

tasks.title: Physics determinism and stability harness
tasks.detail: Fixed-step physics with recorded scenarios replayed in CI. Frame-rate dependent physics is a bug that only shows on someone else's machine.
tasks.acceptance: A recorded scenario replays identically at 30, 60 and 144 fps.

tasks.title: Physics performance budget
tasks.detail: Grid count, body count and substep cost under one budget, with degradation that is a decision rather than a stutter.
tasks.acceptance: Ten active grids with two hundred bodies each stays inside the physics budget.

tasks.title: Playable proof: walk to the cockpit at speed
tasks.detail: Rule 6. The gate, run and recorded.
tasks.acceptance: Walk from the stern to the cockpit while the ship accelerates, rolls and flies through atmosphere; a cup set down stays on the table; step out onto a pad on a rotating planet and inherit the right frame.

tasks.title: Source character and animation libraries, and audit their licences
tasks.detail: ADR-0005 rules out buying assets and rules out generating people: a rigged human with a face is not something a rule produces, and a convincing walk cycle is captured or authored. So this is a sourcing task, and it comes first because every task after it assumes a skeleton and a set of clips already exist. Free, licensed libraries only, with the terms read rather than remembered -- the surface work asserted the Megascans licence from memory and was wrong about it. One skeleton chosen and committed to, because retargeting everything later is worse than choosing badly now. Manifest and validator, same discipline as surfaces: a clip on disk with no recorded source and licence fails the build.
tasks.acceptance: A rigged character and a locomotion set are in the project, every one of them has a manifest entry naming its source and its licence, and an unaccounted asset fails CI naming the file.

tasks.title: Character controller with momentum
tasks.detail: Acceleration, deceleration, turning radius and footing rather than a capsule that changes velocity instantly. A body has mass and the controller has to admit it.
tasks.acceptance: Stopping from a run takes distance, turning at speed carries momentum, and neither is a curve someone drew.

tasks.title: One skeleton for first and third person
tasks.detail: Two skeletons is two sets of bugs and a first person view whose body is a lie. One rig, camera attached to the head, IK correcting what the camera can see.
tasks.acceptance: Look down in first person and see the same body a third-person camera sees, doing the same thing.

tasks.title: Full-body IK and foot placement
tasks.detail: Feet land on the ground that is actually there, at the angle it is at, on stairs, slopes and debris.
tasks.acceptance: Walk across broken terrain and a stairway with no foot sliding and no foot intersecting geometry.

tasks.title: Locomotion state machine and blend framework
tasks.detail: Idle, walk, run, sprint, crouch, prone, strafe, turn-in-place, with distance-matched transitions rather than fixed blends.
tasks.acceptance: No locomotion transition slides the feet, at any speed or direction change.

tasks.title: Locomotion in variable gravity
tasks.detail: Walking on a moon, in a station's spin gravity, and in a ship under thrust — stride, jump arc and fall speed all derived from local gravity.
tasks.acceptance: The same controller produces correct movement at 0.16 g, 1 g and 1.5 g with no special-cased animation.

tasks.title: Zero-gravity movement and EVA
tasks.detail: Push off, drift, arrest with a thruster pack, grab handholds. A different control problem, not a different character.
tasks.acceptance: Cross a compartment in zero gravity by pushing off and catching a handhold, with momentum conserved throughout.

tasks.title: Interaction framework
tasks.detail: One mechanism for everything a person can touch: buttons, levers, doors, seats, terminals, containers. Highlighting, reach, occlusion and the animation that sells it.
tasks.acceptance: A new interactable is one data declaration and inherits highlighting, reach and animation with no bespoke code.

tasks.title: Seats, harnesses and vehicle entry
tasks.detail: Getting into and out of a seat as a physical transition inside a moving frame, with the controller handing off to the vehicle.
tasks.acceptance: Board a hovering ship, take the seat and fly, with no teleport and no cut, and get out again while it is still moving.

tasks.title: Ladders, climbing and mantling
tasks.detail: Vertical movement that respects the geometry rather than snapping to it.
tasks.acceptance: Climb a ladder inside an accelerating ship and mantle onto a ledge, both with correct hand placement.

tasks.title: Carrying and manipulation animation
tasks.detail: Two-handed carry, one-handed carry, and the effect of mass on gait. Tied to M08's object handling.
tasks.acceptance: Carrying a heavy crate visibly changes stance and speed, driven by the object's mass.

tasks.title: Suits, helmets and life support on the body
tasks.detail: A person outside a breathable atmosphere needs a suit, and the suit is a component set with oxygen, temperature and pressure like any other.
tasks.acceptance: Step into vacuum without a sealed suit and die on the modelled schedule, with warnings that come from the suit's components.

tasks.title: Damage, injury and incapacitation
tasks.detail: Localised injury with effects on movement and capability, and a recovery path that is not a health bar refilling.
tasks.acceptance: A leg injury changes gait and speed until treated, and treatment consumes something.

tasks.title: Facial and upper-body animation framework
tasks.detail: Look-at, gesture, and expression driven by state rather than by canned clips, because every NPC in the living world will need it.
tasks.acceptance: A character tracks a moving object with head and eyes while walking, with no clip authored for it.

tasks.title: Character definition and variation
tasks.detail: Body proportions, faces, clothing and equipment as data, so a crowd is not twelve copies of one person.
tasks.acceptance: A hundred generated characters are visually distinct and all animate correctly on the shared rig.

tasks.title: Animation LOD and crowd cost
tasks.detail: Full evaluation up close, reduced further out, and something very cheap at distance, with transitions nobody sees.
tasks.acceptance: Two hundred visible characters stay inside the animation budget with no visible LOD switch.

tasks.title: Footstep, foley and movement audio
tasks.detail: Surface-aware footsteps, cloth, equipment, and breathing that responds to exertion and to whether there is air outside.
tasks.acceptance: Surface material is identifiable from footstep audio, and audio changes correctly in a suit and in vacuum.

tasks.title: Camera framework
tasks.detail: First person, third person, and the transitions, with collision, stabilisation and the shake budget that stops it becoming nauseating.
tasks.acceptance: Switching view is continuous, the camera never enters geometry, and motion sickness testing passes with three people.

tasks.title: Animation regression suite
tasks.detail: Recorded traversals with foot-sliding, penetration and pop metrics computed automatically, because animation regressions are invisible in a diff.
tasks.acceptance: A deliberately broken blend is caught by CI with a named metric.

tasks.title: Playable proof: room to cockpit and back
tasks.detail: Rule 6. The gate, run and recorded.
tasks.acceptance: Out of a room, up a ladder, across a pad in wind, into a ship, into a seat, fly, land, get out — one shot, no cut, nothing sliding.

tasks.title: Modular kit framework
tasks.detail: Rooms, corridors, junctions and shafts as a connectable kit with sockets, so interiors are assembled rather than modelled. The prerequisite for generated ships, stations and buildings all at once.
tasks.acceptance: An interior assembled from the kit has no gap, no z-fight at any seam, and correct collision throughout.

tasks.title: Interior generation from a layout grammar
tasks.detail: A generator that lays out an interior from a purpose and a footprint — circulation first, then rooms, then detail — rather than stamping prefabs.
tasks.acceptance: Twenty generated interiors of the same purpose are all navigable, all different, and none has an unreachable room.

tasks.title: Ship interiors on the modular kit
tasks.detail: Ship internals assembled from the same kit, constrained by the hull, with the component graph from M05 physically present in them.
tasks.acceptance: Every component in a ship's graph has a physical location inside it that can be walked to and worked on.

tasks.title: Cockpit generated from the component graph
tasks.detail: The strongest case for generating rather than authoring, and it comes out of a promise already made: docs/quality-bar.md says every gauge traces to a real component. A hand-authored cockpit can lie about that. One laid out from the ship's own graph cannot -- a readout exists because a component exists, a breaker exists because a power path does, and a ship fitted differently gets a different panel without anyone redrawing it. Layout from the seat outward: reach envelope from the seated eye point, consoles on ergonomic arcs, sightlines to the canopy preserved, labels beside every control. Cable and pipe runs routed between components rather than drawn.
tasks.acceptance: Two ships with different component fits produce different cockpits with no hand editing; every readout in both traces to a component in the graph; and every control is reachable from the seated position without the sightline to the horizon being blocked.

tasks.title: Station interiors
tasks.detail: Larger, with spin gravity, public and private volumes, docking connections and the traffic that implies.
tasks.acceptance: Walk from a docked ship into a station, across it, and into another docked ship, all in the correct frames.

tasks.title: Building interiors for settlements
tasks.detail: Habitation, industry and civic interiors, generated for the settlement layer, with the environment-driven composition from LW SS7.2 visible inside as well as outside.
tasks.acceptance: A habitat on an airless world has an airlock, a pressurised interior and visible life support; the same archetype on a temperate world does not.

tasks.title: Portals and interior streaming
tasks.detail: Interiors stream and cull through portals, so a city block of walkable buildings costs what is visible rather than what exists.
tasks.acceptance: A hundred walkable interiors in view cost no more than the handful actually visible through their openings.

tasks.title: Doors, airlocks and pressure boundaries
tasks.detail: Doors as constraints with power, pressure differential and failure. An airlock is a state machine that can kill you.
tasks.acceptance: Cycling an airlock takes time, equalises pressure, and opening the wrong door vents the compartment.

tasks.title: Interior lighting framework
tasks.detail: Lights as powered fixtures. When the district loses power, the lights go out — which is the first-person tell LW SS7.1 requires.
tasks.acceptance: Cutting power to a building darkens its interior and emergency lighting comes up on its own reserve.

tasks.title: Interior navigation mesh generation
tasks.detail: Navigation built from the assembled kit at runtime, across frames, so NPCs can move through interiors that were generated a moment ago and are themselves moving.
tasks.acceptance: A character navigates from any point in a generated interior to any other, including inside a moving ship.

tasks.title: Interior audio: reverb, occlusion, propagation
tasks.detail: Rooms sound like rooms, doors muffle, and a corridor carries sound the way a corridor does.
tasks.acceptance: Reverb and occlusion change correctly walking between three connected spaces without hand-placed volumes.

tasks.title: Set dressing and clutter framework
tasks.detail: Rule-driven placement of the objects that make a room look inhabited, responding to the room's purpose and its owner's circumstances.
tasks.acceptance: A workshop, a bunk and an office generated from the same kit are immediately distinguishable, and a wealthy one differs from a poor one.

tasks.title: Interior collision and traversal quality pass
tasks.detail: Every surface a person can reach behaves: no invisible walls, no geometry you can walk through, no ledge you catch on.
tasks.acceptance: An automated traversal agent covers every reachable point of ten generated interiors without getting stuck.

tasks.title: Playable proof: street to cockpit through a building
tasks.detail: Rule 6. The gate, run and recorded.
tasks.acceptance: Street, into a building, up through it, onto a roof pad, into a docked ship, to its cockpit — no load, no fade, no frame over budget.

tasks.title: The planet from orbit
tasks.detail:
The owner's report: planets from space look 'awful and like almost low poly/animated', not like Star Citizen. The capture bears it out and the cause is not polygon count. From about 12,000 km the whole planet resolves to ~540 patches at depth 3 to 4, so vertices sit 10 to 20 km apart; the terrain material takes its ground palette straight from VertexColor; and the sea is generated on the same vertex grid as the land. Every coastline is therefore interpolated across a 10-20 km grid, on both sides at once, which is exactly the rectangular shoreline in the frame. It is colour resolution, and adding triangles is the expensive way to fix shading.

Two further defects, separate causes: no clouds over the disc at all, because the volumetric layer's TracingMaxDistance is 250 km and the viewer is far outside it; and no scattering halo on the limb, which is mostly honest physics -- 60 to 100 km of air on a 6,344 km radius is about 1% of the disc -- rather than a bug, though it can be made to read.

The shape of the fix: a planet-wide albedo sampled from the same climate and height functions the patch generator already uses, at a resolution independent of the mesh, cross-faded in as patches coarsen. The material already carries what that needs -- NodeSize from UV1.y, ToCamera from the camera, and its own comment warning that the blend must be driven by the same quantity the LOD decision uses or the two disagree. One source fixes land and sea together, because they share the grid.

Why nothing caught this: T059's acceptance is a mountain range 80 km away, seen from the ground. No task in this roadmap ever asked what the planet looks like from space, which is why it has never been measured.
tasks.acceptance: From orbit, a coastline shows no step larger than the terrain's own detail at that distance -- measured as the longest run of identically coloured pixels along a land-sea boundary, against the same capture today -- and the disc carries cloud. A person shown the frame without context does not call it low-poly.

notes.text: [2026-09-12] MY DIAGNOSIS IS WRONG, and the experiment says so. I claimed the blocky coastlines were vertex colour resolution: from orbit the planet is ~540 patches at depth 3-4, so vertices 10-20 km apart, and the terrain material reads its palette from VertexColor. The A/B refutes it. Same flight, same camera, one arm at the default 250 px screen error and one at 60 px (-terrainerror=60, confirmed applied in the log: 'terrain: refining against 60 px of screen error'). The refined arm built 3,614 patches by frame 301 against the coarse arm's 474 -- about EIGHT TIMES the geometry -- and the coastline metric did not move: longest run of identical pixels along rows across the disc, median 8 px both, p90 107 against 108, worst 552 against 553, and the two frames look the same to the eye. Eight times the vertices changed the blockiness by one pixel. So vertex spacing is not what quantises the coastline and the far-field albedo I designed would have been built on a dead cause. WHERE TO LOOK INSTEAD: upstream of the mesh. The candidates are the climate and biome field the palette is sampled from (if it is evaluated on a coarse grid per patch, refining the mesh cannot help -- which is exactly the symptom), and how SurfaceColour bins land against sea. The step size should then be a property of that field's resolution, not of the patch depth, and that is testable: sample the field directly at two resolutions and see where the coastline granularity comes from, without a run. CAVEAT ON THIS RUN, stated because it nearly invalidated it: the patch cache had just been deleted so both arms streamed cold, and I killed the refined arm partway to stop it filling the disk again. The orbit screenshot was written before the kill and the patch counts show the tree really did subdivide, so the comparison holds -- but the frame counts and hole counts from these arms are worthless.

[2026-09-12] THE CAUSE, FOUND -- it is the climate lattice, not the mesh. LedgerPatchGenerator samples climate on a ClimateGrid x ClimateGrid lattice per patch and bilinearly interpolates it to the 65x65 vertices (line 432: 'Sampled on the coarse grid and interpolated'). ClimateGridFor(Extent) = clamp(round(3 + Extent*20), 3, 13). Worked through for this planet (cube face edge ~9,965 km): depth 3 patch is 1,246 km wide with a 6x6 lattice -- ONE CLIMATE SAMPLE EVERY 249 KM. On screen the disc is ~900 px for a 6,344 km radius, so 1 px is ~14 km and 249 km is ~18 px of minimum feature size before interpolation smears it further. The measured coastline steps (p90 107 px, worst 552 px) sit in exactly that range. Biome weights -- and therefore the land/sea palette -- cannot resolve finer than that lattice NO MATTER HOW MANY VERTICES A PATCH HAS, which is why refining the tree 8x (3,614 patches against 474) moved the metric by one pixel. THE COMMENT ABOVE THE FUNCTION ALREADY RECORDS THIS EXACT FAILURE being fixed once for root patches: 'three samples across a root patch is three across a whole cube face, and the orbit and space captures came back with flat-coloured continents: correct interpolation of a grid far too coarse to have a biome boundary in it'. The scaling was added then; the 13 ceiling is what is left of it, and it is too low for a patch that fills the screen from orbit. THE FIX SHAPE: make the lattice track the patch's APPARENT size rather than its extent alone, so a coarse patch being looked at from space gets a real sampling while the thousands of distant fine patches keep paying for three -- which is the trade the comment says was intended. COST, which must be priced before it ships: each climate sample marches forty steps upwind through the height field plus four subsidence steps, and patch generation already runs 6-83 ms on a worker. Going 6x6 to 33x33 on a coarse patch is 36 to 1,089 samples. It is off the critical path (the game thread only uploads) so it bounds throughput, not frame time -- but starving the streamer while the planet is being drawn from orbit would trade one defect for another. Measure before shipping.

(1) The metric I wrote into this task -- 'longest run of identically coloured pixels along a land-sea boundary' -- was implemented as the longest run per row across the disc, and that measures HOW WIDE THE CONTINENTS ARE, not how blocky the coastline is. MEASURED THE FRAME INSTEAD OF THEORISING, AND EIGHT CAUSES ARE NOW DEAD. Sampled 229,600 pixels inside 0.75R of out/planet-fine-orbit.png and median-cut them: eight dominant clusters, five land and three sea, and NOT ONE IS GREEN. Land is a single warm ramp, rgb(185,171,156) down to rgb(127,119,112), every one R>G>B. Normalised to R=1 the land spans G/R 0.898-0.937 and B/R 0.796-0.882 -- a hue band NARROWER THAN THE SCAN LIBRARY ITSELF. Against the scans' measured means: tundra rocky_ground (0.922/0.854) sits dead centre, while desert gravel (0.790/0.607), rainforest (0.791/0.625), snow (1.000/1.001) and boreal moss (1.054/0.254) all fall OUTSIDE the measured range -- though desert is 20.9% of land and ice cap 22.1%. So eight surfaces are arriving as one, varying in brightness only. RULED OUT, each by reading the code that would have to be at fault: (1) the climate field -- out/climate.txt reports 19.9% grassland, 16.8% savanna, 20.9% desert, 13.1% tundra, 22.1% ice cap, 7.3% forest over 19,435 land points, and snow 0.0% of land below 30 deg, 38.5% at 30-60, 100% above 60; that field is varied and plausible. (2) Moisture -- I predicted a dry planet collapsing to desert; mean moisture is 0.700 and 63% of rows exceed 0.65, the opposite. (3) Patch cache staleness -- ContentKey mixes FormatVersion and every cache directory is from tonight. (4) Baked-material staleness -- M_Terrain.uasset is untracked (a build product) and its mtime is newer than both the material source and the biome config. (5) The missing-material fallback -- Fallback() only logs an error and returns nullptr, and no such error is in either orbit log. (6) The elevation-ramp fallback SurfaceColour -- its ramp is GREEN (beach 126,116,92 through grass 74,88,52) with bluish snow 206,210,216; the disc shows neither, so that branch is not drawing it. (7) The 8-into-7 channel mapping -- GroundChannels sends ice cap to INDEX_NONE (snow) and the other seven to channels 0-6; nothing is clamped. (8) Rock taking over the tints -- Slope is dot(VertexNormalWS, Radial), so from orbit Slope is about 1, RockWeight = saturate((0.90-1.0)/0.25) = 0, and with SoilBid in [1,2] against RockBid in [0,1] the height-bid contest gives RockShare = saturate(Rock.Height - Soil.Height - 0.5) = 0. THE REFRAME THAT MATTERS: the 'green' biomes are not green. grassy_soil_xbklfix (temperate grassland) has a mean albedo of [0.508,0.458,0.389] and savanna's is [0.464,0.400,0.337] -- warm grey-tan dirt. That makes this a composition problem, not a broken pipeline, and it is why refining the tree 8x, the climate lattice and the orbital cloud march all changed nothing: every one of them was upstream of a fault that is not there. STILL UNSEPARATED, and the next measurement: those pixels are lit AND seen through 6,400 km of atmosphere, both of which compress hue toward neutral. An unlit -terrainvis=biome capture from orbit (needs -livematerials, since the debug arms exist only in the in-memory material, not the baked asset) shows the biome weights as RGB with no sun and no tint, which separates 'the field is collapsed' from 'the shading and the air wash it out'. ATTRIBUTED TO THE CUMULUS DECK, BY MEASUREMENT RATHER THAN INFERENCE, AND THE DEFECT NAMED. There is no per-deck arm, so I attributed by shape instead of adding one. The cloud-only pixels -- bright with the deck, not bright without it, 39,402 of them -- are ISOTROPIC: horizontal run lengths mean 8.72 px, vertical 9.02, elongation 0.97. Cirrus is stretched 0.88 along a fixed axis in the material and would have shown a large asymmetry; it shows none. With the opacities (cumulus 0.9, cirrus 0.03) that settles it: the blobs are CUMULUS. A deck at 3% opacity cannot paint bright white. No rebuild and no new flag were needed. THE DEFECT, in units: cloud masses measure p50 6 px, p90 20 px, max 93 px on a 1,804 px disc for a 6,344 km radius, so about 7 km per pixel -- masses 40 to 60 km across, p90 140 km, ALL AT ONE SCALE. Real cumulus is individual cells one to ten kilometres across that organise into systems hundreds of kilometres wide; there is structure at both ends and none in between. What renders is uniform mid-sized blobs, evenly scattered, no size variation and no organisation, which is precisely what a single noise field cut at a single threshold gives. That is the 'almost low poly / animated' reading. Current settings: Cumulus.Coverage = 0.15 + 0.6*Wetness (38% here), Opacity 0.9, CumulusScale 0.0000048, DeckNoise Levels 3. THE FIX SHAPE, not yet taken: the cumulus field needs scale variation and organisation -- more octaves so cells vary in size, and/or a low-frequency mask gating WHERE cells form so they gather into weather systems with clear air between. It is not a coverage change; lowering coverage would give fewer blobs of the same wrong size. WHAT MUST HAPPEN BEFORE ANY OF IT SHIPS: this is the seventh conclusion in this session and the previous six all died on contact with a measurement. The floor is 0.47%, the statistics to judge against are land-ish fraction (62.41/62.42 on repeat arms) and coast crossings per row (18.43/18.39), and any cloud change must be judged on those two plus the run-length distribution above, not on a screenshot.

WEATHERSCALE IS NOT THE LEVER: NEGATIVE, MEASURED, AND THE ARM STAYS AT ITS DEFAULT. I proposed raising the organising field's scale because its features (about 40,000 km) are larger than the planet's circumference, so from orbit it is one gradient and organises nothing. Added -weatherscale=N as a measurement arm (a multiple of the default; default untouched at 2.5e-8) and ran three arms on one cache, judged against the established 0.47% floor. CONTROL (1x, -livematerials): land 62.42%, 18.43 coast crossings per row, bright runs n 5183 p50 7 p90 23 max 93 mean 10.2 -- and it matches the pre-edit baked frame at 0.47%, exactly the floor, so the edit did not disturb the default path. 10x (features about 4,000 km): land 73.93%, crossings 66.83 per row, bright runs n 1855 p50 1 p90 3 max 7 mean 1.6. That is the OPPOSITE of the intended effect. The deck did not gather into systems with varied cell sizes; it shattered into single-pixel speckle, and the frame is a salt-and-pepper haze over the whole disc, plainly worse than what ships. WHY, and it is worth keeping: the material already fades fine noise to its mean between 10 and 60 km (the Far term) precisely so orbital pixels do not alias -- its comment says the speckled sepia veil was that bug. The weather field is added at FULL AMPLITUDE AFTER that fade, so shrinking its features re-introduces exactly the sub-pixel variation the anti-aliasing path exists to remove. WeatherScale is entangled with the aliasing defence, not free to tune. So the defect stands as measured (cumulus masses 40-60 km, all one scale, no organisation) but this parameter is not the fix, and anything that gives the field smaller features must pass through Faded() or it will alias the same way. The 30x arm is running only to confirm the trend is monotonic. NOTHING SHIPPED: the default is unchanged and -weatherscale= is an instrument. This is the eighth proposal in this session to die on a measurement, and the first one killed BEFORE shipping rather than after.

WEATHERSCALE CLOSED, MONOTONIC IN THE WRONG DIRECTION -- the third arm confirms there is no value worth trying. Bright-run distribution across the three arms on one cache: 1x (default) p50 7, p90 23, max 93, mean 10.2; 10x p50 1, p90 3, max 7, mean 1.6; 30x p50 1, p90 2, max 5, mean 1.3. Every step makes the deck FINER and more fragmented rather than more organised, and the speckle floods an increasing share of the disc. The mechanism stands as recorded -- the weather field is added at full amplitude AFTER the Far fade that averages fine noise to its mean for orbital pixels, so shrinking its features re-introduces precisely the sub-pixel variation that fade exists to remove. ANY future attempt to give the organising field finer structure must route it through Faded() first, or it will alias identically. Default remains 2.5e-8; -weatherscale= stays as an instrument with this result in its comment. THE DEFECT IS STILL REAL AND STILL UNFIXED: cumulus arrives as 40-60 km masses all of one size (p50 6 px, p90 20, max 93 on a 1,804 px disc at about 7 km per pixel), evenly scattered, no size variation and no organisation, and that is what reads as 'almost low poly / animated' from orbit. The remaining candidates, none tested: more octaves in the cumulus DeckNoise (currently Levels 3) so cells vary in size within the existing scale; or an organising term that is faded correctly with distance instead of added after the fade.

CUMULUS SCALE AND OCTAVES: NEGATIVE, AND IT ALMOST FOOLED ME. Added -cumulusscale=N and -cumulusoctaves=N as measurement arms (defaults untouched; the control reproduces the previous control at 0.46% against a 0.47% floor, on land fraction, crossings and the full run distribution). The 832 km arm (-cumulusscale=0.25 -cumulusoctaves=5, confirmed applied in the log) APPEARED TO PASS the criterion I had fixed in advance: bright-run spread p90/p50 from 3.3 to 7.7, max 93 to 296, mean 10.2 to 34.0. IT DID NOT. Land fraction 43.71% and crossings 6.32 per row are the NO-CLOUD numbers (floor-c reads 43.71% and 6.33; the earlier noclouds arm 43.70% and 6.36), and differencing confirms it: the 832 km arm differs from the no-cloud reference by 1.04%, about twice the floor, while the control differs from it by 48.22%. THE DECK VANISHED RATHER THAN REORGANISED. My bright-run metric could not tell cloud from bright land -- in the control the bright class is cloud blobs (n 5,192, small), in this arm it is the cream continent itself (n 1,574, large) -- so the criterion passed for entirely the wrong reason. WHY, and it constrains every future attempt: coverage is a THRESHOLD on the noise field, and both knobs move that field's distribution relative to a fixed cut. Both arms engaged (log: 'cumulus coverage forced to 0.55 (weather says 0.38)' and 'cumulus at 0.25x scale (base about 832 km) with 5 octaves'). THE COMPENSATION WORKED AS A MECHANISM: isolated cloud came back to 14.28% of the disc against the shipping deck's 17.22%, so the deck is present and comparable rather than deleted as in the uncompensated arm (0.10%). THE SHAPE WENT THE WRONG WAY, decisively: runs n 4,517 -> 8,846, p50 6 -> 3, p90 20 -> 8, max 93 -> 32, mean 8.7 -> 3.7. MORE fragments, SMALLER, not fewer and larger. The frame is a mottled camouflage of small patches over the whole disc, plainly worse than what ships. WHY, and it is the same mechanism for the third time: a coarser base with more octaves still leaves the finest octave near 52 km while the extra octaves put more energy close to the cut, so a fixed threshold carves the field into many small pieces instead of few large ones. Coarser base plus more octaves does not give larger masses; it gives more edges. WHAT IS NOW CLOSED: three routes, all failing through the same fixed-threshold mechanism -- WeatherScale (monotonic the wrong way), cumulus scale/octaves (deletes the deck), and cumulus scale/octaves at matched coverage (fragments it). I do not intend to keep sweeping these parameters; the 0.70 and 0.85 arms are running only to close the sweep and will move the cloud FRACTION, not the fragment size. WHAT THE EVIDENCE POINTS AT INSTEAD: the defect is not the scale of the noise, it is that coverage is a HARD THRESHOLD ON A SINGLE FIELD. Every knob available moves the field relative to a fixed cut. Varied mass sizes need the CUT to vary spatially -- a low-frequency modulation of the threshold rather than of the field. The Weather term was designed to be exactly that ('moves every deck's coverage threshold up and down -- overcast where it is high, clear where it is low') and is tuned to 40,000 km, larger than the planet, which is why it modulates nothing. So the honest next experiment is not another scale: it is giving the THRESHOLD a field at 2,000-4,000 km with real amplitude, routed through Faded() so it does not alias, while the cloud noise itself stays where it is. Defaults remain untouched; everything added is an instrument.

BOTH OF MY CLOUD METRICS ARE WRONG, IN OPPOSITE DIRECTIONS -- recording this before any more arms, because it invalidates how I have been judging every cloud experiment tonight. METRIC ONE, brightness: a pixel counts as cloud if it is bright in the arm and not bright in the no-cloud reference. It reported cover 0.70 as 0.94% cloud -- nearly cloudless -- when differencing shows that frame differs from the cloudless reference on 49.01% of pixels (a genuinely cloudless arm, cum-832, differs by 1.04%). It failed because raising coverage drives the deck toward SOLID OVERCAST, and thick overcast over dark ocean is not bright; the material's own comment says a band at full density is twenty optical depths thick. So the brightness gate stopped seeing cloud that is unambiguously there. METRIC TWO, difference: a pixel counts as cloud if it differs from the cloudless reference by more than 12. It reports the SHIPPING deck as 92.51% cloud, when the control frame plainly shows clear ocean between blobs. It fails because the deck perturbs nearly every pixel somehow -- cloud shadow, aerial perspective, the lighting shift of an overcast sky -- so it measures 'touched by the deck', not 'is cloud'. FOUR IMAGE METRICS HAVE NOW MISLED ME IN ONE SESSION: median-cut cluster centroids, hue-band width, bright-run spread, and this difference mask. Each looked principled and each answered a question I had not asked. The pattern is that I keep inventing a proxy for a material rather than measuring the material. WHAT I CAN STILL SAY, from the frames rather than the statistics: cover 0.70 at 832 km is NEAR-TOTAL OVERCAST -- a uniform tan blanket with small dark holes where ocean shows through, which is precisely the 'fog and not a cloud field' the material's comment warns about. Cover 0.55 was fragmented camouflage. Both are worse than what ships, so the coverage route is closed on visual evidence I trust more than either number. CONSEQUENCE FOR THE QUEUED ATTEMPT FOUR (-weatheramp, pushing the threshold harder): I am NOT running it as written. Its whole premise is that the cut should swing decisively, and cover 0.70 has just shown what the overcast end of a decisive swing looks like. It would likely alternate blanket and empty -- the two failures already seen -- and I have no instrument left that could tell me whether the result was good. An experiment whose outcome I cannot measure is not worth the machine time. WHAT THE NEXT SESSION NEEDS FIRST: a defensible measure of cloud shape. The candidates are a cloud mask taken from the material itself (a -terrainvis-style unlit pass that outputs the cumulus band mask directly, which is ground truth rather than a proxy), or a human judgement on a contact sheet of arms. Until one exists, further cloud parameter arms are unmeasurable and should not be run.

THE COVERAGE SWEEP IS CLOSED, MONOTONE INTO FAILURE, ON EVIDENCE I CAN SEE. Three arms at an 832 km cumulus base, coverage forced (each confirmed applied in its log): 0.55 gives fragmented camouflage -- more and smaller patches than the shipping deck. 0.70 gives near-total overcast, a tan blanket with small dark holes where ocean shows through. 0.85 gives a TOTAL LID: a uniform tan cover over the whole disc with only pinprick holes, no coastline, no ocean, no structure whatever. That is precisely the failure the material's own comment names -- 'a sky that was solid everywhere the threshold had not zeroed outright, which is a fog and not a cloud field'. So coverage compensation does not rescue a coarsened cumulus field; it walks from fragmentation straight through to overcast with nothing usable between. Combined with the earlier arms, FOUR PARAMETER ROUTES ARE NOW CLOSED: WeatherScale (monotone the wrong way, shatters into speckle), cumulus scale and octaves (deletes the deck outright, 17.22% to 0.10%), the same at matched coverage (fragments it), and the coverage sweep itself (fragmentation to overcast). Every one failed through the same mechanism: coverage is a hard cut on a single noise field, and every knob available only slides the field across that cut. I judged these last three by eye rather than by statistic on purpose -- four separate image metrics contradicted each other tonight, and the frames are unambiguous where the numbers were not. WHAT IS BUILT INSTEAD OF A FIFTH SWEEP: -cloudmask, which puts the cumulus band alone in the extinction pin so the frame IS the cumulus field rather than a brightness proxy for it. It is being validated against two cases whose answers are already known (the shipping deck should show the familiar blob field; the known-fragmented setting should show fragments). If it cannot separate those by eye it is no better than the metrics it replaces and should be said so. The defect itself remains exactly as measured and entirely unfixed.

THE INSTRUMENT WORKS, AND IT MOVES THE SUSPICION OFF CUMULUS. -cloudmask engaged cleanly (log: 'cumulus alone in the extinction pin', no probe interference) and the frame shows something not seen all session: WHITE CUMULUS WITH SOFT EDGES OVER A VISIBLE CONTINENT AND BLUE OCEAN. Cloud and ground are separable by eye without any brightness proxy, which is what the four contradictory metrics were groping at. WHAT IT IMPLIES, AND IT CORRECTS MY OWN ATTRIBUTION: the shipping deck's flat tan wash is NOT what cumulus alone produces. With middle and cirrus removed, the same cumulus field at the same coverage reads as white cloud over a legible planet. So 'the cumulus deck is what makes the disc read as scattered blobs' is right about the SHAPES -- the blob field is cumulus -- but wrong about the TAN. The washed-out colour is coming from the two decks I ruled out, and I ruled them out by inference rather than measurement: cirrus on its 0.03 opacity and its 0.88 streak stretch, middle on its 4% coverage. Neither was ever isolated and looked at. THE CHEAP TEST THIS OPENS: isolate middle and cirrus the same way, or run the shipping deck with cirrus alone removed. Cirrus is the candidate -- 43% coverage, nearly independent of surface weather, drawn out into streaks across the whole disc, sitting at 6,058-8,538 m above everything else. A thin sheet at 43% over the entire planet is exactly what would wash colour out of the ground beneath it while contributing little shape of its own. If removing it restores the ground's colour, the defect is cirrus and four sessions of cumulus parameter sweeps were aimed at the wrong deck. NOT OVERCLAIMING: this is one frame from one arm, and twelve conclusions died tonight, four within minutes of my asserting them. What is established is that the instrument separates cloud from ground; what is suggested, and needs its own arm, is that cumulus is not the deck that flattens the disc.

INSTRUMENT VALIDATED, AND IT RETRO-EXPLAINS THE WHOLE COVERAGE SWEEP. The second validation arm (-cloudmask with the known-fragmented settings: -cumulusscale=0.25 -cumulusoctaves=5 -cumuluscover=0.55) shows a clean continent, blue ocean and mint shelf with ALMOST NO CLOUD -- a few wisps at the limb. Against the first arm's white blob field over a legible planet, the two are unmistakable by eye, which is exactly what the four contradictory pixel metrics could not deliver. The instrument discriminates and I will use it from here. WHAT IT SAYS ABOUT THE SWEEP I ALREADY RECORDED: cov-55, the SAME cumulus settings with all three decks drawn, was mottled camouflage across the whole disc. -cumulusscale feeds only the cumulus band, so that camouflage was NOT cumulus. It was middle and cirrus. Every frame in that sweep was a mixture I was reading as a single deck. And the arc now makes sense mechanically: a coarsened cumulus field sits below the coverage cut at the default 0.38 (hence cum-832's near-total disappearance), climbs back to wisps at 0.55, and crosses the threshold nearly everywhere at 0.70 and 0.85 -- which is why those read as near-overcast and then a total lid. The deck was not fragmenting and then thickening; it was absent, then partial, then everywhere, with the other two decks supplying the texture I was attributing to it throughout. SO THE ATTRIBUTION IN MY EARLIER COMMITTED NOTES IS WRONG IN ITS SECOND HALF. 'The cumulus deck is what makes the disc read as scattered blobs' holds for the blob SHAPES in the shipping configuration -- that was measured with -noclouds against a 0.47% floor and reproduced across two chains. But 'the deck converts the disc to a mid-tone wash' does not follow, and the -cloudmask frames say cumulus alone renders as white cloud over a visible continent. The wash belongs to middle or cirrus. chain197 is running the direct test: the shipping deck, then -cirruscover=0, then -middlecover=0, judged by eye. THIS IS CORROBORATION, NOT PROOF. Twelve conclusions died tonight and several looked this good at this stage.

FOUND IT: CIRRUS IS THE WASH. The override fired (log: 'Cirrus coverage forced to 0.00 (weather says 0.43)'; the reference arm in the same build logs none, and that reference matches the earlier control at 0.48% against a 0.47% floor, so the baseline is the same planet). Removing cirrus alone changes 38.18% OF THE DISC, worst channel 155 -- roughly eighty times the floor. And the frame is what this task has been chasing since the owner first reported it: white clouds with soft edges, BLUE OCEAN, a legible continent with its mint continental shelf. The flat tan wash is simply gone. WHAT THE DECK WAS DOING: cirrus is 43% coverage, near-independent of surface weather, a thin streaked sheet at 6,058-8,538 m lying over everything else on the planet. Thin enough to contribute almost no shape of its own (opacity 0.03) and broad enough to drain the colour out of every surface beneath it. That is exactly why it evaded every measurement: it does not look like cloud in the frame, it looks like the ground being wrong. MY OWN ERROR, RECORDED PLAINLY: I dismissed cirrus TWICE tonight by inference rather than by isolating it -- once on opacity (0.03 cannot paint bright white blobs, which was true and irrelevant) and once on shape (the cloud-only pixels were isotropic at elongation 0.97, so not streaked, which was also true and also irrelevant, because I was measuring the pixels cirrus does not paint). Both inferences were sound about what cirrus contributes as CLOUD and useless about what it does as a FILTER. Four parameter sweeps -- WeatherScale, cumulus scale and octaves, the same at matched coverage, and the coverage sweep -- went into the cumulus deck because of those two dismissals. THE CORRECTED DIAGNOSIS: cumulus owns the blob shapes (measured with -noclouds against the floor, reproduced across two chains); CIRRUS OWNS THE WASH, which is the half that actually reads as 'low poly / animated'. WHAT THIS IS NOT: a fix. The deck is identified, not remedied. Lowering its coverage, thinning it further, or changing what it does to transmitted light are all changes to how every sky in the game looks from orbit and from the ground, and that is the owner's call on a before-and-after, not mine to ship off one frame at two in the morning.

DECK ATTRIBUTION COMPLETE: MIDDLE IS INNOCENT, CIRRUS OWNS IT ALONE. Both overrides fired and logged ('Middle coverage forced to 0.00 (weather says 0.04)', 'Cirrus coverage forced to 0.00 (weather says 0.43)'), against a reference in the same build that matches the earlier control at 0.48%. Removing the middle deck changes 0.49% of the disc, worst channel 29 -- indistinguishable from the 0.47% floor, i.e. nothing. Removing cirrus changes 38.18%, worst channel 155. So the wash is one deck and one deck only, and no further isolation arms are needed. WHAT REMAINS BEFORE ANY REMEDY IS RECOMMENDED, and it is the reason I am not proposing one yet: every frame in this investigation is from ORBIT. Cirrus at 43% coverage also lies over the ground view, where a thin high sheet is frequently what keeps a sky from reading as empty -- and lowering its coverage, thinning it, or changing what it does to transmitted light would change every sky in the game from eye height as well as from space. Choosing a remedy from orbital frames alone would be precisely the narrow-metric error that cost four parameter sweeps tonight: each of those was judged on a statistic that answered a question I had not asked. chain198 is running the same two arms (shipping decks, and -cirruscover=0) capturing the SURFACE frame rather than the orbital one, so the trade is visible on both sides before the owner is asked to choose. THE OPTIONS, costed but not taken: (a) lower Cirrus.Coverage from its 0.15 + 0.45*random -- currently 43% here -- which keeps the deck but thins its reach; (b) lower its 0.03 opacity further, which keeps its coverage but weakens the filtering; (c) change what it does to transmitted light rather than how much there is. All three are aesthetic decisions about the owner's sky and none should ship off a single orbital frame at two in the morning.

A FALSE ALARM I RAISED AND KILLED, recorded so it is not inherited. The ground capture's HUD reads 'air 0.0 kPa, angle of attack 160.7 deg, lift 0.00 STALL' while the ship stands on the pad beside buildings, which looks like an atmosphere reporting no air at the surface of a world that plainly has some -- and it appears in the REFERENCE arm, so no flag of mine caused it. It is not a bug. LedgerHUD.cpp:86 prints AirNow.DynamicPressure, not static pressure, and dynamic pressure is half rho v squared: exactly 0.0 kPa for a parked ship. The same run logs the atmosphere as 'nitrogen-oxygen, 96898 Pa at 272.1 K, scale height 8.01 km, top 96.1 km', so the surface carries 96.9 kPa and the HUD is correctly reporting that a stationary vehicle has no airspeed. The 160.7 degree angle of attack and the STALL flag are the same artefact -- both meaningless without relative wind. Nothing to raise against M04, whose gate is passed. WHY IT IS WORTH A NOTE ANYWAY: this is the fourteenth thing tonight that looked like a finding and dissolved on inspection, and it failed the same way as most of the others -- I read a LABEL ('air ... kPa') and inferred a QUANTITY (static pressure) without checking which quantity the code actually prints. The session's recurring error is not carelessness about measurement, it is confidence about what a measurement means.

THE GROUND CHECK PASSES: REMOVING CIRRUS DOES NOT EMPTY THE SKY. The override fired in the ground arm (log: 'Cirrus coverage forced to 0.00 (weather says 0.43)') with the reference logging none. From eye height the difference is exactly what the deck is: the high wispy streaks across the upper sky go, and everything that makes the sky read as a sky stays -- the blue zenith-to-horizon gradient, the bank of cumulus sitting on the horizon, the depth between them. It does not come back empty. THAT MATTERED AND COULD HAVE GONE THE OTHER WAY. A thin high sheet is often the thing that stops a sky looking like a painted dome, and had the ground frame come back flat I would have had to tell the owner that fixing the orbital view costs the surface one. It does not, so a cirrus remedy is viable from both viewpoints rather than a trade between them. WHAT IS NOW ESTABLISHED END TO END: cumulus owns the blob shapes from orbit (measured with -noclouds against a 0.47% floor, reproduced across two chains); CIRRUS owns the colour wash that reads as 'low poly / animated' (38.18% of the disc, worst channel 155, against the same floor); the middle deck is innocent (0.49%, indistinguishable from noise); and removing cirrus costs the ground view only its high streaks. STILL NOT A FIX, AND DELIBERATELY. The three options -- lower Cirrus.Coverage from 0.15 + 0.45*seeded (43% here), lower its 0.03 opacity, or change what it does to transmitted light rather than how much of it there is -- are aesthetic decisions about the owner's sky, and they differ in what they cost at the surface. The owner now has both views and should pick; I have shipped nothing and every default is untouched.

A TRAP IN THE GROUND NUMBERS, DEFUSED. A plain difference on the ground pair reads 80.99% of pixels changed (95.74% in the upper sky), which looks like removing cirrus wrecks the surface view and flatly contradicts the frames. It does not: >2 is the same 'touched by the deck' threshold that earlier called the shipping planet 92.51% cloud. Graded by magnitude the picture is unambiguous -- UPPER SKY mean change 18.2, >12 on 26.1% of pixels, >32 on 20.7%, >64 on 11.8%; HORIZON BAND mean 4.3, >12 on 4.0%, >32 on 0.3%, >64 on none; GROUND mean 4.0, >12 on 2.5%, >32 on 1.1%. So the real change is concentrated exactly where the cirrus streaks were, and the horizon and ground shift by a mean of about four parts in 255 -- a tint nobody would notice. The frames and the numbers agree once the numbers are asked the right question. WHY THIS IS WORTH A NOTE: anyone re-running a simple diff on that pair will see 81% and conclude the ground view is destroyed. It is not. Quote the graded figures. AND THE ONE PIECE OF GOOD NEWS ABOUT METHOD IN THIS SESSION: this is the first verification tonight that CONFIRMED a reading rather than demolishing it. The difference was not luck -- it was asking for magnitudes instead of a single threshold, which is the specific correction the earlier failures pointed at.

M04'S GATE CERTIFIES THE VERY DECK THAT RUINS THE PLANET. Auditing M03/M04 rather than trusting their gatePassedAt stamps, I read both gate evidence files (roadmap/public/evidence/, 241 files -- they exist and are substantial). These are not rubber stamps: every M03 check names specific tests plus captures, and every M04 check names tests AND harness report lines with measured values and explicit verdicts. The evidence is stronger than anything M02 currently has. BUT M04 CHECK 4 READS: 'Three cloud decks resolve at the altitudes the atmosphere profile predicts' -- Success Ledger.Cloud.TheDecksSitWhereTheThermometerPutsThem, and from airshow-1.txt 'cirrus 6058 to 8538 m, cover 0.43'. THAT IS RECORDED AS A PASS. It is the same deck, at the same altitude, at the same 43% coverage, that tonight's isolation proved accounts for 38.18% of the orbital disc against a 0.47% floor and drains the colour out of every surface beneath it. The gate asks whether each deck sits where the thermometer puts it. It never asks what a deck DOES to what is under it. So M04 can be passed exactly as written while the planet it produces looks wrong from space, and no regression is involved -- the acceptance simply does not measure the thing that matters. THAT IS A DIFFERENT KIND OF 'NOT DONE' FROM AN UNFINISHED TASK, and it is worth separating: (a) REGRESSION -- do the named tests still pass tonight? chain199 is re-running the full suite with the same invocation the gates used (-nullrhi, so tonight's frame-time trouble cannot touch it); (b) SCOPE -- a gate that certifies altitude and coverage while the visible result is wrong. (b) cannot be fixed by running anything; it needs the acceptance restated, which is the owner's call in the same way the M02 cold-start boundary and the check-11 statistic are. I am not rewriting a passed gate's acceptance on my own judgement -- that is the one move this project's gates exist to prevent.

CIRRUS OPTICAL DEPTH ~1: A REAL IMPROVEMENT, SMALLER THAN THE PHYSICS ARGUMENT PROMISED, AND IT INVERTS MY RECOMMENDED LEVER. The arm engaged ('Cirrus extinction forced to 0.0100 per metre (default 0.0300)'), on a build whose reference matches the cirrus-finding reference at 0.49% -- the floor -- so the comparison is sound. FIRST, A METRIC THAT NEARLY FOOLED ME AGAIN: distance from the no-cirrus reference barely moved, 38.09% to 37.80%, which reads as 'the change did nothing'. It is the same failure as every other >2 threshold tonight -- it counts pixels the deck TOUCHES, and cirrus at 43% coverage still touches everything however thin it is. The direct comparison says 16.67% of pixels changed with worst channel 64, and the frame plainly changes: blue ocean returns across most of the disc, the continent reads with its mint shelf, and cirrus remains visible as white streaks. Presence is not strength; grade by magnitude. GRADED PROPERLY, against the no-cirrus control: as it ships (depth ~3) mean tint 14.95, >12 on 32.0% of the disc, >32 on 16.4%, >64 on 3.3%. At depth ~1: mean tint 11.00, >12 on 27.1%, >32 on 7.7%, >64 on 2.5%. So cutting extinction by TWO THIRDS cut the mean tint by only a QUARTER, though it halved the heavy filtering (>32). The frame agrees: the ocean comes back, the continent is still veiled. WHY SUB-LINEAR, AND WHAT IT IMPLIES: where the deck is fully covered it is optically thick enough that lowering per-metre extinction moves transmittance little; the gain is mostly at the edges. If that holds, COVERAGE IS THE STRONGER LEVER THAN OPACITY -- which inverts the recommendation I gave the owner earlier, where I put opacity first as the smallest blast radius. Smallest blast radius is not the same as most effective, and I should have said which I was optimising. NOT SHIPPING THIS VALUE YET. 'The comment says 1 is right' plus a 26% tint reduction is not the same as 'the planet now looks right', and the frame still shows a veiled continent. The 0.5 arm will say whether the trend continues or flattens; if it flattens, the honest fix is coverage, or coverage and opacity together. Ground checks for both candidates are queued -- a remedy that empties the sky at eye height is not a remedy.

tasks.title: Material standard and shading model audit
tasks.detail: One documented PBR standard: what maps, what ranges, what conventions. Half the reason a game looks amateur is materials that disagree about what roughness means.
tasks.acceptance: Every material in the project conforms, and a validator flags any that does not.

tasks.title: Master material framework with layering
tasks.detail: Layered materials with blend masks, so a hull is metal plus paint plus wear plus dirt rather than one baked texture.
tasks.acceptance: A single hull material produces a clean ship and a filthy one from parameters alone.

tasks.title: Wear, dirt and weathering framework
tasks.detail: Procedural edge wear, dirt accumulation by cavity and by exposure, streaking below seams, heat discolouration near thrusters, driven by an object's actual history rather than authored in. Under ADR-0005 this is not a finishing touch, it is the single largest quality lever available: the gap between generated geometry and shipped-game geometry is mostly this layer, all of it curvature and occlusion arithmetic, and none of it needing an artist.
tasks.acceptance: A ship that has flown through dust looks like it, and cleaning it removes exactly that. The same asset with the wear layer disabled and enabled, at identical framing and exposure, is the before-and-after this task is judged on.

tasks.title: Decal framework
tasks.detail: Projected detail on hulls, terrain and interiors — markings, damage, leaks, signage — with correct normals and a budget.
tasks.acceptance: A thousand decals in view cost inside budget and none swims or z-fights.

tasks.title: Lighting: Lumen configuration and fallback
tasks.detail: Global illumination that works from a lit cockpit at night to a sunlit dune, with a measured decision about where it costs more than it gives. Design v1.1 turned it off for the slice; this is where that is revisited with numbers.
tasks.acceptance: Three reference scenes are correctly lit within budget, and the decision is recorded with measurements.

tasks.title: Shadow quality across scales
tasks.detail: Contact shadows in a cockpit, cascades across a landscape, and shadows from a moon on a planet — three problems that must share one setup.
tasks.acceptance: No shadow acne, no peter-panning and no cascade seam at any of the three scales.

tasks.title: Reflection framework
tasks.detail: Screen-space, captures and ray-traced where it pays, with a policy for what gets which. Water, canopies and polished hulls each want a different answer.
tasks.acceptance: A reflective hull, a canopy and the sea are all correct from a viewpoint that shows all three.

tasks.title: Exposure, tone mapping and colour pipeline
tasks.detail: One colour pipeline from lighting to display, handling a range from starlight to a sunlit ice field without clipping or hunting.
tasks.acceptance: Flying from a dark hangar into daylight adapts smoothly with no overshoot, and no scene clips.

tasks.title: Anti-aliasing and upscaling
tasks.detail: Temporal AA tuned against the specific problems here — thin cockpit geometry, high-frequency terrain, particles — plus an upscaler evaluated rather than assumed.
tasks.acceptance: No ghosting on cockpit instruments during rapid motion and no shimmer on terrain at any distance.

tasks.title: Particle and VFX framework
tasks.detail: Thrusters, damage, weather, dust and debris on one budgeted system, with LOD and culling and no orphaned emitters.
tasks.acceptance: Worst-case effects load stays inside budget and a two-hour session leaks no emitters.

tasks.title: Volumetric lighting and atmospherics in interiors
tasks.detail: Light shafts, dust in the air, smoke that fills a compartment — the difference between a lit room and a rendered one.
tasks.acceptance: A single window lights a dusty interior convincingly at three times of day, inside budget.

tasks.title: LOD and impostor chain for everything
tasks.detail: One policy covering ships, buildings, characters and props, with automatic generation and no visible switch.
tasks.acceptance: No LOD transition is visible at any distance for any asset class.

tasks.title: Character rendering: skin, cloth, hair, eyes
tasks.detail: The hardest thing to make not look like a mannequin, and the thing a player looks at closest.
tasks.acceptance: A character at conversation distance holds up in three lighting conditions.

tasks.title: Cockpit rendering quality pass
tasks.detail: Where the player spends most of their time: glass, displays, backlighting, reflections on the canopy, and the sun through it.
tasks.acceptance: A cockpit at dawn, at noon and at night each hold up, with legible instruments in all three.

tasks.title: Post-processing chain
tasks.detail: Bloom, motion blur, depth of field, aberration and grain, each with a reason and a budget, and each defensible against being turned off.
tasks.acceptance: Every post effect has a measured cost and a documented reason, and the chain costs no more than its budget.

tasks.title: Runtime Virtual Texture for surface composition
tasks.detail: Compose the blended surface into an RVT so the expensive blend happens once per texel rather than once per pixel, and so decals and roads have something to write into. Moved here from M02 (2026-09-11): the terrain material measured at most 0.7 ms, so the saving was never there; decals and roads are the reason, and they arrive with this work.
tasks.acceptance: Terrain material cost falls measurably against the direct-blend version with no visual difference.

notes.text: Measured before building. A -flatterrain control arm swaps the surface for an untextured constant on identical geometry; the GPU difference over the same fixed-step flight is the whole budget an RVT competes for. It is at most 0.7 ms anywhere on the flight, and 0.1 and 0.0 ms in the surface and town phases where terrain fills the screen. There is nothing to recover: an RVT would add page rendering, memory on top of a 512 MB patch cache, and a cache invalidated by terrain that uploads 762 patches a second. Size is not the objection -- non-adaptive RVT gives 2.39 m/texel over a cube face, adaptive gives 9.3 mm. Evidence and the control-arm capture in docs/comparisons/terrain-material-cost/.

Blocked on a consumer, not on effort. The performance premise is measurably false -- the whole terrain material costs at most 0.7 ms, and 0.0 where terrain fills the screen. The surviving justification is that decals and roads need something to write into, and there are none yet. Revisit when the biome and settlement work needs a target, and size the RVT for the play area rather than the planet.

[2026-09-11] The blocker, found in the engine rather than argued: a runtime virtual texture is drawn by the scene proxies that opt into it, and in UE 5.8 those are the landscape, static-mesh and dynamic-mesh proxies (bSupportsRuntimeVirtualTexture = true in LandscapeRender.cpp, StaticMeshSceneProxy.cpp and BaseDynamicMeshSceneProxy.cpp) -- the procedural mesh component the terrain streams into is not one of them, so an RVT would simply not see the ground. The path exists: the terrain's second backend, -terraincomponent=static, builds a UStaticMesh per patch, and that proxy does draw into RVTs. What it costs: that backend regenerates every patch instead of re-uploading from the in-memory section cache, so the comparison the acceptance asks for (material cost with and without the RVT, no visual difference) has to be run on it, and it is only worth running when something needs a surface to write into (roads, decals) or when the T053 seven-channel material measures expensive. The terrain material's last measured cost was at most 0.7 ms; re-measure on the static backend before building the RVT volume (a box aligned to the viewer's up, re-centred as they move).

[2026-09-11] Moved from M02 to M11 (Rendering fidelity) by the owner's decision. The premise measured false for terrain cost (the whole material is at most 0.7 ms), and the surviving reason -- roads and decals needing something to write into -- belongs with the work that makes them; building it now would also mean moving the terrain off the procedural mesh the streaming, cache, caves and collision are measured on. Status set to todo: parked with its consumer, not blocked.
